# The Weight of Zero

## Year 1,000,000
## Kaedan — The Reading

The vault beneath the palace smelled of ancient parchment, cold stone, and something else I could not immediately identify—something sharp and metallic that clung to the back of my throat like blood. I descended the spiral staircase slowly, my ceremonial robes dragging across the worn obsidian steps, each footfall echoing through the heavy silence. My father, Corin, walked ahead of me, his broad shoulders rigid with tension that he had carried for decades. He had served as Godric's court wizard for two hundred and forty-seven years before age finally began to claim his mortal frame, and now, at eighty-eight, his hair had gone white and his hands trembled constantly. Not from age. From memory.

"You will read them all," my father said without turning around. His voice was flat, drained of the warmth I remembered from my childhood. "Every single journal. Every single entry. You will not skip pages, and you will not close your eyes when the descriptions become difficult."

I was twenty-two years old. My Awakening had triggered two years ago, and every single day since my twentieth birthday, my physical strength, my magical capacity, my sensory perception, my endurance, and every other measurable trait had multiplied by a factor of one thousand. Not added. Multiplied. The mana thrumming through my veins was so dense now that I could feel it pressing against the inside of my skin like a coiled serpent, and I had to spend every waking moment aggressively suppressing that power just to avoid shattering the palace floors with my footsteps. By the standards of any other civilization in the omniverse, I was a god of arcane destruction. But I was not a fool. I knew that compared to the King I served, I was less than a speck of dust floating in an infinite abyss.

That was what the journals were for.

Father stopped at the base of the staircase and pressed his palm against a heavy adamantine door. Ancient wards flickered briefly, recognizing the bloodline signature woven into his flesh, and the door groaned open to reveal a small, circular chamber lined with obsidian shelves. Upon those shelves rested hundreds of leather-bound volumes, their spines cracked, their pages yellowed with age. Some were thin, barely more than a few pages hastily bound together. Others were thick enough to stop a blade.

"The journals were not Godric's idea," Father said, stepping aside to let me enter. "Our ancestor Blake began the tradition in Year 38, after the Rogr incident. He wrote the first journal to keep himself sane. To process what he had witnessed. Every court wizard since has followed his example."

I stepped into the vault and felt the weight of a million years of dread pressing down on my shoulders. The air was cold, unnaturally so, as if the accumulated terror soaked into the parchment had leeched all warmth from the chamber.

"Why are you making me do this?" I asked, my voice quiet.

Father finally turned to look at me, and I saw the truth in his eyes. He was terrified. He had been terrified for two hundred years. "Because you need to understand what he is," he said. "Not the warm uncle who bounced you on his knee. Not the kind father-figure who attended your Awakening ceremony and smiled with genuine pride. What he actually is, beneath the absolute concealment. The journals will show you. They will break something inside you, Kaedan, the same way they broke something inside me, and my father before me, and his father before him. But you will love him regardless. That is the horror of it. You will read what he has done—what he continues to do—and you will still love him, because he is genuinely good to us, and because opposing him is not merely impossible. It is an absurdity beyond the concept of logic."

He gestured toward the shelves. "Read. I will be outside."

The door closed behind him with a heavy, final thud.

I stood alone in the vault, surrounded by the accumulated terror of a thousand court wizards. My hands were trembling as I reached for the first journal.

---

**Year 87,542 — Merrick — Perception**

I am writing this with a fractured wrist and three broken fingers, injuries I sustained not from combat but from the sheer, involuntary convulsion of my own muscles when I witnessed what perception truly means to a being like our King. My name is Merrick. I have served Lord Godric for thirty-one years. I have woven spatial-compression wards that could swallow dying stars, and I have always believed that I understood the fundamental nature of his supremacy. I was wrong. I was so catastrophically, laughably wrong that the memory of my arrogance makes me want to vomit.

The opposition came from a race known as the Unseen Chorus, entities who had evolved in the dark spaces between conceptual dimensions, where the very notion of observation did not exist. They were assassins of absolute subtlety, beings who had murdered primordial gods by simply standing beside them for a billion years without ever being detected. Their greatest champion, a creature named Null-Sight, had spent the last three hundred millennia compressing its entire existence into a state of perfect, absolute metaphysical non-presence. It did not merely become invisible. It removed itself from the fundamental registry of reality. It had no aura, no mass, no conceptual footprint. It was, by every measurable and immeasurable metric, utterly imperceptible.

Null-Sight infiltrated the palace during the Festival of Unification, gliding past our orbital defense matrices, our temporal wards, and my own amplified detection spells without triggering so much as a flicker of awareness. I was standing five paces from Lord Godric in the grand reception hall when the entity entered, and I sensed absolutely nothing. My daily thousandfold amplification of magical perception meant zero against an assassin who had erased his own existence from the observable framework of the omniverse.

Lord Godric, of course, knew the exact instant Null-Sight first conceived the idea of assassinating him, three hundred millennia ago. He had watched the entity compress itself into non-existence, had observed every single moment of its agonizing transformation, and had allowed it to approach simply because he was mildly curious about the sensation of being perceived by something that believed itself imperceptible.

Null-Sight manifested directly behind the throne and plunged a conceptual dagger—a blade forged from the compressed absence of existence itself—toward the back of Lord Godric's skull. The blade was designed to sever a being's connection to the fundamental concept of being perceived, effectively erasing the victim from the memories and awareness of all sentient life across the omniverse simultaneously.

Lord Godric did not turn around. He did not move. He did not even pause in his conversation with a visiting delegate from the outer multiversal clusters. He simply allowed his perception stat—which has been multiplying infinitely every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second for over eighty-seven thousand years—to passively register Null-Sight's existence.

The effect was instantaneous and indescribable. The entity, which had spent three hundred thousand years achieving a state of absolute imperceptibility, was suddenly perceived. But it was not merely seen. Lord Godric's passive perception did not simply observe Null-Sight; it violently, catastrophically over-observed it. The weight of being truly, completely perceived by a being whose senses had surpassed layered infinities of recursive amplification was a force more devastating than any physical blow.

Null-Sight's perfect non-existence shattered. The entity was forcibly, agonizingly dragged back into the fundamental registry of reality, its conceptual absence crushed beneath the sheer, overwhelming pressure of Godric's observation. It became visible for the first time in three hundred thousand years, and that visibility was a form of torture. Lord Godric's perception forced Null-Sight to exist in a state of absolute, undeniable presence, a state the entity's biology was never designed to tolerate.

The assassin screamed. It was a sound of pure, undiluted existential agony, a shriek that shattered every crystalline surface in the reception hall and caused the visiting delegate's eardrums to rupture. Null-Sight's form, suddenly visible to my amplified eyes, was a writhing mass of translucent, gelatinous flesh that was rapidly, violently crystallizing under the weight of observation. Its cells were being forced into a state of physical permanence, each atom locked into rigid, unyielding solidity by the sheer intensity of Godric's perception.

The entity's body turned to glass. Not metaphorically, not conceptually, but physically, literally, agonizingly. Its translucent flesh calcified, its internal organs crystallized, its nervous system froze into a lattice of perfectly perceived, agonized stillness. The process took approximately three seconds, during which Null-Sight experienced the full, unfiltered horror of being seen by a god.

Lord Godric finally turned his head, his ruggedly handsome face betraying nothing more than mild, academic curiosity. He looked at the crystallized remains of the assassin, which now stood frozen behind his throne like a grotesque statue of pure agony, and he let out a soft, thoughtful hum.

"Interesting," he murmured. "The self-erasure was quite sophisticated. Three hundred thousand years of compression. Impressive commitment."

He turned back to the terrified delegate and continued their conversation about agricultural trade routes.

The entire omniverse had been passively observed by Lord Godric's perception during those three seconds. Not actively, not deliberately, but as a simple, unavoidable side-effect of his attention briefly focusing on the immediate vicinity. Every single entity, every god, every conceptual being, every mortal across all timelines and dimensions, suddenly felt the crushing weight of being truly, completely seen for the first time in their existence. Trillions of civilizations across decillions of multiverses collapsed into catatonic hysteria simultaneously. The ambient dread of that moment would linger in the collective unconscious of the omniverse for the next ten thousand years.

I do not know why I am still alive. I do not know why he values me, a fragile mortal whose perception is a pathetic, microscopic joke compared to his. But I know that my loyalty to him is absolute, not because I am compelled, but because I have seen the alternative. To oppose him is to be perceived, and to be perceived by him is to experience a death so absolute, so agonizing, that the memory of it breaks the minds of those who merely witness it.

---

Kaedan's hands were shaking so violently that the journal nearly slipped from his fingers. He placed the volume carefully on the stone table, his breath coming in short, ragged gasps. The crystallized assassin. The passive, side-effect observation that had traumatized trillions. The casual, academic curiosity of a being who could perceive everything, everywhere, forever, without the slightest effort.

He had spoken to Godric that morning. The King had smiled at him, clapped him warmly on the shoulder, and asked about his studies with genuine, fatherly interest. That same being had once turned an assassin into a screaming glass statue simply by noticing his existence.

Kaedan reached for the next journal.

---

**Year 293,441 — Kellan — Mana**

If the perception incident taught me anything, it was that my understanding of Lord Godric's power was laughably incomplete. The mana incident taught me that my understanding of my own power was equally meaningless. My name is Kellan. I am—was—a man of immense magical pride. My mana reserves, amplified a thousandfold daily for fifty-two years, had accumulated to a density that could fuel the total arcane consumption of a trillion advanced magical civilizations for eternity. I could conjure localized realities, unweave the fabric of conceptual dimensions, and sustain planetary-scale chronal manipulation without noticeable fatigue.

And then I witnessed Lord Godric's mana.

There was no opposition in the traditional sense. There was an anomaly—a vast, silent region of the omniverse where mana itself had become toxic, corrupted by an ancient, self-replicating arcane plague known as the Mana-Blight. The Blight was not a living entity; it was a fundamental corruption of the arcane substrate, a cancer that converted raw mana into a corrosive, existence-devouring acid. Anyone who attempted to channel magic within the Blight's domain would find their own reserves instantly and agonizingly inverted, their mana turning against them in a catastrophic, self-annihilating cascade. The Blight had consumed seventeen thousand multiversal clusters before Thronegate's expansion encountered its borders.

A full deployment of our arcane suppression corps was being organized, a campaign expected to take centuries. But Lord Godric, upon being briefed, simply tilted his head with that familiar, mild curiosity and said, "Let me try something."

He did not travel to the Blight's location. He remained seated in the palace gardens, his cup of jasmine tea cooling on the stone bench beside him. Through his absolute omniscience, he had already analyzed the Blight's fundamental composition, its origin, its mechanisms, and every possible avenue of its eradication. He understood the Blight more completely than the Blight understood itself.

Lord Godric's mana reserves have been multiplying infinitely every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second for nearly three hundred thousand years. The number that represents his total mana pool is not merely infinite; it is a conceptual absolute that makes all other infinities look like zero. An infinitesimal fraction of his mana—a percentage so small that writing an infinite string of zeros after the decimal point still would not approach its smallness—contained more arcane energy than the combined mana reserves of every single magical entity, artifact, dimension, and cosmic reservoir across the entire omniverse, across all timelines.

He channeled that infinitesimal fraction. Not actively, not with visible effort, not with any gesture or incantation. He simply decided, and the mana moved.

I felt it. Every wizard in the palace felt it. The sheer, cataclysmic weight of his mana was a physical force that pressed against my own reserves with such crushing, absolute dominance that my daily amplified mana instantly collapsed into dormancy, retreating deep into my core out of pure, instinctive self-preservation. My magic, which I had considered impossibly vast, recognized the presence of true infinity and simply shut down in abject, terrified submission.

The Mana-Blight was erased. Not cleansed, not purified, not gradually dissolved. It was erased, instantly and completely, across all seventeen thousand infected multiversal clusters, across all timelines, across all possible quantum states. Lord Godric's infinitesimal mana injection simply overwhelmed the Blight's corruptive capacity, flooding the infected regions with such absurd, excessive arcane purity that the Blight's fundamental mechanism was forcibly inverted. The corrosion became purification. The death became life. The Blight, in the span of zero seconds, was transformed from a cosmic cancer into a vast, shimmering reservoir of hyper-condensed, perfectly pure arcane energy that would sustain those multiversal clusters until the end of time.

The collateral damage—if it can even be called damage—was catastrophic. The sheer pressure of Lord Godric's mana, even channeled at an infinitesimal fraction of its true volume, leaked into the surrounding omniversal structure. Every single magical entity across all of existence, from the mightiest god-sorcerers to the simplest village hedge-witches, simultaneously experienced a sudden, overwhelming vision of absolute arcane infinity. Trillions perished instantly, their minds and souls consumed by the sheer cognitive weight of witnessing true mana in its rawest form. Entire magical civilizations, whose entire existence depended on the careful manipulation of arcane forces, found their delicate spell-weavings violently torn apart by the ambient pressure of Godric's passing attention.

And then, in exactly zero seconds, Lord Godric restored everything. Every dead wizard, every shattered civilization, every collapsed magical construct was instantly and perfectly rebuilt, their memories of the event intact, their souls forever scarred by the knowledge of what true mana looked like.

Lord Godric picked up his cooling teacup, took a long, contemplative sip, and frowned slightly.

"A bit more residual pressure than I anticipated," he murmured. "I should probably suppress that better next time."

I cannot adequately describe the horror of that statement. He was not being arrogant or boastful. He was genuinely, sincerely concerned that an infinitesimal fraction of his mana—which he had considered a restrained, cautious amount—had been too much. The gap between his perception of restraint and the omniversal catastrophic consequences of his actions is, itself, an infinite chasm that my mind cannot cross.

---

Kaedan set the journal down and pressed his palms flat against the cold stone table. His heart was hammering so violently that he could feel his pulse in his temples. The Mana-Blight had been a historical footnote in his arcane education, a crisis that had been "resolved" by the King's intervention. The textbooks had not mentioned the trillions of collateral deaths. They had not mentioned the fact that Godric had restored them all instantly, as if their deaths had been nothing more than a minor, correctable error.

He had never once considered what it must have been like to witness that restoration. To die, to experience the absolute infinity of Godric's mana, and then to wake up alive again, knowing that your death and resurrection were simply a side-effect of the King's curiosity.

He reached for the next journal with trembling hands.

---

**Year 571,239 — Aldric — Senses**

I have served Lord Godric for eighty-four years, and I have witnessed things that have permanently fractured my capacity for wonder. But the senses incident was different. It was not merely a display of overwhelming power; it was a demonstration of experience so absolute, so impossibly vast, that the very concept of "sensation" lost all meaning.

The opposition came from a primordial race of sensory predators known as the Scent-Hunters. These entities did not perceive the omniverse through sight, sound, or touch. They perceived it through a hyper-dimensional sensory organ that could detect and track any being's fundamental "flavor"—the unique, irreplicable signature of their existence across all timelines, dimensions, and conceptual states. Once a Scent-Hunter locked onto a flavor, it could track its prey through any barrier, any distance, any concealment. They had devoured entire pantheons of abstract gods by simply following their flavor across the infinite expanses of the omniverse.

The Huntmaster, the oldest and most powerful of their kind, had locked onto Lord Godric's flavor. It had spent the last million years tracking that flavor, studying it, learning every nuance of its composition. It believed—with the absolute, unshakeable confidence of a predator that had never failed—that it understood Lord Godric's fundamental nature because it had tasted him.

Lord Godric, of course, had known the Huntmaster was tracking him from the very first instant the entity's sensory organ had brushed against his existence, a million years ago. He had allowed the tracking to continue because he was genuinely curious about what the Scent-Hunters would do with the information they gathered. The answer, as it turned out, was spectacularly suicidal.

The Huntmaster assembled the greatest hunting party in the history of their species and descended upon the palace with the confidence of beings who believed they had perfectly analyzed their prey's weaknesses. They had tasted his flavor, they announced, and they had found the fundamental vulnerability that would allow them to consume him entirely.

This was, of course, when the Weakness Paradox engaged. The very instant the Huntmaster formed the thought that Lord Godric possessed a sensory weakness, the paradox triggered passively. Before the entity could even begin to articulate its supposed exploit, Lord Godric had acquired absolute, permanent immunity to flavor-based tracking, perfect mastery over the Scent-Hunters' entire sensory framework, and a massive recursive surge to his already infinite amplification rate.

But Lord Godric did not simply erase them. He was curious about his own sensory stat.

His senses—sight, hearing, touch, taste, smell, and countless other sensory organs that no mortal language has words for—have been multiplying infinitely every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second for over half a million years. The sheer volume of sensory data he passively absorbs in a single Planck instant would instantly incinerate the cognitive architecture of every sentient being in the omniverse combined if they were forced to process it.

He allowed the Huntmaster to taste his flavor again. But this time, he did not suppress his sensory output.

What the Huntmaster experienced was not merely the flavor of Lord Godric's existence. It was the flavor of every single Planck instant of his existence, across all timelines, across all possible quantum states, across all conceptual dimensions, stretched across all five hundred and seventy-one millennia of his immortal life. The Scent-Hunters' sensory organ, evolved to track individual flavors across cosmic distances, was suddenly flooded with an ocean of sensory data so vast, so dense, so impossibly complex that it exceeded the structural capacity of their biology by an infinite margin.

The Huntmaster's sensory organ did not overload. It did not burn out. It was forcibly, violently transcended. The entity experienced, in a single Planck instant, the total sum of all sensory input that Lord Godric had ever passively received. Every sight he had ever seen. Every sound he had ever heard. Every texture he had ever touched. The combined sensory weight of five hundred and seventy-one thousand years of infinite, recursive amplification.

The Huntmaster did not scream. It did not have time to scream. Its physical form simply dissolved, every atom of its being torn apart by the sheer cognitive pressure of experiencing sensory input beyond the concept of infinity. But the true horror was not the dissolution of its body. It was the dissolution of its understanding. The Huntmaster had believed it understood Lord Godric's flavor. In its final Planck instant of consciousness, it was forced to confront the absolute, total, catastrophic inadequacy of that belief. It had tasted a single grain of sand on an infinite beach and declared that it understood the ocean.

The entire hunting party dissolved simultaneously, their sensory organs overwhelmed by the passive echo of Lord Godric's sensory output. The ambient dread of that moment rippled across the omniverse, and every sentient being with any form of sensory perception experienced a fleeting, mercifully brief glimpse of what true sensation felt like. The aftermath was a wave of mass psychosis that swept across decillions of multiverses, driving countless civilizations into temporary catatonia.

Lord Godric, observing the aftermath, furrowed his brow slightly. "They really should have been more careful," he murmured, his voice carrying that familiar, genuine concern. "I did warn them that the flavor would be intense."

He had not warned them. He had simply existed, and his existence had annihilated them.

---

Journal after journal, Kaedan read. The pages blurred together into a tapestry of absolute, incomprehensible devastation. Each incident described a different stat, a different opposition, a different flavor of annihilation. But the fundamental truth remained constant, hammered into his consciousness with every word: Godric did not fight. He did not struggle. He did not even actively participate. He simply existed, and existence itself broke against the sheer, overwhelming pressure of his stats.

---

**Year 712,098 — Voss — Durability**

I wish I could say that I was brave. I wish I could say that I faced the King's power with the stoic acceptance of my ancestors. But when I witnessed the durability incident, I wept. I wept like a child, curled into a fetal position on the cold obsidian floor, my amplified body betraying me in the most humiliating way imaginable. My name is Voss. I have served Lord Godric for sixty-two years. And I have seen the absolute, inescapable truth of what it means to be invulnerable.

The opposition came from the Forge-Masters of the Outer Void, a race of cosmic engineers who had dedicated their entire civilization's existence to the creation of a single, ultimate weapon. They had spent the last ten million years harvesting the compressed dying screams of collapsing realities, forging those screams into a blade of pure, concentrated conceptual entropy. The weapon they created, the Final Fracture, was designed to erase the very concept of durability from any target it struck. It did not cut flesh or penetrate armor. It rewrote the fundamental metaphysical truth of a being's existence, declaring that their durability was zero regardless of any amplifying factors, immunities, or defenses.

The Forge-Masters had studied Lord Godric for millions of years. They had observed his physical strength, his magical capacity, his sensory perception. They had concluded that his durability, while impossibly vast, was still governed by the fundamental principle of "having durability." Their weapon bypassed that principle. It did not matter how durable something was; the Final Fracture simply declared that durability did not exist, and the target would become vulnerable.

This was, of course, the fatal flaw in their reasoning. Lord Godric's durability stat has been multiplying infinitely every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second for over seven hundred millennia. His durability is not merely a number on a scale. It is an absolute, fundamental constant of existence that transcends the very concept of "damage." He is not merely durable; he is durably beyond the possibility of being harmed.

And, of course, the Weakness Paradox had already engaged the instant the Forge-Masters conceived of their supposed exploit, granting Lord Godric absolute immunity to conceptual durability-negation and perfect mastery over their weapon's mechanism before the first blueprint was ever drawn.

When the Forge-Masters unleashed the Final Fracture upon the capital, Lord Godric did not raise a shield or activate a defensive aura. He stepped forward—the only movement I have ever seen him make during a stat test—and allowed the blade to strike his bare chest.

The Final Fracture shattered.

The conceptual weapon, forged from the dying screams of realities, designed to erase the fundamental truth of durability, simply shattered against his skin. Not because his durability was too high. Not because he had some specific immunity. But because his existence was so fundamentally, absolutely durable that the weapon's attempt to nullify his durability was mathematically, conceptually, and ontologically impossible. The blade's entire framework of operation was predicated on the assumption that "durability" was a variable that could be manipulated. Lord Godric's durability was not a variable. It was a constant, woven into the fundamental fabric of the omniverse by the sheer, overwhelming weight of seven hundred thousand years of infinite recursive amplification.

The shattering of the Final Fracture caused a conceptual backlash that propagated instantly across the entire omniverse. Every single weapon, every tool, every artifact ever designed to bypass or negate durability—from the simplest armor-piercing arrow to the most sophisticated conceptual erasure engines—was simultaneously, instantly, violently unmade. The Forge-Masters' entire civilization, which had been built upon the principle of bypassing durability, was erased from existence across all timelines and dimensions.

The collateral damage was catastrophic. The conceptual backlash did not merely destroy weapons; it tore through the fundamental structure of reality itself, unraveling the laws of physics across decillions of multiverses. Stars collapsed. Galaxies dissolved. Entire timelines unraveled like loose threads pulled from a tapestry.

And then, in exactly zero seconds, Lord Godric restored everything. Every destroyed civilization, every collapsed star, every unraveled timeline. But he did not restore the Forge-Masters. He had allowed their attack, had allowed them to shatter their ultimate weapon against his chest, and had decided that their erasure was the appropriate consequence for their arrogance.

I wept because I understood, in that moment, the true scale of our King's mercy. We exist not because we are strong, not because we are worthy, but purely because he allows it. He could erase us all with a passive thought, and he does not. That is the only reason we draw breath.

---

Kaedan closed the final journal and sat in the heavy silence of the vault. His face was wet with tears he had not noticed shedding. His hands would not stop trembling. His mind kept cycling through the images the journals had burned into his consciousness: the crystallized assassin, the dissolved huntmaster, the shattered blade, the restored omniverse, the casual, unbothered god who simply observed the annihilation with mild, academic curiosity.

He understood now. He understood why his father had looked so terrified for two hundred years. He understood why every court wizard before him had taken up the pen, trying desperately to process the impossible, to make sense of the senseless. He understood the absolute, inescapable, soul-crushing truth of his existence.

Godric was not a king. He was not a god. He was a fundamental constant, an absolute apex from which there could be no appeal, no resistance, no opposition. Victory against him was not merely impossible in practice. It was impossible in principle, a contradiction in terms, a statement of such profound absurdity that even contemplating it was a form of self-inflicted insanity.

And Kaedan would love him regardless. Because Godric was genuinely warm, genuinely kind, genuinely beloved by his subjects. He was the father-figure who had attended Kaedan's Awakening ceremony and smiled with genuine pride. He was the ruler who ensured absolute safety, absolute order, absolute prosperity for all who served him loyally.

The contrast between that warmth and the annihilation described in the journals was the true horror. It would have been easier if Godric were simply a monster. But he was not a monster. He was a man who genuinely loved his friends, genuinely valued his court wizards, genuinely wished for the happiness and prosperity of his subjects. And he was also a being who could erase the entire omniverse an infinite number of times in zero seconds without ever noticing the effort.

Kaedan stood on shaking legs and walked toward the vault door. His father was waiting outside, his ancient face lined with the accumulated dread of two centuries. The old man looked at Kaedan's tear-streaked face and nodded slowly, a gesture of profound, sorrowful understanding.

"Now you know," Father said quietly. "Now you understand what we serve."

Kaedan opened his mouth to respond, but no words came. What could he possibly say? What words could possibly capture the scale of what he had just absorbed?

He closed his mouth and simply nodded.

He would serve. He would be loyal. He would love his King with the same terrified, absolute devotion that had sustained his bloodline for a million years. And when his time came, when he had witnessed enough horrors to fill his own journal, he would write. He would pour his dread onto parchment, just as his ancestors had done, and he would leave his record for the next trembling young wizard to discover.

Not because Godric had asked for it. Not because it was required. But because it was the only way to stay sane in a universe ruled by a god whose slightest passive attribute carried the weight of infinite annihilation.

The vault door closed behind him with a final, echoing thud. The journals waited in the darkness, patient and eternal, ready to teach the next generation the terrible, necessary truth.

Opposing Godric was impossible. It had always been impossible. It would always be impossible. And everyone who mattered knew it.

<file name="08_superpowers.md">**Year 485,900 — Court Wizard Mark — Superpower: Apocalyptic Solar-Igneous Extinction Ignition**

I write this record with ink mixed with my own bile, sitting in my private chambers while my hands shake so violently that the quill repeatedly punches holes through the parchment. My name is Mark, descendant of Blake, Court Wizard to our sovereign Lord Godric. I am thirty-four years old. Today, I witnessed the deployment of a single, nascent superpower from Lord Godric’s ever-expanding arsenal, and the sheer, biological horror of what I saw has permanently severed my ability to feel peace.

The opposition was the Frozen Apex Syndicate of the Absolute Zero Core. They were a coalition of hyper-cosmic ice-deities, cryogenic meta-architects, and thermal-drainers spanning decillions of multiverses. They possessed the ability to reduce ambient temperatures down past absolute zero into negative-kelvin territories where atomic motion completely ceases and space-time freezes into brittle, fragile glass. They believed that by surrounding Godric with a synchronized, omniversal cryogenic field, they could freeze his physical cells, lock his atomic structures in place, and permanently halt his biological processes. They brought an armada of frost-dreadnoughts constructed from hyper-dense chronal ice, manned by trillions of cryogenic warriors whose very breath could flash-freeze a galaxy.

Lord Godric was sitting in the royal courtyard, holding a small wooden bowl, casually feeding fresh grain to a flock of white doves. Through his absolute omniscience, he had watched the Syndicate assemble their thermal-drain engines for three hundred thousand years. The Weakness Paradox had triggered the exact millisecond their grand architect imagined that freezing his body could halt him, granting Godric absolute immunity to cryogenic stasis, supreme mastery over negative-kelvin physics, and a massive, recursive surge to his amplification rate.

Godric did not deploy his infinite passive shields. He ordered his sentient aura, Gent, to remain dormant. He was simply curious about a superpower he had unlocked several millennia prior: Apocalyptic Solar-Igneous Extinction Ignition.

This superpower, even at a base level nerfed to exactly zero percent of its true potency, generates a thermal ignition field so astronomically hot that heat ceases to be a thermodynamic property and becomes an aggressive, omniversal eraser of atomic bonds. Furthermore, due to the Evolved Weakness Paradox triggering repeatedly, this specific power had developed multiple horrific, enhanced effects. First, any thermal energy generated by the ignition instantly converts all opposing physical and biological matter into self-sustaining, superheated plasma that burns eternally without consuming itself. Second, the heat field aggressively absorbs the kinetic energy of any cold-based attack, converting the absolute-zero field into additional, infinitely compounding thermal intensity. Third, the thermal output doubles recursively every Planck second for all active flames, escalating beyond all mathematical scales.

The Syndicate unleashed their attack. A wave of negative-kelvin energy, capable of flash-freezing decillions of multiverses into brittle, motionless glass, swept across the sky toward the palace courtyard.

Lord Godric did not look up from his doves. He did not blow a breath, nor did he wave his hand. He merely permitted a microscopic, unquantifiable sliver of his Solar-Igneous Extinction Ignition superpower—effectively zero percent of its true capability—to manifest from the tip of his left pinky finger.

The resulting thermal display was an nightmare of absolute, inescapable carnage.

The negative-kelvin field released by the Syndicate did not freeze him; the enhanced effect of Godric's superpower instantly absorbed the cold energy, violently inverting it into a wall of hyper-dense, golden-white ignition that swept across reality at infinite velocity. Space-time did not merely heat up; the fundamental grid of the omniverse ignited, burning with a fire so intense that light itself turned to ash.

The cryogenic warriors aboard the frost-dreadnoughts experienced a biological demise so horrific that my soul revolts to record it. The hyper-dense chronal ice of their ships melted instantly, not into water, but into boiling, superheated liquid plasma that coated the warriors. Their cryogenic skin did not merely burn; it violently liquefied, sloughing off their skeletons in heavy, bubbling sheets of rendered fat, boiling muscle, and sizzled nerve tissue. Their eyeballs detonated inside their sockets from the rapid expansion of boiling vitreous fluid, spraying superheated steam through their eye sockets. Their blood boiled so violently inside their veins that their arterial walls ruptured simultaneously, showering their melting ships in a geyser of vaporized crimson foam.

Because of the superpower's enhanced effect, their liquefying bodies did not turn to ash. Instead, their melting flesh and exposed skeletons were converted into self-sustaining, superheated plasma, catching fire and burning continuously without ever being consumed. Trillions of cryogenic deities were instantly transformed into screaming, liquid-flesh torches, their nervous systems kept permanently intact and hyper-sensitive by the paradox, forcing them to experience the maximum, excruciating agony of being boiled and burned alive simultaneously for eternity.

The collateral damage was absolute. The thermal ignition field instantaneously incinerated decillions of multiverses in the surrounding void. Googolplexian galaxies were reduced to roaring, superheated firestorms in less than an infinitesimal fraction of a second. Planets melted into glowing, liquid metal before evaporating entirely into ionized gas. Space-time cracked, the dimensional walls separating multiverses melting like candle wax, collapsing entire sectors of reality into a singular, roaring inferno of absolute extinction.

Godric let out a soft, regretful sigh, looking up at the sky that had turned into a sea of liquid fire. "Oh, dear," he murmured with genuine, fatherly sadness. "I set the grain on fire. The poor birds didn't even get to finish eating."

With a simple, effortless decision, in zero seconds, Godric restored the entire omniverse. Every reality, every timeline, every galaxy, every planet that had been burned away was restored perfectly, as though the ignition had never occurred. The sky cleared, the courtyard returned to its pristine marble state, and the white doves settled back onto the stone, pecking peacefully at the fresh grain.

Everything was restored except the Frozen Apex Syndicate. Their leadership and high commanders were left floating in a localized pocket of open space above the palace—a writhing, screaming cluster of perpetually burning, liquid-flesh skeletons, their bodies constantly melting and boiling, their voices producing a continuous, high-pitched shriek of unimaginable thermal torture that would never end, because Godric willed it so.

Lord Godric stood, brushed a stray grain off his tunic, and walked toward me. His salt-and-pepper beard was uncharred, his simple garments pristine. He reached out and pat my shoulder with a warm, comforting hand. "Mark, my boy," he said gently, his rich baritone dripping with sincere affection. "You look faint. Go to the kitchens and tell the head chef I said to give you a cup of chilled spiced wine."

I bowed and left. I drank the wine, but my throat felt as though it were swallowing liquid lead. I write this so that those who come after me will understand: Godric’s superpowers are not weapons he wields. They are apocalyptic absolute laws that shatter the fundamental mechanics of existence, leaving behind only screaming, immortal horror.</file>

Use "Godric Stat Experiment" prompt as baseline writing rule for the journal.

Write 3 detailed journals by 3 court wizards who witness Godric "testing" his superpower (only 1 superpower per journal. Choose superpowers that are distinctly different from each other).
