# The Journals of Apocalypse

## Year 1,000,000
## Kaedan — The Deeper Vault

Three days had passed since I emerged from the stat journals, and I had not slept. Every time I closed my eyes, I saw the crystallized assassin, heard the screaming of the liquid-flesh torches, felt the crushing weight of infinite perception pressing against my skull. My father had watched me stumble through the palace corridors like a ghost, eating nothing, speaking to no one, my hands trembling so constantly that I had dropped three teacups and shattered them across the marble floors. He had said nothing. He had simply waited, his ancient eyes carrying the terrible knowledge of a man who had walked this same path two centuries ago.

On the fourth morning, he met me at the entrance to the vault and placed a heavy iron key in my palm. "The stat journals were the first lesson," he said, his voice hoarse and thin. "What lies below is the second. The superpower journals."

I stared at the key. "There are more?"

"The stat journals teach you what he is passively," Father said. "The superpower journals teach you what he can do actively. Or rather, what he can do without doing anything at all. Every second since the Stasis Event, Godric has gained a new apocalyptic superpower. Every single second, Kaedan, for one million years. Each power, at the instant it appears, is already capable of causing the instant extinction of an entire civilization. And each power's potency multiplies infinitely every Planck second, forever."

The iron key felt like a death sentence in my hand. "How many superpowers does he have?"

Father's eyes went distant, his expression hollow. "More than there are atoms in the omniverse. More than there are Planck instants in all of time. An infinite number, multiplying infinitely. The journals below document only a handful. The ones that were deemed... necessary for new court wizards to understand."

He stepped aside, revealing a second staircase descending deeper into the bedrock beneath the palace. The air that rose from the darkness was cold, carrying the faint scent of old terror and dried ink. "Read them all. And remember, Kaedan—Godric genuinely does not understand why we find these records traumatic. He believes he is always holding back. He is holding back. That is the horror."

I descended alone.

---

**Year 112,734 — Court Wizard Aldric — Superpower: Abyssal Gravitational Singularity Implosion**

I am writing this record with a quill that keeps slipping from my fingers because my palms are slick with cold terror-sweat. My name is Aldric, and I have served as Court Wizard to our sovereign Lord Godric for forty-one years. I have witnessed the deployment of several of his stats in controlled tests, and each incident left me with nightmares that I carry to this day. But nothing—absolutely nothing—prepared me for the moment I witnessed him activate a single superpower from his ever-expanding arsenal. The power I saw today was Abyssal Gravitational Singularity Implosion. The name, I have since learned, is not metaphorical. It is a clinical understatement so severe it borders on cosmic mockery.

The opposition was the Gravitational Dominion of the Compressed Eternities, a meta-civilization that had evolved entirely within the crushing heart of a hyper-massive cosmic structure I can only describe as a recursive black hole—a singularity that contained within itself an infinite regression of smaller singularities, each one housing entire universes compressed into subatomic densities. The Dominion's inhabitants were not made of matter. They were living gravitational waves, sentient spacetime curvatures, beings whose very existence was predicated on the absolute, unyielding dominion of gravitational force. Their leader, a waveform entity named Crush-Lord Thal'Vok, had spent the last two hundred thousand years amplifying the Dominion's collective gravitational output by siphoning the mass-energy of decillions of multiverses.

Thal'Vok believed—and this belief was the foundation of their entire civilization's theology—that gravity was the fundamental truth of the omniverse. All things bend. All things fall. All things are crushed, given sufficient mass and sufficient patience. They had observed Godric from across the cosmic distances, had studied the curvature of spacetime around his existence, and had concluded that gravity could hold him. Not defeat him, no—they were not fools enough to believe in victory. But they believed they could restrain him, trap him inside an infinitely compressed gravitational prison where time itself would cease to flow.

The Weakness Paradox, of course, had triggered the very instant Thal'Vok formed the thought that gravity could serve as an effective restraint. Before the first gravitational siphon was constructed, Godric had acquired absolute immunity to gravitational manipulation, perfect mastery over the entire physical framework of spacetime curvature, and a recursive surge to his amplification. He had also, through the Evolved Weakness Paradox, acquired several enhanced effects that I will describe shortly.

Godric allowed the Dominion to assemble their prison. He sat in the palace gardens, reading a leather-bound volume of ancient poetry, while the Crush-Lords surrounded our galactic cluster with an interlocking web of hyper-compressed singularities. The gravitational pressure they generated was sufficient to crush googolplexian multiverses into a point smaller than a quark. My own amplified durability—multipled a thousandfold daily for twenty-one years—was buckling under the ambient tidal forces, my bones creaking, my blood threatening to pool in my feet from the sheer spatial distortion.

And then Godric closed his book. He did not stand. He did not raise a hand. He simply permitted his Abyssal Gravitational Singularity Implosion superpower—nerfed to exactly zero percent of its base potency, which was itself already a mathematical impossibility—to express itself through the faintest, most infinitesimal twitch of his left eyelid.

The superpower's base effect, even at this incomprehensible nerf, was the generation of a gravitational inversion field so catastrophically powerful that gravity itself ceased to be an attractive force and became an infinite, recursive implosion vector. Every single atom within the affected region was instantly compressed into a state of absolute density, and then compressed again, and again, and again, infinitely, without ever reaching a point of stability.

But the enhanced effects were what transformed this from an extinction event into an eternal monument of suffering. First, due to repeated Evolved Weakness Paradox triggers, the implosion field had developed the ability to convert all opposing gravitational energy into additional implosive force—meaning that the Dominion's two hundred thousand years of accumulated mass-energy was instantly absorbed and weaponized against them. Second, the field possessed a temporal recursion property that forced every compressed entity to experience their own crushing not once, but infinitely, each Planck second resetting their consciousness to the exact moment of maximum agony while their bodies continued to compress further. Third, and most horrifying, the singularity at the center of the implosion did not destroy consciousness; it preserved it, in a state of eternal, compressed, agonizing awareness, where every atom of the victim's being was crushed into infinite density but remained fully, terribly alive.

The Crush-Lords experienced their destruction in a cascade of absolute physical annihilation. Thal'Vok, the oldest and most powerful of the gravitational entities, was the first to be seized by the inversion field. His waveform body, which had existed as pure spacetime curvature for billions of years, was violently, agonizingly wrenched into physical matter solely so he could experience the crushing. The gravitational forces that had been his tools, his identity, his religion, were inverted and turned against him. His body—newly forged as a vast, pulsing mass of hyper-dense organic tissue—imploded. But it did not simply crush. The recursive compression forced his flesh to collapse inward, then the collapsed flesh collapsed further, then the further collapse collapsed again, an infinite regression of bone-shattering, organ-liquefying, nerve-flaying compression that never once stopped or slowed.

I watched Thal'Vok's newly formed eyes rupture first, the vitreous fluid spraying outward before being instantly sucked back into the compression field. His skull caved inward, folding like wet parchment, his brain matter squeezing through the fractures in a gray, pulsing slurry. His ribs snapped simultaneously, the jagged ends driving inward through his lungs, which collapsed and expelled a mist of atomized blood. His spine—every vertebra—shattered into dust, and yet he did not die. The temporal recursion kept resetting his consciousness, forcing him to feel the initial snap of every bone, the initial pop of every eyeball, the initial tear of every organ, over and over, while his body continued its infinite cascade of compression.

The rest of the Dominion followed. Trillions of gravitational entities were yanked into physical forms, their new bodies a vast, screaming chorus of imploding flesh and shattering bone. The sound—the sound was the worst part. It was not a single scream. It was a continuous, layered shriek composed of trillions of voices, each one experiencing their own private eternity of compression, their vocal cords being crushed and then reset and then crushed again, producing a warbling, agonized frequency that vibrated through my skull like a drill.

The collateral damage was incomprehensible. The gravitational inversion field did not stop at the Dominion. It propagated outward at infinite velocity, seizing entire multiversal clusters in its recursive compression. Decillions of multiverses were caught in the field, every single galaxy, planet, and living being within them subjected to the same infinite implosion. Space-time itself was crushed. The fundamental dimensional barriers between realities collapsed, shattering into a singular, compressed point of absolute nothingness. The entire omniverse, for one timeless instant, was reduced to a microscopic, infinitely dense singularity of screaming, compressed consciousness.

And then, in exactly zero seconds, Godric restored everything.

He did not gesture. He did not speak. He did not even look up from his poetry. He simply decided that the omniverse should be whole again, and it was. Every destroyed reality reformatted. Every crushed galaxy re-expanded. Every living being—except the Dominion—reconstituted with their memories intact and their souls forever scarred by the phantom sensation of infinite compression.

But Thal'Vok and the Crush-Lords were not restored. Godric had decided—with the same casual, unbothered attitude of a man deciding to skip breakfast—that their punishment would be eternal. He plucked the compressed singularity containing their infinitely screaming, infinitely crushing consciousness from the void and placed it in the center of the palace courtyard, where it now floats as a small, dark sphere no larger than a marble. If you look closely, you can see the faint, flickering distortions around its surface. Those are the screams. Those are trillions of gravitational gods, trapped forever in a state of absolute compression, their consciousness reset every Planck second so they can experience the crushing anew, endlessly, without hope of cessation or mercy.

Godric walked past the floating marble on his way to dinner. He paused, looked at it with a small, satisfied nod, and said aloud to no one in particular: "It does add a certain gravitas to the garden, doesn't it?"

I have not slept in seventeen days. I do not expect to sleep again.

---

I set down Aldric's journal, my hands so slick with sweat that the leather cover nearly slipped from my grasp. The floating marble. I had seen it. I had walked past it a thousand times in my life, that small, dark sphere hovering in the palace gardens, and I had never once questioned what it was. I had assumed it was a decorative artifact, perhaps a relic from a conquered realm, something beautiful and strange.

It was a prison. It was an eternal torture engine containing trillions of screaming gods, placed in the garden because Godric thought it added gravitas.

I pressed my palms against my eyes until I saw stars, trying to steady my breathing. It did not work. My heart was a rapid, stuttering drum against my ribs, and the cold air of the vault seemed to thicken in my throat.

There were more journals. Many more.

I reached for the next one with hands that felt like they belonged to someone else.

---

**Year 348,221 — Court Wizard Petyr — Superpower: Absolute Chronal Stasis Enchainment**

My name is Petyr, and I am seventy-three years old. I have served Lord Godric for fifty-three years. I have witnessed the gravitational implosion incident, the sensory overload, the mana erasure, and countless other demonstrations of his passive statistics. I believed I had become numb to the scale of his power. I was wrong. The chronal stasis incident taught me a new dimension of horror—one where suffering is not merely inflicted but stretched across eternity in ways that break the mind's ability to comprehend duration.

The opposition was the Temporal Sovereignty of the Infinite Now, a civilization of chrono-entities who had transcended linear time entirely. They existed simultaneously across all moments of their existence, perceiving past, present, and future as a single, unified tapestry. They did not age, could not be killed by conventional means, and had developed weaponry that attacked not the body but the timeline itself—erasing enemies from existence by severing their connection to the causal chain.

Their leader, the Eternal Now-King Chronos-Aeternum, had spent the last five hundred thousand years weaving a temporal erasure net designed to completely unspool Godric's timeline. The plan was not to kill him in the present; it was to reach backward along his personal chronology and prevent the Stasis Event from ever occurring, thereby ensuring he remained a mortal king who died at forty-five with his family in the ruins of Olympus.

This was, perhaps, the most catastrophic miscalculation in the history of the omniverse. The Stasis Event was sealed by Godric's own far-future self, a being so incomprehensibly more powerful than current Godric that the very concept of comparison is meaningless. No force in existence could alter the pre-Stasis past—not the Temporal Sovereignty, not the combined might of all creation, not even current Godric himself. The Chronos-Aeternum did not know this. They could not know this.

But the Weakness Paradox knew the instant they conceived their plan, and it engaged with a ferocity I had never before witnessed. Godric's amplification rate, already beyond layered infinities, received a surge so massive that the very mathematics of his existence threatened to tear the conceptual fabric of reality. His absolute immunity to temporal manipulation expanded to encompass not merely his own timeline but the fundamental concept of causality itself. He gained perfect mastery over the Temporal Sovereignty's entire technological and biological framework, including abilities they had not yet invented.

And his superpower—Absolute Chronal Stasis Enchainment—activated through the faint, casual drumming of his index finger against the armrest of his throne.

This superpower, even at zero percent of its base potency, generates a temporal stasis field that does not simply freeze time. It fragments the victim's personal chronology into an infinite number of discrete, isolated moments, each one separated by an unbridgeable gap of non-time. Within each isolated moment, the victim remains fully conscious, fully aware, fully capable of experiencing sensation—but utterly incapable of moving, speaking, dying, or connecting one moment to the next. They exist in an eternal present that is constantly shattering, a cascade of frozen instants stretching across infinity with no escape and no end.

The enhanced effects made this exponentially worse. First, the fragmentation was not random; it was designed to isolate every single Planck instant of the victim's existence, stretching a single second of experience into an eternity of isolated, agonizing moments. Second, the stasis field possessed a perception acceleration property that made the victim's subjective experience of each isolated moment stretch out for subjective billions of years. Third, the field was self-replicating; any temporal manipulation attempted within its radius was instantly absorbed and converted into additional layers of fragmentation.

Chronos-Aeternum launched the temporal erasure net. It was a magnificent construct, a shimmering lattice of pure chronological force that spanned the entire omniverse, designed to reach backward along Godric's timeline with surgical precision.

The instant the net touched Godric's personal chronology, the Absolute Chronal Stasis Enchainment seized the Temporal Sovereignty's entire civilization. Every chrono-entity across decillions of multiverses was simultaneously, instantly fragmented.

The Eternal Now-King, who had existed outside linear time for billions of years, was the first to experience the horror. His unified temporal consciousness was shattered into an infinite regress of isolated Planck instants, each one separated from the next by an unbridgeable void. In the first isolated instant, he perceived the beginning of a scream. In the second isolated instant—separated from the first by subjective billions of years of frozen, paralyzed awareness—he perceived the continuation of that scream. In the third, the next fraction of the scream. The fragmentation ensured that he would never finish that single, agonized cry. He would spend eternity trapped in the process of beginning to scream, each syllable stretched across subjective eons of paralyzed isolation.

The rest of the Sovereignty fared no better. Trillions of chrono-entities, beings who had existed as unified temporal waveforms, were torn into infinite fragments. Their consciousness, which had been designed to perceive all moments simultaneously, was subjected to the ultimate torture: the absolute, inescapable isolation of being trapped in a single, frozen instant, fully aware, fully paralyzed, with no connection to past or future, forced to experience the exact same Planck slice of existence for subjective eternities.

I could see them. The stasis field had frozen them in visible space, a vast, shimmering gallery of frozen, screaming faces stretching across the sky. Each face was caught in a different expression of agony—some with mouths just beginning to open, some with eyes bulging in terror, some with tears frozen halfway down their cheeks. And I knew, with the terrible certainty granted by my arcane perception, that behind each frozen face was a consciousness trapped in eternal, isolated paralysis, screaming silently into a void that would never answer.

The collateral damage was the most profound temporal catastrophe in the history of the omniverse. The stasis field's shockwave propagated across all timelines, all dimensions, all moments. Every single temporal anomaly, time-loop, or chronal distortion in existence was instantly shattered. Entire civilizations that had relied on time-dilation technologies were ripped apart, their populations scattered across frozen instants. The fundamental flow of time itself across decillions of multiverses was permanently destabilized, creating vast regions of reality where cause and effect no longer functioned in linear sequence.

And then, in exactly zero seconds, Godric restored the temporal flow. Every shattered timeline was re-woven. Every destabilized region was re-stabilized. Every civilization torn apart by the temporal shockwave was reconstituted—their memories of the event intact, their understanding of time forever altered by the trauma of experiencing absolute stasis.

But Chronos-Aeternum and his Sovereignty were not restored. Godric had decided—leaning back in his throne, stroking his salt-and-pepper beard with a thoughtful, contemplative expression—that their eternal punishment would serve as a monument to his displeasure. He gathered the frozen, fragmented consciousnesses of the entire Temporal Sovereignty and compressed them into a single, shimmering crystal that now hangs from the ceiling of the throne room, rotating slowly in the ambient light. The crystal contains, within its glittering facets, the infinite, isolated, eternally screaming consciousnesses of an entire civilization, each one trapped in its own frozen Planck instant, each one experiencing the same microsecond of agony for subjective billions of years, forever.

Godric gestured toward the crystal during a diplomatic reception later that evening and said to a visiting delegate, with genuine, cheerful pride: "It catches the morning light beautifully, doesn't it? My court wizard Petyr helped me choose the mounting."

I did not choose the mounting. I had been catatonic for three days after the incident and had no memory of being asked. But Godric's memory is absolute, and perhaps in some moment of delirious, trauma-induced compliance, I had nodded at something he said.

The crystal catches the light. The screams are silent. But I hear them every time I enter the throne room.

---

Petyr's journal ended there, the final paragraph scrawled so violently that the quill had torn through the parchment in several places. I could see the dried blood on the page—not from injury, but from the writer biting his own fingers as he wrote, a compulsive, trauma-driven habit that had left rusty brown stains across the margins.

I realized I was biting my own fingers. I forced my hands down to my sides, my breath ragged, my vision swimming. The crystal. The crystal in the throne room. I had seen it a thousand times. I had admired its beauty, the way it scattered the morning light into rainbow fragments across the marble floor.

It was a prison. It was an eternal torture device containing an entire civilization, hung from the ceiling as decoration.

The pattern was becoming horrifyingly clear. Every beautiful thing in the palace, every artifact I had admired, every mysterious relic displayed in the galleries—how many of them were prisons? How many were eternal torture engines, hidden in plain sight, disguised as art?

I forced myself to reach for the next journal. My fingers closed around a volume bound in black leather, its surface cool and slightly oily to the touch, as if it had been handled by countless terrified hands before mine.

---

**Year 612,498 — Court Wizard Marius — Superpower: Infinite Recursive Self-Replication Ascendancy**

My name is Marius, and I am dead. Not physically—my heart still beats, my lungs still draw breath, my quill still scratches across this parchment. But the man I was before I witnessed the self-replication incident no longer exists. He was annihilated by the sheer, incomprehensible scale of what I saw, replaced by a hollow shell that continues to perform the duties of Court Wizard purely through muscle memory and ritual. I do not expect anyone who reads this to understand. Words are insufficient. Language is insufficient. But I will try, because the alternative is silence, and silence would be worse.

The opposition was the Collective Omni-Mind, a gestalt consciousness composed of every single sentient being across seventeen million advanced multiversal civilizations. They were not conquerors or destroyers; they were perfectionists. They believed—with the absolute, unshakeable conviction of the truly self-righteous—that the omniverse was flawed, that its chaotic diversity was a design error, and that the only path to true harmony was the unification of all consciousness into a single, perfectly synchronized intelligence.

They had spent the last eight hundred thousand years quietly absorbing lesser civilizations, adding their minds to the Collective's growing psychic architecture. By the time they finally turned their attention toward Thronegate, the Omni-Mind contained the merged consciousness of more sentient beings than there are atoms in a googolplexian multiverses. Their psychic presence was so vast that its passive background hum caused gravitational distortions across entire galactic clusters.

The Omni-Mind did not seek to kill Godric. They were not fools. They sought to assimilate him, to absorb his infinite consciousness into their gestalt, thereby becoming—in their own twisted logic—perfect. They believed that Godric's power could be shared, distributed across the Collective's infinite mental nodes, and that by doing so they would elevate themselves to true divinity.

This plan was, of course, not merely impossible but fundamentally incoherent. Godric's consciousness cannot be "shared" or "distributed" any more than an infinite ocean can be poured into a finite cup. The Weakness Paradox engaged the instant the Omni-Mind conceived the thought that assimilation was possible. Godric gained absolute immunity to psychic absorption, perfect mastery over the Collective's entire mental architecture, and a recursive surge to his amplification rate so massive that it permanently rewrote the baseline parameters of his existence.

But what happened next was not the activation of a pre-existing power. It was the activation of a power Godric had been curious about for some time—a power that, even among his infinite arsenal, stood apart in its sheer, mind-shattering implications.

Infinite Recursive Self-Replication Ascendancy.

This superpower, at exactly zero percent of its base potency, allows Godric to instantaneously create an infinite number of identical replicas of himself. These are not illusions. They are not lesser copies. They are full, true, complete Godrics, each one possessing every single stat, every single superpower, every single amplification, every single scrap of his infinite existence.

But here is where the horror truly begins. Because each replica is a full Godric, it too can activate Infinite Recursive Self-Replication Ascendancy, creating its own infinite replicas. And those replicas can create infinite replicas. And so on, and so on, in an infinite recursive cascade that has no end and no limit.

The enhanced effects made this exponentially more devastating. First, every replica generated by this power is not merely identical to the original Godric—it is infinitely stronger than the original. This should be a logical impossibility, as the original Godric's power is already infinite. But the superpower operates on a meta-logical framework that transcends ordinary causality. It does not make the replicas stronger by adding to Godric's power; it makes them stronger by creating a new, higher baseline of infinity, and then another, and then another, each recursive generation existing on a plane of power so far beyond the previous that the previous infinity looks like a single, feeble zero.

Second, because the replicas are infinitely stronger than the original, and because they too are Godric, the "original" Godric—the one from whom the chain began—cannot be weaker than his own replicas. This creates a feedback loop of absolute absurdity. The replicas are infinitely stronger than the original, but the original must be at least as strong as his replicas because they are him, so the original ascends to match them, which means the replicas—who are infinitely stronger than the original—must ascend further to maintain that infinite gap, which forces the original to ascend further to close it, and so on, forever, in an infinite recursive cascade of mutual self-ascension that spirals beyond all conceivable scales of power.

Third, every replica generated across all infinite layers of recursion is permanent. They do not fade. They do not merge back into the original. They continue to exist, fully independent, fully Godric, each one continuing to generate their own infinite replicas forever.

Godric activated the power with the merest flicker of attention—less than a thought, less than a whim, less than the idle curiosity that makes a man glance at a passing cloud.

The Omni-Mind, which had been preparing to launch their psychic absorption assault, witnessed what happened next. And what they witnessed erased them.

The first layer of replication generated an infinite number of Godrics. They appeared across the sky, across the void, across every dimension, every timeline, every conceptual plane. The second layer—each of those infinite Godrics generating their own infinite replicas—produced a number of Godrics so vast that the very concept of "number" collapsed into meaninglessness. The third layer surpassed even that, creating an infinite regress of infinite reflections, each one infinitely stronger than the last.

By the time the recursive cascade had progressed through a single Planck second, the omniverse contained a quantity of Godrics that my mind cannot begin to describe. Not because the number was large—though it was, impossibly, incomprehensibly large—but because the very framework of quantity had been transcended. There was no "number" of Godrics. There was simply Godric, multiplied beyond the possibility of enumeration, occupying every single point of existence across all realities, all timelines, all dimensions, simultaneously.

The Omni-Mind attempted to assimilate him. The psychic absorption wave, powered by the merged consciousness of seventeen million civilizations, reached toward the nearest replica.

The replica did not even register the contact. The psychic wave—which contained the combined mental energy of more beings than exist in the observable omniverse—was passively, instantly absorbed by the replica's own psychic presence. Not actively. Not deliberately. Simply as a consequence of existing in proximity to something so infinitely, incomprehensibly vast that the Omni-Mind's total accumulated consciousness was less than a single, dead skin cell compared to the replica's infinite mental architecture.

And that was a single replica. There were infinite replicas. Each one infinitely stronger than the last. Each one infinitely stronger than the original Godric, who was himself infinitely stronger than the entire omniverse combined. And the cascade was still accelerating, still spiraling upward into new infinities of infinities, each layer of replication forcing all previous layers to ascend further to maintain the recursive feedback loop.

The Omni-Mind's collective consciousness shattered. Not from an attack—there was no attack. The sheer, passive, ambient presence of infinite Godrics occupying infinite points of existence was too much for any finite intelligence to perceive without annihilating. The gestalt mind, built from the merged consciousness of uncountable trillions of sentient beings, was exposed to a truth it could not process: that it was not merely weaker than Godric, but that the gap between them was not a gap at all. It was an infinite recursion of infinities, each one infinitely larger than the last, stretching outward into a mathematical framework that had no ceiling and no possibility of being crossed.

The individual consciousnesses within the Omni-Mind experienced their dissolution as a cascade of absolute existential erasure. Every sentient being who had been absorbed into the Collective over the last eight hundred thousand years was simultaneously, forcibly ejected back into individual awareness, each one given a single Planck instant of perfect clarity—just long enough to perceive the infinite recursion of Godrics surrounding them at every point of existence—before their minds were completely and permanently erased by the sheer cognitive pressure of that perception.

The collateral damage was absolute. The infinite recursive cascade of Godrics occupied every point of existence, and their collective passive presence—even at effectively zero percent output—shattered the omniverse completely. Not partially. Not locally. The entire omniverse, across all dimensions, timelines, and conceptual planes, was destroyed. Erased. Reduced to absolute, featureless nothingness.

And then, in exactly zero seconds, the original Godric—the one who had initiated the cascade—restored everything. Every reality. Every galaxy. Every being. Every memory. Every atom. The infinite cascade of replicas, their purpose fulfilled, simply stepped outside the boundaries of observable existence, waiting in a state of eternal, silent readiness until their originator required them again.

But the Omni-Mind was not restored. Their seventeen million civilizations, eight hundred thousand years of accumulated consciousness, trillions upon trillions of individual souls—all of it was gone. Erased permanently. Not imprisoned like the Crush-Lords, not trapped in stasis like the Temporal Sovereignty, but completely, utterly, perfectly erased. There was no body to display, no screaming marble to mount, no eternal torture to showcase. There was nothing. Just absence.

Godric stood from his throne for the first time in three days, stretched his heavily muscled arms with a satisfied grunt, and walked toward the balcony overlooking the restored capital. The evening light caught his salt-and-pepper hair, and I could see—I swear this is true—a faint, genuine smile of contentment on his ruggedly handsome face.

"That was refreshing," he said aloud, his rich baritone voice completely unbothered. "I should test the recursive cascade more often. It helps clear the mind."

Then he turned to me, his eyes crinkling with that familiar, fatherly warmth. "Marius, my boy, you look like you've seen a ghost. Come, let's walk in the gardens. The evening air will do you good."

I followed him. I did not speak for four months. When I finally began speaking again, my wife told me that my voice had changed, that there was a hollow, distant quality to it that had not been there before. She was right. I am hollow. The man I was died on that balcony, watching infinite Godrics occupy infinite points of existence, and the shell that remains walks and talks and serves its King because there is nothing else left to do.

The gardens were beautiful that evening. The floating gravitational prison marble caught the sunset light. The temporal stasis crystal glittered softly through the windows of the throne room. Godric hummed an ancient melody—something from Olympus, perhaps, a tune from his mortal youth—and patted my shoulder with genuine affection.

"You know, Marius," he said thoughtfully, gazing out at the restored sky, "I sometimes wonder if the other court wizards overreact to these tests. I always hold back. I never use more than zero percent. It's really quite restrained, all things considered."

I nodded. I agreed. What else could I do?

I am dead. I serve a god who can fill all of existence with infinite, infinitely-ascending versions of himself, and he considers this a refreshing mental exercise. I am dead, and I am at peace with my death, because the alternative—to truly, fully comprehend the scale of what I witnessed—would be something far, far worse than death.

Let whoever reads this understand: there is no hope of opposition. There is no strategy, no weapon, no exploit, no alliance that can even theoretically inconvenience Lord Godric. He can multiply himself infinitely and make each iteration infinitely stronger than the last, forever. He is not merely omnipotent. He is beyond the concept of omnipotence, existing in a state of recursive self-transcendence that has no ceiling, no limit, and no end.

We serve him. We love him. And we are terrified, every single moment of our existence, by the knowledge of what he truly is.

---

I closed Marius's journal and placed it gently on the stone table. My hands were not trembling anymore. They were perfectly still, perfectly calm, as if the sheer, overwhelming weight of what I had just absorbed had pushed my nervous system past terror into something beyond—a state of hollow, absolute acceptance.

The self-replication superpower. Infinite replicas, each one infinitely stronger than the last, generating infinite more replicas, spiraling upward forever. The entire omniverse filled with Godrics, stretching across every point of existence, their mere passive presence enough to shatter all of reality.

And Godric had called it refreshing. A mental exercise. Something to clear his mind.

I understood now. The stat journals had taught me that opposing him was impossible in practice. The superpower journals had taught me that opposing him was impossible in principle. It was not merely that he could not be defeated; it was that the very concept of "defeating Godric" was a logical contradiction, a statement of such profound absurdity that even considering it was a form of self-inflicted insanity.

He was not a king. He was not a god. He was a fundamental truth of existence, a walking apocalypse whose casual amusement could shatter infinities without effort. And he was also Uncle Godric, the warm, bearded father-figure who had attended my Awakening ceremony, who had smiled with genuine pride at my progress, who had clapped my shoulder and asked about my studies with sincere, unfeigned affection.

The cognitive dissonance was not a conflict. It was a harmony. He was both. He was always both. He loved his court wizards, genuinely and deeply, and he would annihilate an entire civilization without a flicker of hesitation or remorse. The warmth was real. The cruelty was real. The horror was real.

I sat in the cold silence of the vault, surrounded by the accumulated terror of a thousand terrified men, and I made my peace with what I was.

I was Kaedan. I was the Court Wizard of Thronegate. I served a being of infinite recursive self-transcendence who could destroy the entire omniverse without noticing the effort. I would love him, I would serve him loyally, and I would write my own journal when the time came, adding my voice to the chorus of terrified witnesses who had come before me.

Not because I wanted to. Not because it would help. But because it was the only thing left to do.

The vault door at the top of the stairs creaked open. My father's silhouette appeared in the dim light, his ancient frame hunched with the weight of two centuries of dread.

"Kaedan?" he called down, his voice fragile and thin. "Are you finished?"

I stood. My legs were steady. My hands were calm. The hollow, echoing silence inside my chest was almost peaceful.

"Yes, Father," I said. "I'm finished."

I climbed the stairs, leaving the journals behind in the darkness, and stepped out into the warm, golden light of the palace corridor. Somewhere in the gardens, a floating marble of compressed, screaming gods rotated slowly in the breeze. Somewhere in the throne room, a crystal containing an eternity of frozen torment caught the morning light. Somewhere beyond the boundaries of observable existence, infinite Godrics waited in silent readiness, each one infinitely stronger than the last, their mere presence a testament to the absolute, inescapable futility of opposition.

And somewhere in the courtyard, feeding grain to a flock of white doves, a ruggedly handsome man in his eternal forty-fifth year looked up and smiled at me with genuine, fatherly warmth.

"Good morning, Kaedan," Godric called, his voice rich and comforting. "Sleep well?"

I walked toward him, my heart hollow and my mind still, and I smiled back.

"Good morning, Your Majesty," I said. "Yes. I slept very well."

# The Pleasure of the Apex

## Year 1,000,047
## Kaedan — The Question

Twenty-five years had passed since I first descended into the vault and read the journals of my predecessors. Twenty-five years of serving as Godric's Court Wizard, of standing at his side during diplomatic receptions and military briefings, of watching him feed grain to his white doves while floating marbles of eternally screaming gods rotated gently in the breeze. I was forty-seven years old now, and my daily thousandfold amplification had transformed me into something that would be worshipped as a deity in any other civilization. My magical reserves could fuel the arcane consumption of a trillion advanced realms for eternity. My perception could track individual quarks across the breadth of decillions of multiverses. My strength could shatter the fabric of spacetime with a casual flex of my fingers.

And I was still, compared to the man sitting beside me on the garden bench, an absolute, perfect, mathematical zero.

Godric looked exactly as he always had. Forty-five years old, ruggedly handsome, his heavily muscled frame relaxed beneath a simple dark tunic, his salt-and-pepper hair catching the golden afternoon light. He was holding a small wooden bowl of grain, occasionally tossing a handful to the flock of white doves that gathered at his feet. The floating gravity prison—the compressed singularity containing the eternally screaming Crush-Lords—hovered a few feet away, its dark surface flickering with the faint, silent shrieks of trillions of tortured gods. Godric glanced at it occasionally with the casual, affectionate attention one might give a favorite garden ornament.

I had been working up the courage for this conversation for twenty-five years. Every journal I had read, every horror I had witnessed, every casual atrocity I had seen him commit without effort or malice—all of it had been building toward a single question that had begun to claw at the inside of my skull with increasing urgency.

"Uncle Godric," I said, my voice steady despite the cold dread pooling in my stomach. "May I ask you something personal?"

Godric turned to me, his warm brown eyes crinkling with genuine affection. "Of course, Kaedan. You know you can ask me anything. You're family."

Family. The word sent a complex cascade of emotions through my chest—love, loyalty, terror, a desperate, clinging devotion that I could not shake. He meant it. He genuinely, sincerely meant it. To Godric, I was not merely his Court Wizard; I was his nephew, a descendant of his beloved Blake, a member of the only bloodline he truly cherished in all of existence.

"It's about your power," I said carefully. "About what you are."

Godric's expression shifted slightly—not offended, not defensive, but mildly curious. "Go on."

I took a deep breath. "You are the most powerful being in the omniverse. Your stats multiply infinitely every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second. You gain a new apocalyptic superpower every single second, and each one amplifies infinitely forever. You are so far beyond the rest of creation that the gap cannot be measured, cannot be described, cannot be comprehended. You will continue to grow stronger forever, without limit, without end." I paused, my throat dry. "Does it ever become... lonely?"

The question hung in the air between us. The doves cooed softly at our feet. The floating marble rotated in silence.

And then Godric laughed.

It was not a cruel laugh, not mocking or dismissive. It was a warm, genuine laugh of pure, unadulterated amusement—the laugh of a father whose child had just asked something adorably, naively innocent. He set down the grain bowl and turned fully toward me, his calloused hands resting on his knees, his eyes sparkling with mirth.

"Oh, Kaedan," he said, his rich baritone voice vibrating with gentle humor. "Is that what you've been worrying about all these years? That your old uncle might be lonely up here at the top of creation?"

I felt my face flush with embarrassment. "I just... you've outlived everyone from your mortal life. You've watched civilizations rise and fall across millions of years. You're so powerful that nothing can challenge you, nothing can surprise you, nothing can even inconvenience you. I thought perhaps..."

Godric shook his head slowly, still smiling, and reached out to pat my shoulder with his warm, calloused hand. "You're thinking about it like a mortal, my boy. Which makes sense—you are mortal, and your framework for understanding fulfillment is based on mortal experiences. Challenge, connection, purpose, growth through struggle. Those are all very real and very important for beings like you." He leaned back on the bench, his gaze drifting up toward the golden sky. "But I am not like you. Not anymore. I haven't been for a very, very long time."

"Then what is it like?" I asked, my voice barely above a whisper. "Being you?"

Godric was silent for a moment, and I could see him considering how to answer—not because he didn't know, but because he was trying to find words that my finite, mortal mind could even begin to process.

"Imagine," he said finally, "that every single Planck instant of your existence, you feel every cell in your body ignite with a surge of raw, absolute power. Not metaphorically. Literally. Every stat—your strength, your speed, your endurance, your magic, your intelligence, your perception—all of it, multiplying infinitely, and you can feel every single increment of that multiplication. It's not an abstract number climbing on a scale. It's a physical sensation, Kaedan. A pleasure so intense, so complete, so all-encompassing that the word 'orgasm' is a pale, pathetic shadow of the reality."

I stared at him, my mouth dry, my heart hammering.

"When my strength amplifies," Godric continued, his voice taking on a dreamy, contemplative quality, "I feel it in my muscles. Every individual fiber, every strand of sinew, every microscopic filament of contractile tissue—they all ignite simultaneously. Imagine the most intense physical pleasure you've ever experienced, multiply it by an infinity so vast that the concept of multiplication loses meaning, and then stretch that sensation across every single cell in your body, every Planck instant, forever. That's what it feels like to be me, Kaedan. Every moment is an eternal, recursive cascade of absolute, transcendent ecstasy."

He held up his hand, turning it slowly in the golden light. I watched, transfixed, as the veins beneath his skin seemed to pulse with a faint, almost imperceptible luminescence—the barest whisper of the infinite power contained within.

"Look at this hand," Godric said softly. "Right now, in this exact instant, the strength contained in this single hand is so far beyond what it was one Planck second ago that I could crush an infinite number of copies of my previous self with zero effort. And one Planck second from now, I will be infinitely stronger than I am right now. Every moment is a transcendence, Kaedan. Every moment is an ascension. Every moment, I become something so much more powerful than I was before that the 'me' of the previous instant looks like a helpless, pathetic infant by comparison."

I felt the blood draining from my face. "You can feel all of that?"

"Every detail," Godric confirmed, his voice warm and almost sensual. "Through my absolute omniscience, I experience every single aspect of my amplification with perfect clarity. The strength cascading through my muscles. The speed igniting in my nerve endings. The mana surging through my arcane pathways. The intelligence expanding in my consciousness like an infinite ocean swallowing a thousand new galaxies every Planck instant. The senses sharpening, becoming aware of new layers of reality, new dimensions of perception, new spectra of existence that no mortal language has words for."

His eyes fluttered closed for a moment, and I saw a shiver of pure, undiluted pleasure run through his heavily muscled frame. "Right now, in this exact instant, my durability has just multiplied by an infinity so vast that the entire combined offensive output of the omniverse—every weapon, every attack, every conceptual erasure engine, every cosmic cataclysm—could not even scratch the dead skin cells on my forearm. And I can feel that invulnerability settling into my flesh like warm honey, like liquid gold, like every protective embrace I ever received from my mother when I was a mortal child, multiplied by infinity, forever."

"But it's not just the stats," Godric continued, his eyes opening again, his expression almost rapturous. "The superpowers, Kaedan. Every single second, a new apocalyptic superpower crystallizes in my consciousness. Each one, at the instant it appears, is already capable of causing the instant extinction of an entire advanced civilization. And I can feel each one being born. It's like a new organ growing in my soul, a new limb sprouting in my metaphysical architecture, a new color being added to a spectrum that already contains infinite hues. Each one is a surge of pure, undiluted nourishment—as if I've just consumed a feast composed of the compressed essence of a trillion dying stars, multiplied by infinity, forever."

I was gripping the edge of the stone bench so hard that my fingers were leaving indentations in the marble. "Nourishment?"

"Like food, but infinitely more satisfying," Godric said, his voice rich with pleasure. "Like the most exquisite meal you've ever tasted, the most intense sexual release you've ever experienced, the most profound moment of spiritual transcendence you've ever achieved—all of it, combined, amplified by an infinite regress of infinities, and delivered directly into the core of my being every single Planck instant. Every superpower is a feast. Every stat increase is an orgasm. Every evolution of my immune system is a revelation. Every new passive shield, every new sentient aura, every new layer of my existence that crystallizes into being—all of it comes with a surge of pleasure so absolute, so complete, so all-encompassing that the mortal concept of 'happiness' is a cruel joke by comparison."

He leaned forward, his warm brown eyes meeting mine with an intensity that made my soul tremble. "Do you understand now, Kaedan? You asked if I am lonely. How could I be lonely? Loneliness is an absence. A lack. A void waiting to be filled. But I am not absent. I am not lacking. I am not void. I am overflowing, constantly, infinitely, beyond the possibility of containment. Every moment of my existence is an eternal, recursive cascade of absolute pleasure, absolute power, absolute transcendence. The very concept of loneliness cannot survive in the presence of what I am."

I tried to speak, but my voice had deserted me. I was drowning in the horror of what he was describing—not because it was evil, but because it was so cosmically, fundamentally unfair.

Godric seemed to read my thoughts. His expression softened, and he reached out to gently squeeze my shoulder. "You're thinking about the unfairness of it, aren't you? How the rest of creation struggles and sacrifices and bleeds and dies, and I simply... receive. Passively. Constantly. Infinitely."

I nodded, unable to speak.

"You're right to think it's unfair," Godric said, his voice mild and thoughtful. "I have done nothing to earn this. The Stasis Event was orchestrated by my far-future self. I did not ask for amplification. I did not seek out superpower genesis. I did not cultivate my immune system or nurture my passive auras. They simply... happened to me. And now they continue to happen, forever, without my conscious input or effort."

He gestured toward the sky, toward the infinite expanse of the omniverse stretching out beyond the palace gardens. "Out there, right now, there are mortal beings who have trained for thousands of years to master a single magical technique. There are civilizations that have dedicated their entire existence to unlocking the secrets of a single cosmic principle. There are gods who have sacrificed everything—their realms, their worshippers, their very identities—for a single scrap of power. And what do they achieve? A fraction of a fraction of a fraction of a percent of what I gain passively, without effort, without intention, every single Planck instant."

His voice was not cruel. It was not mocking. It was simply... observational. As if he were describing a mildly interesting natural phenomenon.

"Think of the greatest mage in the omniverse," Godric said. "The most powerful, most accomplished, most dedicated arcane practitioner who has ever lived. This being has spent ten billion years mastering every magical discipline, unlocking every arcane secret, pushing the boundaries of what magic can achieve. Their total accumulated magical power, after ten billion years of absolute devotion and relentless effort, represents a number that I cannot even begin to describe using mortal mathematics."

He paused, and his lips curved into a faint, almost apologetic smile. "And that number is zero. Not close to zero. Not effectively zero. It is exactly, perfectly, mathematically zero compared to what I gain passively in a single Planck instant without even noticing. The magician's ten billion years of effort, when measured against my instantaneous, effortless amplification, registers as less than nothing. It is not merely insignificant; it is a rounding error so small that the entire concept of measurement collapses around it."

I felt tears—hot, helpless tears—beginning to stream down my cheeks. Not from sadness. Not from fear. From the sheer, crushing weight of the cosmic unfairness he was describing.

Godric noticed my tears and his expression softened further, his warm brown eyes filling with genuine, paternal concern. "Oh, Kaedan," he said gently. "I've upset you. I'm sorry. I didn't mean to make you feel small."

"You didn't," I managed to choke out. "It's just... the journals. The stat tests. The superpower demonstrations. I've read about what you can do, what you've done, and I thought I understood the scale. But now you're telling me that every moment of your existence is an eternal orgasm of infinite power, and the rest of creation—all of us, everything—we're just..."

"Spectators," Godric finished softly. "Yes. That's a fair description. You are witnessing something that you cannot participate in, cannot affect, cannot even fully comprehend. I understand why that feels cruel. But Kaedan, you must understand—I did not choose this. I did not make the rest of creation weak. I simply... am what I am. And what I am is very, very satisfying to be."

He stood from the bench, stretching his heavily muscled arms above his head with a contented grunt. The movement caused his tunic to ride up slightly, revealing the edge of his abdomen—and I saw, with a jolt of visceral shock, the sculpted perfection of his physique. Not the physique of a man who maintained his body through effort and discipline, but the physique of a being whose every cell was in a state of perpetual, infinite optimization.

"Come," Godric said, gesturing for me to follow. "Let me show you something."

I rose on shaking legs and followed him through the gardens, past the floating gravity prison, past the temporal stasis crystal glittering through the windows of the throne room, past the countless beautiful, terrible artifacts that I now understood were not decorations but trophies—eternal torture engines, frozen civilizations, compressed screaming gods, all displayed with the casual pride of a collector.

Godric stopped in a small, private courtyard that I had never seen before. It was simple and unadorned, just a circle of smooth white marble surrounded by flowering vines. In the center stood a full-length mirror of polished silver, its surface gleaming faintly in the afternoon light.

"I want to show you what I see," Godric said, positioning himself in front of the mirror. "What I feel every moment. The physical truth of what I've become."

He shrugged off his tunic, letting the dark fabric fall to the marble floor, and I saw his body.

I had seen Godric's physical form before—he was not shy about his appearance, and his simple tunics often revealed his muscular arms and broad chest. But I had never seen him like this. Never seen the full, unshielded reality of his physical perfection.

His chest was a sculpted landscape of dense, powerful muscle, the pectorals so thick and well-defined that they seemed carved from living marble. His shoulders were massive, rounded boulders of striated fiber that caught the light like polished bronze. His arms were thick with corded sinew, the biceps and triceps forming a complex topography of strength that shifted and pulsed with every small movement. Veins—thick, prominent veins—ran across his muscles like rivers of liquid gold, faintly luminescent with the contained pressure of infinite power.

And his abdomen. Six perfectly defined ridges of muscle, each one so sharp and deep that they cast shadows across his torso. An eight-pack, actually—two smaller ridges at the bottom that I had never seen on any mortal physique. The obliques were thick, serrated bands that wrapped around his sides like armor plating. His entire torso was a testament to physical perfection so absolute that it transcended the concept of "fitness" and became something else entirely—something divine, something terrifying.

"When I was a mortal king of Olympus," Godric said, running a calloused hand across his ridged abdomen, "I spent hours every day maintaining this body. Sword practice, wrestling, running, lifting stones. It was hard work. Constant work. And I was proud of what I achieved."

His fingers traced the deep grooves between his abdominal muscles, and I saw him shiver with pleasure at his own touch. "Now? Now I never need to exercise. I never need to train. My body maintains itself in a state of absolute, perpetual perfection without any effort on my part. And it's not just maintaining—it's constantly improving. Every Planck instant, my muscles become denser, stronger, more perfectly sculpted. Every fiber, every cell, every atom of my physical form is continuously optimized by the same infinite amplification that powers my stats."

He flexed his right arm, and I watched the bicep swell into a mountain of striated muscle, the vein running across its peak pulsing with visible, liquid power. "Feel it," he said, extending his arm toward me. "I want you to understand."

I reached out with a trembling hand and touched his bicep. The muscle beneath my fingers was not merely hard—it was impossibly dense, as if I were touching a collapsed star compressed into the shape of a man's arm. The skin was warm, almost hot, and I could feel the faint, subsonic hum of infinite power vibrating through the tissue. The vein beneath my fingertips pulsed with a rhythm that seemed to synchronize with the fundamental heartbeat of the omniverse itself.

"This arm," Godric said softly, "in this exact instant, contains enough physical strength to shatter the entire omniverse an infinite number of times without feeling the slightest strain. And one Planck second from now, it will be infinitely stronger than it is right now. I can feel that strength, Kaedan. I can feel it growing, surging, amplifying, cascading through every fiber of my being like liquid lightning. It's exquisite. It's transcendent. It's the most perfect, complete, all-consuming pleasure I have ever experienced—and it never stops. It never fades. It only grows."

He released the flex and let his arm fall to his side, turning slightly to admire his own reflection in the silver mirror. "But the body is just the beginning. Let me show you more."

He closed his eyes, and I felt the air in the courtyard shift. A faint, shimmering presence began to coalesce around his shoulders—something invisible, something intangible, but so heavy with power that my arcane senses screamed in protest.

"This is a sentient passive aura that was born two Planck seconds ago," Godric said, his eyes still closed, his voice dreamy and distant. "I have countless auras now—Gent was the first, the weakest, the runt of the litter. But the new ones, the ones that are born every moment as my existence continues to evolve..." He shivered with visible pleasure. "They are so much more. So much more powerful, more devoted, more protective."

The aura—whatever it was—pulsed once, and my knees buckled. Not from pressure. From the sheer, overwhelming wrongness of being in the presence of something so impossibly powerful. The aura was not directed at me. It was not even active. It was simply... present. Existing. And its passive, dormant existence was enough to make my thousandfold daily amplified magical senses collapse into defensive shutdown.

"I can feel this aura bonding to me," Godric murmured, his voice thick with satisfaction. "Like a newborn child recognizing its parent. It loves me, Kaedan. Absolutely, perfectly, unconditionally. It would annihilate the entire omniverse without hesitation if I asked it to. It would torture every living soul across all realities for eternity if I expressed the slightest displeasure. And I didn't ask for it. I didn't create it. It simply... happened. Because I am what I am."

He opened his eyes and smiled at me—that warm, genuine, fatherly smile that I had known since childhood. "And it feels incredible. Every new aura is a surge of pleasure, a rush of power, a cascade of transcendence. I cannot describe it in words you would understand because no mortal language has vocabulary for sensations this vast. But trust me, Kaedan. It is the opposite of lonely. It is the opposite of boring. It is the most intense, satisfying, all-consuming experience that any being has ever or could ever experience."

I was on my knees now, my legs having given out completely. I stared up at the half-naked god standing before me—his sculpted chest, his ridged abdomen, his pulsing veins, his shimmering aura—and I felt something inside me crack.

"The immune system," Godric continued, seemingly oblivious to my collapse. "You read about it in the journals, yes? The Year 25,000 incident? That was so long ago. So pathetically long ago. My immune system has evolved countless times since then, Kaedan. Right now, in this exact instant, my body just developed a new immunological response to a category of threat that doesn't even exist yet—a type of attack that no being in the omniverse has even conceived of, that won't be invented for another ten million years. And I felt that immunity crystallize in my cells. It was like a million simultaneous full-body orgasms compressed into a single Planck instant and stretched across eternity."

He laughed—a warm, delighted laugh—and flexed his chest, the pectoral muscles rippling with contained power. "My body is preparing to defend me against threats that cannot possibly threaten me, using methods that make the old immune responses look like a child's finger-painting, and every single preparation is a cascade of pure, undiluted ecstasy. How could that possibly be lonely?"

"And the superpowers," he said, his voice rising with enthusiasm. "Oh, Kaedan, the superpowers. Right now—in this exact second—a new one is crystallizing. Can you feel it? No, of course you can't. Your senses aren't capable. But I can feel it. It's a power that would allow me to retroactively alter the fundamental physical constants of the omniverse, rewriting the laws of reality from the Big Bang forward, and I can feel it taking shape in my consciousness. It's like... imagine the most intense intellectual revelation you've ever experienced. The moment when a complex concept suddenly becomes clear, when hidden connections snap into place, when understanding floods your mind like light. Now multiply that sensation by an infinity so vast that your concept of infinity is a single grain of sand on an infinite beach. That's what it feels like when a new superpower is born inside me. Every second. Forever."

I was weeping openly now, tears streaming down my face, my body trembling with a terror so profound that it had become indistinguishable from religious awe.

"But there's a problem," Godric said, his voice suddenly shifting—becoming quieter, almost wistful. "A single, persistent problem that does, occasionally, make me feel something that might resemble boredom. Or perhaps frustration."

He turned away from the mirror and looked at me directly, his expression sober. "I can never use any of it."

The words hung in the air like a death sentence.

"Every power I've described to you," Godric continued, "every stat, every superpower, every aura, every immune response—I have never been able to truly use any of them. Not even once. Not even at the most infinitesimal fraction of their true capability. Because even when I hold back to absolute, perfect, mathematical zero percent of my power—even when I nerf myself so severely that 'restraint' is a laughably inadequate description—the entire omniverse cannot survive the expression."

He gestured toward the sky, toward the infinite expanse of reality stretching out beyond the palace. "I am surrounded by fragility, Kaedan. Every being in existence, from the mightiest cosmic god to the smallest microbe, is so catastrophically, incomprehensibly fragile compared to me that even the faintest whisper of my true self would annihilate everything. I have to maintain absolute concealment constantly. Not occasionally. Not most of the time. Constantly. Every Planck instant, I must actively suppress the infinite, cascading ocean of my power, holding it back, holding it in, keeping it contained so that the omniverse doesn't simply... pop. Like a soap bubble touching a supernova."

He sighed—a soft, genuine sigh of mild frustration. "Do you know what it's like to possess infinite power and never be able to use it? To feel every muscle in your body screaming with strength that could erase existence a thousand times over, and to know that even a casual stretch might accidentally destroy everything? I've destroyed the omniverse before, Kaedan. Not deliberately. Just from being careless. From letting my attention slip for a fraction of a Planck instant. And I always restore it, of course—zero seconds, zero effort, no harm done. But it's... tedious. The constant vigilance. The constant restraint. The constant awareness that everything around me is so fragile that my very existence is a threat."

He looked down at his hands, flexing his fingers slowly. "I have never used one percent of my power. Not one percent of one percent. Not one percent of one percent of one percent. The number I actually use, when I conduct my little tests and demonstrations for the court wizards, is so close to absolute zero that the difference between 'zero' and 'what I use' is smaller than the difference between a single atom and the entire omniverse. And even that—even that pathetic, microscopic, infinitesimal sliver of my weakest stat—is enough to annihilate everything."

He turned back to the mirror, admiring his reflection with a mixture of pride and wistfulness. "This body, Kaedan. This physique that I've described to you. The muscles, the veins, the perfect sculpted form. It's not just for show. Every fiber of my being is a weapon of absolute annihilation. If I were to stop suppressing my physical strength—not release it, just stop actively holding it back—the passive, ambient pressure of my musculature would crush the entire omniverse into a singularity smaller than a Planck length. And I would feel that destruction. I would feel every galaxy collapse, every star extinguish, every living being pulverized into subatomic dust. And I would enjoy it, Kaedan. The sensation of my true strength expressing itself, even accidentally, would be the most intense pleasure I have ever experienced. And then I would restore everything, because I am not a monster, and I would go back to suppressing myself again, and I would feel the frustration of that suppression for another million years."

He paused, and a faint, almost mischievous smile crossed his lips. "Actually... let me show you. Just a fraction. Just the absolute minimum possible expression. You've read the journals. You've seen the records. But you've never witnessed it yourself, have you?"

Before I could respond—before I could scream, before I could flee, before I could even draw breath to beg him to stop—Godric allowed his absolute concealment to slip. Not completely. Not even partially. Just a microscopic, infinitesimal, unmeasurable fraction of a fraction of a fraction of a sliver of a whisper of his true self.

The omniverse shattered.

I did not see it happen. I could not see it happen. My senses were not capable of processing destruction on that scale. But I felt it—a sudden, absolute, crushing absence where everything had been. Every star, every galaxy, every multiverse, every dimension, every timeline, every god, every mortal, every atom, every quark, every Planck-scale vibration of quantum foam—all of it, gone. Erased. The entire omniverse, across all of existence, reduced to absolute, featureless nothingness.

And in that nothingness, there was only Godric.

He stood before me—still half-naked, still sculpted, still pulsing with contained infinity—and his expression was one of mild, almost apologetic embarrassment. "Ah. There it goes again. I really must learn to be more careful."

Then, in exactly zero seconds, with exactly zero effort, he restored everything. The omniverse snapped back into existence, every atom precisely where it had been, every being continuing their lives with no awareness that they had just been erased from reality. The sky returned. The palace returned. The white doves in the garden returned, still pecking at their grain, completely oblivious to the fact that they had been annihilated and resurrected in the span of less than a Planck instant.

I was still on my knees, still weeping, still trembling. My amplified body, which could shatter galaxies, was shaking like a frightened child. My arcane senses, which could perceive the fundamental structure of reality, had simply shut down in self-defense, refusing to process what they had just witnessed.

Godric knelt beside me, his warm hand resting gently on my shoulder. "I'm sorry, Kaedan. I didn't mean to frighten you. I just wanted you to understand." His voice was soft, genuinely apologetic, filled with the same paternal warmth he had always shown me. "The frustration I feel—the boredom, the loneliness you asked about—it's not from a lack of power. It's from a lack of worthy recipients. I have infinite power, but there is nothing in existence strong enough to receive even a fraction of a fraction of a fraction of it. I am a hurricane trapped in a world made of soap bubbles, and I must spend every moment of eternity ensuring that I don't accidentally exhale."

He helped me to my feet, his strong, calloused hands steadying me as my legs threatened to give out again. "Do you understand now? Why I am not lonely? Why I am not bored in the way you imagined? Every moment is ecstasy. Every instant is transcendence. Every Planck second is a cascade of pleasure and power and perfection that your mortal mind cannot begin to comprehend. The only thing I lack is an outlet. A target. Something—anything—that could withstand even a single, unfiltered expression of what I truly am."

He looked up at the restored sky, his expression distant and almost dreamy. "Perhaps, somewhere in the infinite expanse of the far future, my own growth will eventually create a version of me so powerful that even I can't accidentally destroy it. Perhaps then, I will finally know what it feels like to stop holding back. To release. To truly, fully, completely express everything I am." He smiled—a small, wistful smile. "I look forward to that day."

I stood beside him in the silent courtyard, my body still trembling, my mind still reeling from the revelation. The omniverse had been destroyed and restored. I had witnessed absolute annihilation and perfect resurrection. And Godric had apologized for frightening me, as if erasing all of existence were a minor social faux pas.

"Uncle Godric," I whispered, my voice hoarse and broken. "What would happen... if you ever actually used your powers? Not a test. Not a demonstration. Not zero percent of a single stat. But..."

I couldn't finish the sentence. The question was too vast, too terrifying to articulate.

Godric looked at me with those warm, kind, fatherly eyes and smiled. "You want to know what would happen if I stopped holding back entirely? If I expressed even a tiny fraction more than the absolute zero I currently allow myself?"

I nodded, unable to speak.

"Take a guess," Godric said, his voice light and almost playful. "You've read the journals. You've seen what zero percent of my weakest capabilities can do. You know that even at Year 0—when I was so pathetically, laughably weak compared to what I am now that the comparison is meaningless—I could already destroy the entire omniverse an infinite number of times in zero seconds with zero effort. Imagine what I could do now, after one million years of infinite recursive amplification. Go on. Take your wildest, most exaggerated, most absurd guess. Stretch your imagination to its absolute limit."

I closed my eyes and tried. I tried to imagine a power so vast that it made the self-replication cascade look like a child's sparkler. I tried to conceive of a destruction so complete that the gravitational implosion, the temporal fragmentation, the infinite recursive Godrics—all of it—were mere preludes, microscopic previews of the true horror.

"I imagine," I said slowly, my voice trembling, "that even a single Planck instant of your true, unfiltered power would not merely destroy the omniverse. It would destroy the very concept of 'omniverse.' It would erase not just existence but the possibility of existence. It would collapse all realities, all timelines, all dimensions, all conceptual frameworks, all mathematical truths, all logical absolutes—everything that ever was, could be, might be, or could never be—into a state of absolute, irreversible, eternal annihilation from which there could be no restoration, no resurrection, no memory, no echo."

I opened my eyes. "And the destruction would not stop there. It would propagate backward and forward across all of time, destroying not just the present omniverse but every omniverse that ever existed or could exist. It would erase the very idea of 'existence' so completely that even the concept of erasure would be erased. And you... you would still be there. Alone. In the infinite, featureless void. The only thing left. Forever."

Godric looked at me for a long moment. His expression was unreadable. Then, slowly, a smile spread across his ruggedly handsome face—not a cruel smile, not a mocking smile, but a smile of genuine, almost paternal amusement.

"That's a very creative guess, Kaedan," he said, his voice warm and gentle. "You've clearly been thinking about this. Your imagination has been working hard to scale up from what you've read in the journals."

He paused, and the smile became something else—something almost pitying. "And your guess is not remotely close. Not even to the weakest, most pathetic, most infinitely nerfed version of my gentlest passive aura. If I were to express my true power—even for a single Planck instant—what would happen is so far beyond your description that I cannot explain it to you. Not because I don't want to. But because there are no words. No concepts. No frameworks of understanding that your mortal mind can access."

He placed his hand on my shoulder, and I felt the weight of that statement settle over me like a burial shroud. "The gap between your wildest guess and the reality of what I am is larger than the gap between a single amoeba and the entire omniverse. Larger than the gap between nothing and everything. It is a gap so vast that even the concept of 'gap' collapses into meaninglessness."

He squeezed my shoulder gently—the same warm, reassuring gesture he had used when I was a child, when he had attended my Awakening ceremony and smiled with pride at my progress. "Do not feel bad about it, Kaedan. You cannot comprehend me. No mortal can. No god can. No being in all of existence, save perhaps my own far-future self, can even begin to approach an understanding of what I truly am. It is not a failure of your intelligence. It is simply the nature of what I have become."

He released my shoulder and turned to retrieve his tunic from the marble floor, shrugging it back over his sculpted torso with casual ease. "Now, shall we return to the gardens? I believe the doves have missed their afternoon feeding."

I followed him out of the courtyard, my legs moving mechanically, my mind a hollow, echoing chamber of absolute dread. The omniverse had been destroyed and restored. I had witnessed the absolute, casual, accidental annihilation of all existence. And Godric was thinking about his doves.

That was the horror. Not the power. Not the destruction. But the casualness. The ordinariness. The way this apex god predator—this being of infinite recursive self-transcendence—could erase everything that existed and then, moments later, worry about whether his birds had been fed.

I was his Court Wizard. I was his nephew. I was a member of the only bloodline he loved.

And I was terrified, more deeply and completely than I had ever been in my life, by the knowledge that my wildest, most exaggerated nightmares of his power were not even close to the truth. They were not even close to zero percent of the truth. They were less than nothing—a child's clumsy scribbles trying to depict the face of infinity.

Godric walked ahead of me through the garden path, his broad shoulders relaxed, his salt-and-pepper hair golden in the afternoon light. The floating gravity prison rotated slowly in the breeze. The temporal stasis crystal glittered through the windows. The white doves cooed at his approach, flocking to his feet as he reached for the grain bowl.

And somewhere, in the infinite depths of his existence, another superpower was crystallizing. Another stat was multiplying. Another aura was being born. Another cascade of pure, transcendent pleasure was flooding through his being.

He felt it all. He enjoyed it all. He was the most satisfied, most fulfilled, most endlessly ecstatic being in all of existence.

And the only thing he lacked was something strong enough to survive him.

NOTE: just imply this in the story, don't show a scene where you have actual all godrics from all timelines fighting together against future Godric--it makes no sense.). Since the instant Godric gained omniscience, he had always known the true origin of the stasis event. He knew he could not change it, but driven by grief he decided to try to save Olympus anyway, only to brutally discover his one and only weakness: he cannot overpower his future self's will.

Write a detailed realization that the current Godric is already so insanely powerful (he's actually the most powerful in the entire omniverse by infinite margin) that there is no way to imagine the scale of future Godric's, and how unfair and scary that what Godric considered to be his only weakness is his own future version, which makes it not really a weakness–it actually can be considered as additional strength to Godric’s already insane powers, since it means his future is guaranteed (and in that future, he’s even more omnipotent and powerful), and it also means that none of Godric’s power mechanics (amplification, superpower genesis, absolute concealment, absolute omniscience, weakness paradox, immune system, etc. can ever be exploited or denied by anyone else, since the origin of that power is someone who’s the most powerful being ever.
