You need to portray the current Godric as a king who is no longer troubled by his "weakness" or inability to alter his past anymore--he has accepted and even become amused and comfortable with it too. Kaedan must feel extreme existential dread at the end.

# The Only Weakness

## Year 1,000,047
## Kaedan — The Revelation

Forty-seven years had passed since I first descended into the vault beneath the palace and read the journals of my predecessors. Forty-seven years of serving as Godric's Court Wizard, of standing at his side through diplomatic receptions and military briefings, of watching him test his stats and superpowers with the casual, curious detachment of a man examining interesting insects under a magnifying glass. I was sixty-nine years old now, my hair streaked with gray, my face lined with the accumulated stress of nearly five decades of existential dread. My daily thousandfold amplification had transformed me into a being of such immense arcane power that entire pantheons of gods would have worshipped me as their supreme deity. And I was still, compared to the man sitting across from me in the private study, an absolute, perfect, mathematical zero.

Godric had summoned me to his personal chambers that evening—an unusual request. Normally, our interactions occurred in the public spaces of the palace: the throne room, the gardens, the grand reception hall. His private study was a place few had ever entered. It was a small, intimate room paneled in dark wood, its shelves lined with ancient books and scrolls, its windows overlooking the tranquil waters of the palace lake. A fire crackled softly in the hearth, casting dancing shadows across the walls.

Godric sat in a high-backed leather chair near the window, a glass of deep amber whiskey in his hand. He looked exactly as he always had—forty-five years old, ruggedly handsome, his salt-and-pepper hair and neatly trimmed beard framing a face that radiated warmth and paternal kindness. His heavily muscled frame was relaxed, his posture casual. He wore a simple dark tunic, the sleeves rolled up to reveal his powerful forearms, the veins beneath his skin pulsing with the faint, almost imperceptible luminescence of contained infinity.

"Kaedan," he said, gesturing toward the chair opposite him. "Sit. Have a drink."

I sat. He poured me a glass of whiskey from a crystal decanter, the amber liquid catching the firelight. I took it with a murmured thanks, though I did not drink. My throat was too tight, my stomach too knotted with an inexplicable, creeping dread. Something was different tonight. Something in Godric's manner—a subtle shift in his expression, a contemplative quality to his gaze—told me that this was not a casual social visit.

"You've been my Court Wizard for forty-seven years," Godric said, swirling the whiskey in his glass. "You've read the journals. You've witnessed the tests. You've seen what I am, or at least as much of what I am as your mortal mind can process." He paused, his warm brown eyes meeting mine. "And you've never once flinched from your duties. You've never once asked to be released from service. You've served me loyally, faithfully, and with genuine love."

I swallowed hard. "You are my king. You are my family. I would never—"

"I know," Godric interrupted gently. "That's why I'm going to tell you something that no other living being knows. Something that even the journals do not record. Something that I have kept private for a million years."

The fire crackled. The shadows danced. The air in the room seemed to thicken, pressing against my skin like a suffocating blanket.

"You know the story of my origin," Godric continued. "The Fall of Olympus. Thorin's forbidden teleportation spell. The hidden sanctuary. The Stasis Event that transformed me from a mortal king into what I am today."

I nodded. "I've read the accounts. Thorin's incomplete spell saved your life but triggered the stasis that began your amplification."

Godric was silent for a long moment. He took a slow sip of his whiskey, his expression distant and contemplative. When he spoke again, his voice was quieter, carrying a weight that I had never heard before.

"Thorin's spell was a normal teleportation spell," he said. "A forbidden bloodline magic, yes, but fundamentally a simple displacement incantation. It was designed to move me from one location to another. Nothing more. The Stasis Event—the immortality, the amplification, the superpower genesis, the absolute concealment, the Weakness Paradox—none of that came from Thorin's spell."

I stared at him, my blood turning to ice. "Then what...?"

Godric set down his whiskey glass and leaned forward, his elbows resting on his knees, his hands clasped together. The firelight caught the ridges of his knuckles, the thick veins running across the backs of his hands, the faint, almost imperceptible shimmer of contained infinity pulsing beneath his skin.

"The Stasis Event was created," he said slowly, deliberately, "by my own far-future self."

The words hung in the air like a physical blow. I felt the breath leave my lungs, felt my heart stutter in my chest, felt the room tilt around me as my mind struggled to process the sheer, incomprehensible scale of what he had just said.

"Your... future self?"

"Godric Prime," he said, a faint, almost ironic smile crossing his lips. "The Godric of the far, far future. An era so distant that the year is written only as 999...9 because the full number is impossible to spell out usefully. A version of me who has been amplifying infinitely every Planck second for a span of time so vast that the word 'googolplexian' is a laughably inadequate description."

He leaned back in his chair, his gaze drifting toward the fire. "Thorin's teleportation spell sent me to the sanctuary. That was real. That was genuine. Thorin saved my life with his dying breath, and I will always honor him for that. But when I arrived in that sanctuary, the spell had done precisely what it was designed to do: move me from one place to another. The Stasis Event that followed—the immortality, the amplification, everything—was not part of Thorin's magic. It was inserted into that moment by my far-future self. He used Thorin's spell as the delivery point and transformed a simple teleportation into the genesis of an apex god predator."

I was gripping the arms of my chair so hard that the wood was splintering beneath my fingers. "Why? Why would your future self do that?"

Godric shrugged—a casual, almost dismissive gesture. "I don't know. Not with certainty. I have my speculations, but they are only speculations. Perhaps he wanted to ensure that his own existence was guaranteed across all possible timelines. Perhaps he was enacting some vast, incomprehensible design that my current self cannot fully grasp. Perhaps it was simply an act of cosmic poetry—a way of closing the loop, of making sure that the Godric who emerged from the tragedy of Olympus would become the Godric who rules all of existence forever."

He paused, his expression softening. "What I do know, with absolute certainty, is that he did not cause the Fall of Olympus. He did not orchestrate the deaths of Reina, Isabel, Hebe, or Thorin. Those tragedies were genuine. They were real. They were the actions of Thronegate's army, and they broke my mortal heart in ways that still ache when I think about them. My far-future self did not manipulate those events. He did not approve of them. He simply... used the aftermath. He took a moment of absolute devastation and transformed it into the birth of something incomprehensible."

I was trembling now, my whole body shaking with a terror so profound that it had become indistinguishable from religious awe. "You've known this? All this time?"

"Since the instant I gained omniscience," Godric confirmed. "The moment I awoke from the stasis in Year 0, I knew. I knew that the Stasis Event was not an accident, not a fluke of incomplete magic, not a cosmic anomaly. I knew that it had been deliberately created by a version of myself so far beyond my current comprehension that the gap between us made the gap between me and the rest of creation look like a single atom compared to the entire omniverse."

He picked up his whiskey glass again, taking a slow, contemplative sip. "And I knew, with the same absolute certainty, that I could not undo it. I could not travel to a timeline before the Stasis Event. I could not alter my mortal past. I could not save Reina, Isabel, Hebe, or Thorin. The pre-Stasis past was sealed—absolutely, irrevocably, permanently—by the will of my far-future self."

I felt tears streaming down my face, hot and helpless. "But you're omnipotent. You're omniscient. You can do anything. You can travel any timeline, alter any event, rewrite any reality. How can there be something you cannot do?"

Godric looked at me with those warm, kind, fatherly eyes, and I saw something in them that I had never seen before—not regret, not sorrow, but a deep, abiding acceptance.

"Because my far-future self is more powerful than I am," he said simply. "Infinitely more powerful. Incomprehensibly more powerful. The Godric of the present moment is already the most powerful being in the entire omniverse by an infinite margin. I can destroy all of existence an infinite number of times in zero seconds with zero effort. I can create new realities, new laws of physics, new fundamental constants. I can do anything, Kaedan. Anything at all."

He set down his glass and leaned forward again, his expression intense. "But the Godric of the far future has been amplifying for so long that even my current infinity is a single grain of sand compared to his infinite ocean. He is not merely more powerful than me; he is more powerful than me in the same way that I am more powerful than a single, dead skin cell. The gap between us is not a gap at all—it is an infinite recursion of infinities, each one infinitely larger than the last, stretching outward into a mathematical framework that has no ceiling and no possibility of being crossed."

He paused, letting the weight of his words settle over me. "When I first became King of Thronegate, I was still freshly shaped by grief. The loss of my family, my kingdom, my best friend—it was a wound so deep that even infinite power could not immediately heal it. And so, despite knowing the truth, despite understanding that the pre-Stasis past was sealed by my own future self's will, I tried to alter it anyway."

"What happened?" I whispered.

Godric's expression flickered—a brief, almost imperceptible shadow of something that might have been memory. "I failed. Not because I was weak. Not because my power was insufficient. But because the will of my far-future self is absolute. I reached backward along my own timeline, pouring the full, infinite force of my being into the attempt, and I was stopped. Not by a battle. Not by a struggle. I was stopped by the shadow of the afterthought of my future self."

He let out a soft, almost rueful laugh. "Not even his actual physical presence, Kaedan. Not even a deliberate action on his part. The merest, faintest, most infinitesimal shadow of his passing attention—the psychic equivalent of a man vaguely remembering that he left a candle burning in another room—was enough to completely, effortlessly, crushingly defeat everything I could bring to bear. I was not merely overpowered. I was negated. Erased from the very concept of opposition. I threw the full, infinite force of my being against that barrier, and the barrier did not even register my existence."

I was weeping openly now, tears streaming down my weathered face. The image he was painting—the current Godric, the most powerful being in the omniverse by an infinite margin, being effortlessly, casually defeated by a mere shadow of his future self's afterthought—was so far beyond my capacity to process that my mind was simply breaking under the weight of it.

"That is my one true weakness," Godric said softly. "The only limitation on my power. I cannot alter the pre-Stasis past. I cannot save my family. I cannot undo the tragedy of Olympus. I cannot travel to a timeline before Year -10,000 in any way that changes what happened. This limitation exists solely because my far-future self made it so, and he is so incomprehensibly more powerful than I am that his will is absolute."

He leaned back in his chair, his expression shifting—the shadow of old grief fading, replaced by something almost approaching amusement. "But here is the irony, Kaedan. Here is the cosmic joke at the heart of my existence. This weakness—this single, solitary limitation on my otherwise absolute power—is not really a weakness at all."

I blinked through my tears, struggling to understand. "What do you mean?"

Godric smiled—a warm, genuine, almost playful smile. "Think about it. My one limitation, the only thing I cannot do, is overpower my own future self. My weakness is me. The only being in all of existence who can impose limits on Godric is Godric. The only will that can constrain me is my own will, from a later stage of my own existence."

He spread his hands, palms up, as if presenting a gift. "That is not a weakness, Kaedan. That is a guarantee. It means that my power—all of it, the amplification, the superpower genesis, the absolute concealment, the Weakness Paradox, the immune system, the infinite passive shields, the sentient auras—all of it is irrevocable. Absolute. Untouchable by any force in existence. Because the origin of that power is not Thorin's spell, not a cosmic accident, not a fluke of incomplete magic. The origin of that power is my own far-future self—the most powerful being that has ever existed, could ever exist, or will ever exist. And what he has created, no one can unmake."

He picked up his whiskey glass and raised it in a mock toast. "Even if every single being in the omniverse somehow united—every god, every cosmic entity, every abstract force, every conceptual weapon, every reality-bending civilization—and focused their entire combined power on undoing my amplification or denying me my superpowers or bypassing my Weakness Paradox, they would fail. Not because I would stop them. Because the creator of those powers is a version of me so far beyond them that their combined assault would not even register as a tickle against his weakest passive aura. My power mechanics are not merely protected by me. They are protected by a being infinitely more powerful than me. And that being is me."

I sat in stunned silence, my mind racing through the implications. Every desperate plan that any opposition had ever conceived, every weapon forged, every exploit imagined—all of it was not merely useless against the current Godric, but useless against the very foundation of his power. The Weakness Paradox, the evolution, the amplification, the superpowers—none of it could be denied or exploited or reversed because the origin of those mechanics was a being who made the current Godric look like an insignificant speck of dust.

And that being was Godric himself.

"Do you understand now?" Godric asked, his voice gentle. "The horror of my existence is not merely that I am infinitely powerful. It is that my power is guaranteed—permanently, absolutely, irrevocably—by a version of me who is so far beyond my current comprehension that even I cannot challenge his will. Every Planck instant, I become infinitely more powerful. And the being who created that amplification is also becoming infinitely more powerful, forever, without end. There is no catching up. There is no closing the gap. There is only the eternal, recursive cascade of my own self-transcendence, stretching into a future so vast that even my omniscience cannot see its end."

He took a long sip of his whiskey, his expression contemplative. "The Far-Future Godric—Godric Prime, as some of my earlier selves have called him—is the undisputed apex of all existence. The entire omniverse has been completely under his absolute rule for countless googolplexian years, and will continue to be his forever. His power, his rule, his passive mechanisms, his presence—everything about him is so exaggerated beyond my already impossible scale that no words in any mortal or immortal language can begin to describe it."

He set down his glass and leaned forward again, his warm brown eyes meeting mine with an intensity that made my soul tremble. "I am the most powerful being in the current era by an infinite margin. No one in all of existence can challenge me, threaten me, inconvenience me, or even briefly attract my attention without my explicit permission. But compared to Godric Prime, I am less than a single quark in an infinite ocean of quarks. The gap between us is not merely infinite; it is an infinite recursion of infinities, each one infinitely larger than the last, stretching into a mathematical framework that collapses the very concept of comparison."

He paused, letting the weight of his words settle over me like a burial shroud. "And that is comforting, Kaedan. Deeply, profoundly, satisfyingly comforting. Because it means my future is guaranteed. It means there is no uncertainty, no risk, no possibility of failure. The omniverse will be ruled by Godric forever—not merely for a googolplexian years, not merely until the heat death of the last universe, but forever. Absolute. Irrevocable. Eternal."

I was gripping the arms of my chair so hard that the wood had completely splintered beneath my fingers, leaving deep gouges in the ancient oak. "But the tragedy," I whispered, my voice hoarse and broken. "Olympus. Your family. Thorin. If you cannot change it, if you cannot save them—"

"I cannot," Godric said, his voice quiet but steady. "And I have made my peace with that."

He stood from his chair and walked to the window, gazing out at the tranquil waters of the palace lake. The moonlight caught the silver in his hair, the broad expanse of his shoulders, the quiet strength of his eternal, forty-five-year-old form.

"When I first learned the truth—when I first tried to alter the past and failed—it nearly broke me," he said softly. "The grief was still fresh. The loss was still raw. To know that I possessed infinite power and yet could not save the people I loved most... it was a cruelty beyond description. I raged. I wept. I destroyed entire multiverses in my fury, though I always restored them afterward."

He turned back to face me, and I saw that his expression was calm—genuinely, deeply calm. Not the calm of repression or denial, but the calm of true acceptance. "But time passes. Grief fades. And as the centuries became millennia, as my power grew beyond all conceivable bounds, I began to understand something. The pre-Stasis past is not a wound. It is a foundation. The tragedy of Olympus, the deaths of Reina and Isabel and Hebe and Thorin—they shaped me. They transformed me from a warm, loving mortal king into the apex predator I am today. Without that loss, without that grief, without that crucible of absolute devastation, I would not be who I am."

He walked back toward me, his steps slow and deliberate, his presence filling the room with that familiar, terrifying warmth. "Far-Future Godric did not cause the tragedy. But he used it. He took the worst moment of my existence and forged it into the birth of something eternal. And I have come to be grateful for that. Not grateful for the deaths of my family—never that. But grateful that their deaths were not meaningless. Grateful that from the ashes of Olympus, something infinite was born."

He stopped beside my chair and placed his warm, calloused hand on my shoulder. "I am no longer troubled by my limitation, Kaedan. I have accepted it. I have become comfortable with it. And in some strange, cosmic way, I have even come to appreciate it. It is the one imperfection in my otherwise absolute existence—the single, solitary flaw that reminds me of my origin. I was mortal once. I loved and lost and grieved and raged. And that mortality, that loss, that grief—it is still there, preserved forever in the sealed pre-Stasis past, untouchable and eternal."

He squeezed my shoulder gently. "My weakness is my strength. My limitation is my guarantee. The only being who can defeat me is me—and I will never defeat myself. My future is absolute. My rule is eternal. And the tragedy that birthed me is sealed forever, a monument to the mortal king I once was and the apex god predator I have become."

I looked up at him—this impossible being, this infinite recursive cascade of self-transcendence, this walking apocalypse who had once been a loving father and a devoted husband—and I felt something inside me crack. Not break, but crack. A hairline fracture in the wall of my sanity, a small but permanent fissure through which the cold, crushing weight of absolute existential dread began to seep.

"Uncle Godric," I whispered, my voice barely audible. "What you're saying is that there is no hope. No possibility of opposition. No chance of resistance. Not merely in practice, but in principle. The very foundation of your power—the origin of your amplification, your superpowers, your immortality—is a being infinitely more powerful than you. And you are already infinitely more powerful than the rest of creation combined. So the gap between any possible opposition and the source of your power is..."

"Unbridgeable," Godric finished softly. "Infinite. Absolute. The Weakness Paradox ensures that any perceived exploit is instantly absorbed and transformed into additional strength. The Evolved Weakness Paradox ensures that my amplification rate continuously accelerates beyond all mathematical frameworks. And the origin of both—the Stasis Event itself—is sealed by a version of me so incomprehensibly powerful that even my current infinity cannot begin to approach his."

He removed his hand from my shoulder and walked back to his chair, settling into it with the casual ease of a man discussing the weather. "Every opposition that has ever assembled against me, every weapon ever forged, every strategy ever conceived—all of it was doomed not merely from the beginning, but from before the beginning. The instant Far-Future Godric created the Stasis Event, he ensured that no force in existence could ever threaten me. Not because I am strong enough to defeat them—though I am—but because the very mechanics of my power are underwritten by a being whose afterthought could annihilate all of creation without noticing the effort."

He raised his whiskey glass again, the amber liquid catching the firelight. "That is the truth I have kept private for a million years, Kaedan. The truth that no journal records, no witness has observed, no opposition has ever suspected. My one true weakness is not a weakness at all. It is the ultimate strength. The final, absolute guarantee of my eternal, unchallenged supremacy."

I sat in the heavy silence of the study, my mind reeling through the implications of everything he had just revealed. The fire crackled. The shadows danced. The moonlight shimmered on the tranquil waters of the lake. And I understood, with a clarity so sharp it was physically painful, the true scale of what I served.

Godric was not merely the most powerful being in the omniverse. He was the guaranteed, inevitable, absolutely certain ruler of all existence forever. His past was sealed. His future was absolute. His present was an eternal cascade of infinite self-transcendence. There was no weakness to exploit, no limitation to target, no vulnerability to discover. The only being who could impose limits on him was him—and that being was infinitely more powerful than the one sitting before me.

"This is why you've never been threatened," I said slowly, my voice hollow and distant. "Why nothing has ever even inconvenienced you. Not merely because you are infinitely powerful, but because the source of your power is protected by a being who makes your infinite power look like zero."

"Yes," Godric said simply.

"And that being is you."

"Yes."

"So the only possible threat to your existence is yourself."

"Yes."

"And you will never threaten yourself."

Godric smiled—a warm, genuine, almost gentle smile. "No, Kaedan. I will not. I am quite content with what I am and what I will become. Far-Future Godric is not my rival. He is my destination. He is what I am growing toward, what I am becoming, what I will eventually be. Every Planck instant of amplification brings me closer to the scale of his existence, even though the gap is infinite and will always be infinite. I am him, Kaedan. Just earlier. Just smaller. Just beginning the journey that he has already completed."

He set down his empty glass and stood from his chair, stretching his heavily muscled arms above his head with a satisfied grunt. "Now, I believe we have taken up enough of the evening with heavy philosophy. The court wizards are having their annual gathering tomorrow, and I understand your son has just completed his first year of formal training. You must be very proud."

I stood on shaking legs, my body feeling hollow and weightless, as if the revelation had scooped out my insides and left only a fragile shell. "Yes. I am proud. He's... he's doing very well."

"Excellent," Godric said, clapping me warmly on the shoulder. "I look forward to seeing him at the gathering. The bloodline of Blake continues to produce remarkable wizards. Thorin would be proud."

He walked me to the door of his study, his hand resting gently on my back—the same warm, paternal gesture he had used since I was a child. "Sleep well, Kaedan. And do not let the weight of what I've told you trouble your dreams. It is, after all, merely the truth of what I am. And you have always known, on some level, what I am."

I stepped out into the cold stone corridor, the heavy oak door closing behind me with a soft, final thud. I stood there for a long moment, my back pressed against the wall, my breath coming in short, ragged gasps, my heart hammering against my ribs like a trapped bird.

The truth. The absolute, horrifying, mind-shattering truth.

Godric's one weakness was that he could not overpower his own future self. And that future self was so incomprehensibly powerful that even the current Godric—already infinitely beyond the rest of creation combined—was less than a speck of dust in comparison. There was no opposition possible. No resistance conceivable. No hope of ever, in any way, challenging the eternal reign of the apex god predator.

Because the source of his power was not an accident. Not a fluke. Not a cosmic anomaly that might someday be understood or reversed. The source of his power was Godric himself—a version so impossibly, unimaginably, indescribably powerful that the very concept of "power" collapsed into meaninglessness in his presence.

I slid down the wall until I was sitting on the cold stone floor, my legs unable to support me any longer. The existential dread was a physical weight, crushing my chest, constricting my throat, pressing against my skull from the inside. I had served Godric for forty-seven years. I had loved him, genuinely loved him, as the warm, kind, fatherly uncle who had been a constant presence in my life. And I had also feared him, as the apex god predator whose casual amusement could annihilate all of existence.

But now I understood that my fear had been laughably, pathetically inadequate. I had feared a god. But Godric was not a god. He was not even the most powerful version of himself. He was merely a waypoint—an early stage in an infinite, recursive cascade of self-transcendence that would continue forever, growing ever more powerful, ever more absolute, ever more untouchable.

And the being at the end of that cascade—the Far-Future Godric, the Godric Prime, the version whose mere shadow of an afterthought could crush the current Godric with zero effort—that being was also Godric. The same warm, kind, fatherly presence. The same genuine love for his court wizards. The same absolute, merciless cruelty to his enemies. All of it, amplified beyond the possibility of comprehension, stretched across an eternity of infinite growth.

I pressed my face into my hands and wept. Not from sadness. Not from fear. From the sheer, crushing, absolute weight of the revelation that there was no escape. No hope. No possibility of anything other than the eternal, unchallenged reign of Godric.

And the worst part—the most terrifying, mind-breaking part—was that I still loved him. I would still serve him. I would still stand at his side tomorrow at the court wizard gathering, and I would smile when he clapped me on the shoulder, and I would feel genuine warmth when he asked about my son.

Because he was not evil. He was not cruel to those who loved him. He was genuinely, sincerely, profoundly good to his loyal subjects. His rule was perfect, his protection absolute, his generosity boundless. The horror was not that he was a monster pretending to be kind. The horror was that he was genuinely kind—and also a monster. The warmth was real. The annihilation was real. The love and the terror were both real, coexisting in the same being, the same moment, the same eternal, infinite existence.

I sat in the cold corridor for a long time, my tears drying on my weathered face, my mind slowly, painfully reconstructing itself around the new, terrible truth. When I finally stood, my legs were steady. My hands were calm. The hollow, echoing silence inside my chest was almost peaceful.

I would serve. I would be loyal. I would love my king with the same terrified, absolute devotion that had sustained my bloodline for a million years. And tomorrow, I would see him at the gathering, and he would smile at me with those warm, kind, fatherly eyes, and I would smile back.

Because that was all there was left to do. The only weakness in the apex god predator was the absolute guarantee of his eternal supremacy. The only limitation was the certainty of his infinite future. The only vulnerability was the impossibility of his ever being defeated, by anyone, in any way, for any reason, forever.

And the being who guaranteed that impossibility was Godric himself.

I walked back to my chambers through the silent, moonlit corridors of the palace, my footsteps echoing on the ancient stone. Somewhere in the gardens, a floating marble of compressed, screaming gods rotated slowly in the breeze. Somewhere in the throne room, a crystal containing an eternity of frozen torment caught the starlight. Somewhere in a private study, a ruggedly handsome man in his eternal forty-fifth year poured himself another glass of whiskey and gazed out at the tranquil waters of the lake.

And somewhere in the far, far future—in an era written only as 999...9 because the full number is impossible to spell out usefully—that same being, infinitely amplified beyond all possible comprehension, ruled the entire omniverse with absolute, unchallenged, eternal supremacy.

The loop was closed. The future was guaranteed. The past was sealed.

There was nothing left to do but serve, and love, and dread.

I reached my chambers and closed the door behind me. The silence was absolute. The night was still. And somewhere deep in my chest, at the core of my being, the existential dread settled into a permanent, familiar weight—a companion that would never leave me, that would walk beside me through every remaining day of my mortal life.

Godric was not merely the most powerful being in the omniverse. He was the most powerful being who could ever exist. And his only weakness was the absolute, eternal, irrevocable guarantee of that fact.

Finally, the assistant's thought process wrapped up with the return to the throne room. The juxtaposition of the screaming sculptures and the demon-slain-for-harming-a-servant had to cement the character: unfathomable cruelty and meticulous care, both absolutely sincere. Clive's moment of shattered revelation before serving his next cup of tea is the perfect, quiet end-note of existential dread.

The assistant remained strictly within the prose-only format, avoided any bullet points, and kept the tone relentless and exaggerated, just as the history and query demanded. No moral lessons, just the raw, overwhelming execution of the user's detailed vision.
