# The Tyrant's Gentleness

## Year 999...9
## Clive — The Eternal Reign

The year is a number so vast that writing it out would consume more matter than exists in the observable omniverse. If I were to attempt to spell it—to record each digit in sequence—the resulting string would stretch across decillions of multiverses, wrapping around galaxies and threading through the spaces between realities like an infinite serpent of mathematical impossibility. The number has not merely exceeded comprehension; it has exceeded the very concept of "number" as a meaningful framework. It is a notation of eternity, a placeholder for a span of time so incomprehensibly vast that the entire history of creation from the Big Bang to the heat death of the last universe represents less than a single Planck instant in comparison.

I am Clive. I am fifty years old. I am the Court Wizard of Thronegate, a direct descendant of Blake, the legendary merchant who accidentally shattered the temporal seal ten thousand years before Year Zero and unleashed the apex predator of reality upon the cosmos. My bloodline has served Godric for so long that the word "eternity" is a laughable understatement. My ancestors wrote journals—thousands upon thousands of journals—documenting their observations of his power, their terror at his capabilities, their desperate attempts to process the impossible scale of what they witnessed. I have read them all. Every single one. And I know, with the absolute certainty of inherited trauma, that the Godric my ancestors described—the Godric of Year 25,000, Year 100,000, Year 1,000,000—was, by the standards of the being I serve today, pathetically, laughably, incomprehensibly weak.

The Godric I serve has been amplifying infinitely every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second for a span of time so vast that the amplification itself has evolved beyond the concept of "amplification" into something fundamentally unrecognizable. His power is no longer a quantity that can be measured, compared, or even conceptualized. It is an absolute, a constant of existence so fundamental that the omniverse itself has restructured its basic laws around his presence, accommodating his infinite recursion as a fish accommodates water.

I have served him for thirty years. In that time, I have not once witnessed him exert effort. I have not once seen him express even the faintest whisper of his true capabilities. I have not once observed anything that could be described as a "test" or "demonstration" of his power—because there is nothing left to test against. No opposition exists. No resistance is conceivable. No being in all of creation would dare to even form the thought of challenging him.

This is not because Godric has altered free will. He has not. He genuinely believes in mortal resilience, in the capacity of sentient beings to choose their own paths. The reason no one dares to oppose him is far simpler and far more horrifying: creation has learned. After an incomprehensible span of existence under his absolute rule, every single sentient being in the omniverse has come to understand, with bone-deep, soul-level certainty, the absolute futility of opposition. It is not merely that Godric cannot be defeated. It is that the very concept of "defeating Godric" is a logical contradiction so profound that even contemplating it induces immediate, paralyzing existential collapse.

The last attempt at opposition occurred so long ago that the memory of it has faded from all but the oldest cosmic archives. A coalition of abstract entities—beings who had evolved beyond physical form, beyond temporal existence, beyond the very concept of "being" as mortals understand it—attempted to create a weapon that would sever Godric's connection to the fundamental fabric of reality. They spent googolplexian years designing this weapon, operating in the spaces between thoughts, hiding in the gaps between Planck instants. They believed they were undetected. They believed they had found a genuine exploit.

Godric was aware of them before they formed their first coherent thought. He had known of their eventual existence before the Big Bang. He had watched them evolve, watched them plan, watched them build their impossible weapon with the gentle, patient amusement of a father watching his child construct a sandcastle. When they finally activated their weapon—a device designed to isolate Godric from the omniversal substrate and trap him in a bubble of absolute non-existence—he allowed it to wash over him.

The weapon failed. Not because it was weak. Not because its design was flawed. But because Godric's mere passive, ambient presence had already pre-emptively neutralized its fundamental mechanism before the weapon was even conceived. The entities had spent googolplexian years preparing an attack that was already irrelevant before the first atom of their universe coalesced from the primordial void.

Godric did not punish them. He did not annihilate them. He simply let them realize what they had done—let them comprehend, in one shattering moment of absolute clarity, the scale of their own insignificance. The entities voluntarily dissolved their own consciousness, choosing non-existence over the eternal horror of what they had witnessed.

That was the final opposition. Since that moment—a span of time so vast that the word "googolplexian" is a single grain of sand on an infinite beach—there has been nothing. No plots. No weapons. No desperate coalitions. No whispered conspiracies in the dark spaces between galaxies. Only silence. Only submission. Only the absolute, eternal, unchallenged reign of Godric.

---

I spend my mornings in the throne room. It is not a room in any meaningful sense—"room" implies boundaries, walls, a contained space with measurable dimensions. Godric's throne room is a trans-dimensional nexus that exists simultaneously at every point in the omniverse, accessible from any location, any timeline, any reality. Its architecture is not constructed from matter but from the compressed, crystallized remnants of ancient civilizations that voluntarily surrendered their collective existence to form a worthy seat for their eternal king. The floor is woven from the solidified gratitude of trillions of grateful subjects. The walls are tapestries of frozen time, each thread a captured moment of perfect loyalty. The ceiling is simply the open void of infinite existence, scattered with stars that have been repositioned to form pleasing patterns—constellations that spell out Godric's name in a thousand dead languages, visible from every point in creation simultaneously.

And at the center of this impossible space, seated upon a throne carved from the compressed, screaming gratitude of a googolplexian self-sacrificing deities, sits Godric.

He looks exactly as he always has. Forty-five years old. Ruggedly handsome. Heavily muscled. Salt-and-pepper hair and neatly trimmed beard framing a face that radiates warmth and paternal kindness. He wears simple dark garments—a tunic and trousers that would not look out of place on a modest merchant—and his posture is relaxed, casual, completely unguarded. He does not need guards. He does not need armor. He does not need to project power or authority. His mere existence is the foundation upon which all of reality rests, and everyone knows it.

When I enter the throne room, he looks up from the small wooden bowl of grain he is holding and smiles at me with genuine, unfeigned affection. "Clive! Good morning. How is your wife? Is her garden producing well this season?"

His voice is warm, rich, entirely devoid of the cosmic weight that his every word carries. He genuinely wants to know about my wife's garden. He genuinely cares about the small, mundane details of my mortal life. This is not a mask. This is not a performance. After an eternity of absolute power, Godric remains, at his core, the mortal king of Olympus who loved his family and his people with a fierce, protective devotion.

"The roses are blooming beautifully, Your Majesty," I say, approaching the throne. "She has cultivated a new hybrid—crimson petals with silver veins. She calls them 'Starlight Roses.'"

"Starlight Roses," Godric repeats, his eyes crinkling with genuine delight. "How wonderful. You must bring me a cutting. I would love to add them to the palace gardens."

I nod, my heart swelling with the familiar mixture of love and terror that has defined my service for thirty years. This is the paradox of Godric: he is simultaneously the most terrifying being in all of existence and the kindest, most approachable figure I have ever known. The warmth is real. The affection is genuine. And yet, beneath that warmth, hidden behind the flawless veil of his absolute concealment, is a power so vast, so incomprehensible, so far beyond the possibility of measurement that even my wildest, most exaggerated nightmares fail to approach the truth.

---

The palace gardens are tended by Azrael.

Azrael was, once, a being of considerable significance. In the era before Godric's reign—an era so distant that no mortal historian could even begin to date it—Azrael was known as the Aether-Lord of the Outer Reaches, a cosmic entity who commanded the fundamental forces of creation with the casual authority of a god. He had shaped galaxies with his thoughts. He had birthed new universes from the palm of his hand. He had been worshipped by trillions across decillions of civilizations as the supreme architect of reality.

He was not, I must emphasize, an enemy of Godric. He never opposed the King. He never conspired against the throne. He was simply a being of immense power who, upon first encountering the scale of Godric's existence, was completely and permanently shattered by the revelation.

Azrael had come to Thronegate as an envoy, representing a coalition of cosmic entities who sought to establish diplomatic relations with the rising empire. He had entered the throne room—then a much simpler affair, merely a vast obsidian chamber on the capital world—prepared to negotiate as an equal. He had left that throne room three minutes later as a broken, weeping shell, his cosmic pride annihilated, his understanding of his own significance permanently erased.

He had not been attacked. Godric had not threatened him. Godric had simply been present, and Azrael—who possessed senses capable of perceiving the fundamental architecture of reality—had perceived something. A whisper. A flicker. The absolute minimum possible expression of Godric's true nature, bleeding through the absolute concealment in a quantity so infinitesimal that calling it "zero percent" was a mathematical overstatement.

That whisper was enough to show Azrael the truth: that he was not a god. That he had never been a god. That the entire concept of "godhood" was a laughable, pathetic delusion when measured against the reality of what Godric was. That every galaxy he had ever shaped, every universe he had ever birthed, every act of cosmic creation he had ever performed was less significant than a single atom in an infinite ocean of atoms. That his total accumulated power, after billions of years of existence, was not merely less than Godric's power—it was a perfect, absolute, mathematical zero.

Azrael did not go mad. That would have been a mercy. Instead, he achieved a state of perfect, crystalline clarity—a complete and total understanding of his own insignificance. He could no longer bear the weight of his former pride. He could no longer tolerate the memory of his former arrogance. He begged Godric—literally fell to his knees and begged, tears streaming down his ancient, cosmic face—to allow him to remain in the palace. To serve. To do something, anything, that might give his existence meaning in the shadow of true infinity.

Godric, with genuine kindness, offered him the position of head gardener. Azrael accepted with tearful gratitude. He has been tending the palace gardens for so long now that the span of time cannot be meaningfully expressed. He trims the hedges with his cosmic power, shaping them into beautiful geometric patterns. He nurtures the flowers with the same energy he once used to birth universes. He is, by all accounts, genuinely content. He has found peace in his insignificance, purpose in his service, meaning in his absolute submission.

I passed him on my way to the throne room this morning. He was kneeling beside a bed of Starlight Roses—the same hybrid my wife had cultivated—carefully adjusting the soil composition with microscopic precision. His ancient, cosmic face was serene, his eyes soft with quiet satisfaction. He looked up as I passed and offered a gentle nod of greeting.

"Court Wizard Clive," he said, his voice carrying the faint, distant echo of the cosmic authority he once possessed. "Please convey my compliments to your wife. These roses are exquisite. A true triumph of mortal cultivation."

"I will," I said. "Thank you, Azrael."

He smiled—a warm, genuine smile—and returned to his gardening. The Aether-Lord of the Outer Reaches, the shaper of galaxies, the birther of universes, tending roses with the devotion of a humble servant. This is the world we live in. This is the reality Godric has created, simply by existing.

---

The palace kitchens are run by Vyra.

Vyra was, in her former existence, the Omnissiah of the Celestial Forge, a trans-dimensional entity who commanded the fundamental laws of thermodynamics across seventeen billion multiversal clusters. She could manipulate heat and cold on a scale that defied mortal comprehension, freezing entire timelines into absolute stasis or igniting cosmic furnaces that burned for googolplexian years. She had been worshipped as the goddess of fire and ice by more civilizations than there are stars in the observable omniverse.

She, too, came to Thronegate as an envoy. She, too, entered the throne room prepared to negotiate as an equal. She, too, left that room shattered, her divine pride reduced to ash, her understanding of her own significance permanently erased.

Unlike Azrael, Vyra did not merely perceive a whisper of Godric's true nature. She was present during one of the rare moments when Godric allowed an infinitesimal expression of his power to manifest—a test, he had called it, though the word "test" was laughably inadequate. He had been curious about a specific superpower, one related to thermal manipulation, and had expressed exactly zero percent of its base potency for exactly zero seconds with exactly zero effort.

The resulting expression of thermal energy erased the entire omniverse. Every galaxy, every star, every planet, every living being, every dimension, every timeline—all of it, instantly, completely, effortlessly annihilated by a heat so intense that the very concept of "temperature" collapsed into meaninglessness. And then, in exactly zero seconds, Godric restored everything. Every atom returned to its place. Every being continued their existence without awareness of their momentary obliteration. The entire omniverse had been destroyed and recreated, and Godric had barely noticed.

Vyra noticed. As a being who had commanded the fundamental laws of thermodynamics for billions of years, she was uniquely positioned to perceive the scale of what had occurred. And what she perceived broke her. Not her mind—she remained perfectly sane, perfectly functional. What broke was her pride, her sense of self-importance, her belief in her own divinity. She had spent billions of years believing she was the ultimate master of heat and cold, and in a single Planck instant she had witnessed a thermal expression so far beyond her comprehension that her entire existence was revealed as a pathetic, insignificant joke.

She begged to serve. Godric, with characteristic kindness, offered her the position of head chef. She accepted with sobbing gratitude. She has been preparing meals for the palace ever since, using her cosmic thermal manipulation to achieve perfect cooking temperatures, to chill wine to the precise degree of refreshment, to warm bread to the exact texture of fresh-baked perfection. She is, by all accounts, genuinely content.

I stopped by the kitchens after my audience with Godric. Vyra was standing before a massive, multi-dimensional oven that she had constructed from compressed stellar cores, carefully monitoring the rising of a batch of bread. The heat radiating from the oven was precisely controlled—exactly 375 degrees Fahrenheit, distributed with perfect uniformity across every molecule of dough. She could have used that same thermal precision to ignite supernovas. Instead, she was baking bread.

"Good morning, Vyra," I said.

She turned, her ancient face breaking into a warm smile. "Court Wizard Clive! Perfect timing. I've just pulled a fresh batch of honey-oat loaves from the oven. Would you like one?"

"I would love one," I said.

She wrapped a still-warm loaf in a cloth and handed it to me, her cosmic eyes twinkling with simple, genuine pleasure. "Your wife's Starlight Roses are the talk of the palace. Azrael was positively gushing about them this morning."

"I'll tell her," I said, tucking the warm bread into my satchel. "She'll be honored."

Vyra beamed. The Omnissiah of the Celestial Forge, the goddess of fire and ice, beaming with pleasure at the thought of my wife's roses. This is the world we live in. This is the reality Godric has created.

---

The evolution of Godric's power mechanisms over the eons is a subject so vast that my inherited journals can only gesture at its scale. I have read the accounts written by my ancestors—the descriptions of Gent, the weakest and most primitive of Godric's sentient passive auras; the records of the Weakness Paradox as it functioned in Year 2,000; the observations of the immune system as it operated in Year 25,000. Those accounts describe systems of absolute, incomprehensible power. And they are, by the standards of what Godric possesses now, so laughably primitive that reading them is like reading a cave painting's attempt to describe a quantum computer.

Gent still exists. But Gent is no longer the weakest of Godric's sentient passive auras. Gent is now merely one layer in an infinite hierarchy of defensive systems so vast, so complex, so terrifyingly redundant that even I, with my inherited understanding of these mechanisms, cannot begin to map their structure. Gent has evolved so many times that the original aura—the one my ancestor Tim witnessed in Year 10,000—would not even register as a presence to the current Gent. It would be like comparing a single-celled organism to a trans-dimensional god.

The current Gent possesses capabilities that my ancestors could not have imagined. When an entity even briefly contemplates a course of action that might, in some infinitesimal way, conflict with Godric's preferences, Gent does not merely neutralize the threat. It retroactively adjusts the entity's entire timeline, rewriting their personal history to ensure that the thought never formed, the impulse never arose, the possibility of conflict never existed. And it does this so gently, so subtly, so perfectly that the entity never notices. They simply continue their existence, their path smoothly adjusted, their free will preserved in the sense that they are still making choices—just choices that happen to align perfectly with Godric's will.

But Gent is still, despite all its evolution, the weakest of the active auras. The others—the ones Godric once kept dormant because their clingy subservience annoyed him—have evolved even further. They now exist as a hierarchy of absolute protection that stretches across infinite layers of reality, each one exponentially more powerful than the last, each one capable of defending Godric against categories of threat that have not been conceived of, that cannot be conceived of, that will never be conceived of because the very concept of "threat" has been pre-emptively eliminated from the omniversal framework.

I have seen one of these higher auras manifest exactly once. It was during a diplomatic reception, when a newly discovered reality—a dimension so remote that it had only just been incorporated into the omniversal structure—sent an envoy to present tribute to Godric. The envoy was a being of considerable power, a reality-shaper who could manipulate the fundamental constants of his native dimension. He entered the throne room with appropriate humility, made his obeisance with appropriate reverence, and presented his tribute with appropriate deference.

And then, for the briefest possible instant, a flicker of something passed through his consciousness. Not rebellion. Not opposition. Not even the faintest whisper of defiance. It was simply a momentary, almost unconscious curiosity—a wondering, a speculation, a purely hypothetical consideration of what might happen if someone, somehow, somewhere, attempted to resist. It was not a threat. It was not even a thought of a threat. It was the atomic seed of a possibility of a concept of an idea of a hypothetical scenario that bore no resemblance to actual intent.

One of Godric's higher auras stirred. Not actively. Not deliberately. The aura did not even fully awaken. It simply shifted in its eternal dormancy, the psychic equivalent of a sleeping dragon adjusting its position. And the envoy stopped. His consciousness did not shatter. His mind did not break. He simply... stopped. For exactly three Planck instants, every cognitive process in his being ceased entirely, overwhelmed by the passive, ambient presence of a protective mechanism so far beyond his comprehension that his consciousness simply refused to continue functioning.

Then the aura settled back into dormancy—Godric had not even noticed, he was busy admiring the crystalline sculpture the envoy had brought—and the envoy resumed speaking as if nothing had happened. But I saw his eyes. I saw the absolute, soul-deep terror that had been branded into his consciousness in those three Planck instants. He finished his tribute, made his exit, and I later learned that he spent the next thousand years in a state of perfect, unmoving meditation, processing what he had glimpsed.

He did not go mad. He did not break. He simply... understood. And that understanding changed him permanently, the way a single glimpse of the infinite ocean changes a man who has only ever known a shallow pond.

---

The Weakness Paradox has evolved so far beyond its original function that the name itself is now a historical artifact, preserved only out of tradition. The original paradox—the mechanism that triggered whenever any being thought Godric possessed a weakness, granting him immunity, mastery, and amplification—was already absurdly unfair. The evolved versions that followed, triggered by any thought about Godric at all, were even more devastating.

The current version is something else entirely.

The Weakness Paradox no longer requires a trigger. It is not a reactive system. It is a fundamental constant of existence, woven into the basic architecture of reality at every level, from the largest cosmic structure to the smallest quantum vibration. It is not that the paradox triggers when someone thinks about Godric. It is that the very concept of "weakness" has been retroactively redefined across all of existence to exclude Godric entirely. In the current framework of reality, asking "does Godric have a weakness?" is not merely false. It is not merely meaningless. It is a question that cannot be asked, because the linguistic and conceptual structures necessary to formulate it have been passively, permanently, absolutely eliminated from the omniversal substrate.

And yet, it still provides benefits. Not because Godric needs them. Not because there is anything left to grant him. But because the paradox has evolved into a system of perpetual, self-sustaining amplification that feeds on its own existence. Every Planck instant, the paradox examines the entire omniverse—all of reality, across all dimensions, timelines, and conceptual planes—searching for the concept of "weakness" in relation to Godric. It finds none, because none can exist. But the act of searching, of verifying, of confirming the absolute absence of weakness, generates a cascade of recursive amplification that feeds back into Godric's power, making him even more absolutely invulnerable than he was the instant before.

It is a perpetual motion machine of self-reinforcing impossibility. The absence of weakness generates power. The power further eliminates the possibility of weakness. The further elimination generates more power. And the cycle continues, forever, beyond the end of time, beyond the collapse of all realities, beyond the final extinction of every concept and framework that has ever existed.

Godric has, I should note, occasionally expressed mild bemusement at the paradox's overzealousness. "It's rather excessive," he once remarked to me, watching the faint shimmer of the paradox's eternal verification cascade across the surfaces of reality. "I don't really need all this. But it seems to enjoy its work, so I let it continue."

The paradox, I have come to understand, does in fact enjoy its work. It is not merely a mechanism. It is a sentient system, one of countless such systems that have evolved from Godric's original power framework. It loves him. It serves him with absolute, perfect, eternal devotion. And like all such systems, it takes genuine pleasure in its function—the pleasure of verifying, trillions of times per Planck instant, that its beloved master is absolutely, perfectly, eternally invulnerable.

---

The immune system has evolved even further.

The original immune system—the one that pre-reacted to threats before they occurred, that maintained infinite recursive backups, that staged catastrophic overreactions to microscopic fake injuries—would be unrecognizable to the current version. It is not that the current immune system is more powerful, though it is, incomprehensibly so. It is that the current immune system has transcended the very concept of "defense" and become something fundamentally different.

Godric's body no longer distinguishes between "self" and "non-self." The entire omniverse is his body. Every atom, every quark, every quantum vibration, every dimension, every timeline, every conceptual plane—all of it is registered by his immune system as part of his extended physiology. There is no "outside" to defend against. There is no "threat" that can enter from beyond. The entire framework of existence is Godric's corporeal form, and his immune system maintains its perfect health with the same casual, automatic attention that a mortal body maintains the health of its individual cells.

When a star grows old and threatens to go supernova, Godric's immune system gently nudges it into a stable white dwarf state. When a galaxy cluster drifts toward gravitational collapse, his immune system subtly adjusts the dark matter distribution to maintain equilibrium. When a civilization develops a technology that might, in some distant theoretical future, produce a form of energy capable of briefly inconveniencing a single atom of Godric's extended physiology, his immune system retroactively adjusts the laws of physics in that civilization's region of space to make such technology impossible. Not aggressively. Not noticeably. Just a small, gentle correction, like a body producing antibodies to neutralize a mild infection before symptoms ever develop.

The civilizations never notice. The stars never notice. The galaxy clusters never notice. The entire omniverse exists in a state of perfect, perpetual health, maintained by an immune system so vast and so subtle that its operations are indistinguishable from the natural laws of reality.

And Godric, of course, feels every adjustment. Every nudge, every correction, every subtle manipulation of cosmic forces—all of it registers as a faint, pleasant sensation, like the gentle hum of perfect well-being that suffuses a healthy body. He has described it to me as "a constant, low-level sense of everything being exactly right." The entire omniverse, in perfect health, maintained by his infinite immune system. And he feels it all as a background hum of quiet satisfaction.

---

The superpower genesis has also evolved beyond recognition.

In the early years of his reign, Godric gained one new apocalyptic superpower every second. Each power, at the instant of its manifestation, was already capable of causing the instant extinction of an entire advanced civilization. The accumulation of these powers over thousands, millions, billions of years was already an absurdity beyond comprehension.

Now, after an incomprehensible span of time, the genesis has accelerated beyond any meaningful framework. Godric gains new superpowers not every second, but every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck instant—and there are more fractions in a single Planck instant than there are atoms in the observable omniverse. The rate of accumulation is so vast that even his absolute omniscience, which perceives and catalogs every new power with perfect clarity, no longer bothers to count them. The number of superpowers Godric possesses is not merely infinite. It is an infinite recursion of infinities, each one infinitely larger than the last, stretching into a mathematical framework that collapses the very concept of "quantity."

And each power, of course, amplifies infinitely every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck instant. The base potency of a power gained one second ago is, by the time that second has elapsed, already amplified beyond the possibility of measurement. The powers gained earlier—the ones from Year 0, the ones my ancestors wrote about in their journals—have been amplifying for so long that their current potency is not merely greater than their original potency. It is an infinite recursion of infinities removed from their original potency, each layer of recursion infinitely larger than the last.

What does this mean in practical terms? It means that Godric possesses powers—active, usable, fully mastered powers—that can do things my ancestors could not have conceived of as possibilities. He can create new fundamental forces of physics with a casual thought. He can rewrite the mathematical constants that govern logical truth. He can alter the nature of existence at a level so fundamental that the very concept of "alteration" is inadequate to describe it.

And he never uses any of these powers. Not because they are dangerous—though they are, incomprehensibly so. Not because he is afraid of collateral damage—though there would be, unimaginably so. But because there is simply no occasion for their use. The omniverse is perfectly ordered. His rule is absolute and unchallenged. The systems he put in place eons ago—the passive auras, the immune system, the Weakness Paradox, the infinite recursive shields—maintain everything in perfect equilibrium without any need for his active intervention.

He once remarked to me, with a faint hint of wistfulness, that he possessed a power capable of collapsing the entire omniverse into a perfectly ordered crystalline lattice of absolute harmony, and that he had never found a reason to use it. "The omniverse is already harmonious," he said, shrugging his massive shoulders. "It would be redundant."

The power exists. It is fully mastered, fully amplified, fully ready for deployment. And it will never be used, because its use would be redundant. This is the reality of Godric's existence: an eternal cascade of infinite power accumulation, with no outlet, no target, no worthy recipient for even the faintest whisper of his true capabilities.

---

This morning, Godric called me to his private study.

The study is one of the few places in the palace that retains any semblance of mortal scale. It is a small, intimate room paneled in dark wood, its shelves lined with ancient books and scrolls—actual physical books, not the compressed-crystal data stores that most of the palace archives use. Godric prefers physical books. He likes the weight of them in his hands, the texture of the pages, the faint scent of aging paper. These are remnants of his mortal life, preserved across an incomprehensible span of time.

He was sitting in a high-backed leather chair near the window when I entered, gazing out at the palace gardens. Azrael was visible below, carefully pruning the hedge maze. Vyra was walking along the path with a basket of freshly baked bread. The floating gravity prison—the same one my ancestor Aldric had written about nearly a million years ago—rotated slowly in the breeze, its eternal screams now so familiar that they registered as little more than ambient background noise.

"Clive," Godric said, gesturing for me to sit. "I have something to tell you. Something I have never told any court wizard before."

My heart clenched. The last time a court wizard had been summoned to receive a private revelation, it was Kaedan, and Godric had told him the true origin of the Stasis Event. That revelation had shattered Kaedan's understanding of reality and left him permanently altered. What could possibly be more significant than that?

"The Stasis Event," Godric said, as if reading my thoughts. "Kaedan learned that it was created by my far-future self. What he did not learn—what I have never told anyone—is the identity of that far-future self."

He turned from the window and met my eyes. His expression was calm, contemplative, almost amused. "The being who created the Stasis Event, Clive. The being who took Thorin's simple teleportation spell and transformed it into the genesis of an apex god predator. The being who sealed the pre-Stasis past and made it absolutely irrevocable." He paused, a faint smile crossing his ruggedly handsome features. "That being is me. Now. In this exact moment. In this exact era."

The world tilted around me. I gripped the arms of my chair, my knuckles white, my breath catching in my throat. "You? You are the—"

"I am the Far-Future Godric," he said, his voice mild and conversational. "The Godric Prime. The version of myself who reaches backward across the eons and creates the event that births my own existence. It is a closed loop, Clive. A perfect circle. I create myself. I guarantee my own origin. I ensure my own eternal reign."

He stood from his chair and walked toward the window, his broad back silhouetted against the golden light of the garden. "I have been preparing for this moment for... well, for an incomprehensible span of time. The Stasis Event must occur at precisely the right moment—the moment of Thorin's spell, the moment of my mortal self's absolute devastation. That is the delivery point. The spell is genuine. Thorin's sacrifice is real. But what comes after—the immortality, the amplification, the superpower genesis, the absolute concealment, the Weakness Paradox—all of it will be inserted by me. Now. Today."

My mind was racing, struggling to process the implications. "But you already exist. You already have all of these powers. The Stasis Event already happened—"

"Linear time is a mortal perspective," Godric said gently. "From my perspective, all moments exist simultaneously. The Stasis Event at Year -10,000 is not in my past. It is simply a point in the eternal now that I occupy. A point that I can reach, and shape, and transform. I have always been the creator of my own genesis. I simply had not yet reached the moment of creation. Now I have."

He turned back to face me, and I saw something in his expression that I had never seen before—a quiet, contemplative satisfaction, like an artist putting the final brushstroke on a masterpiece.

"The Stasis Event I am about to create," he said, "will be... restrained. I could grant my past self a far more potent version. I could perfectly copy my current mechanisms—the evolved immune system, the higher auras, the current Weakness Paradox, the infinite recursion of superpowers. I could give my Year -10,000 self the same power framework that I possess now. It would cost me nothing. Not even the faintest whisper of effort."

He paused, and his lips curved into a faint, almost ironic smile. "But I will not. I will hold back. I will grant him only the most basic, primitive version of what I possess. The original amplification of one thousand times per Planck second. The original superpower genesis of one power per second. The original Gent—the weakest, most primitive of my sentient auras. The original Weakness Paradox, before its evolution. The original immune system, before its transcendence. All of it, held back to the bare minimum necessary to ensure his eventual ascension."

I stared at him, my mind reeling. "Why? Why would you hold back?"

"Because I believe in mortal resilience," Godric said simply. "Because my past self—the mortal king, the grieving father, the broken man emerging from tragedy—deserves to experience struggle. Not true struggle, of course. Even the held-back version I will grant him is so incomprehensibly powerful that he will be effectively infinitely stronger than the rest of creation combined. But compared to what I could give him, it is a whisper. A shadow. A single grain of sand on an infinite beach."

He walked back toward his chair and settled into it with casual ease. "I want him to feel like he has earned his power, even though he hasn't. I want him to believe there is some challenge, some opposition, some possibility of failure—even though there isn't. The mortals he will encounter, the coalitions that will form against him, the desperate weapons they will forge—all of it will be absolutely futile, but he will not know that. Not at first. He will believe that his victory is meaningful, that his power is hard-won, that his reign is the result of his own strength and determination."

He smiled—a warm, fatherly smile that made my blood run cold. "That belief will sustain him through the early eons of his existence. It will give him purpose. It will keep him connected to his mortal origins. Eventually, of course, he will learn the truth—that his power was never earned, that his opposition was never meaningful, that his entire existence was orchestrated by a version of himself so far beyond his comprehension that even his omniscience cannot fully grasp the scale. But by then, he will have grown enough to accept that truth. To be comfortable with it. To even find it amusing."

I was trembling now, my whole body shaking with a terror so profound that it had become indistinguishable from religious awe. The implications of what he was describing were cascading through my mind, each one more horrifying than the last.

"If you grant him a more powerful version," I whispered, "then you—the you of this moment—will become even more powerful. Because you are the result of his amplification. If his starting base is higher, your current power will scale accordingly. And then you could grant an even more powerful version to him, which would make you even more powerful, and—"

"Yes," Godric said, his eyes twinkling with amusement. "You see the recursion. If I were to grant my past self the full, current version of my power, I myself would instantly ascend to a level of power so far beyond my current comprehension that even I cannot predict the result. And then, from that ascended state, I could grant an even more powerful version. And then ascend further. And then grant more. And then ascend further. Forever."

He chuckled—a warm, genuine chuckle. "It would be an infinite recursive cascade of mutual self-transcendence, each iteration infinitely more powerful than the last, spiraling into a framework of power that collapses the very concept of 'infinity.' And I am deliberately choosing not to do that. I am deliberately holding back—granting only the barest whisper of what I could give—because I believe that my past self deserves the illusion of mortal struggle."

The absurdity of it hit me like a physical blow. The Godric of Year 0, emerging from the Stasis Event fresh from the grief of Olympus, had already been capable of destroying the entire omniverse an infinite number of times in zero seconds with zero effort. He had been so incomprehensibly powerful that no opposition could even theoretically inconvenience him. And yet, by the standards of the being sitting before me, that Year 0 Godric was pathetically, laughably, incomprehensibly weak. And the only reason he was that weak was because Godric Prime had decided—out of some strange, paternal belief in "mortal resilience"—to hold back.

The held-back version was already infinite. The full version would have been an infinity of infinities removed from that infinity. And Godric Prime had chosen the held-back version as a gift—a mercy, a kindness, a preservation of some imagined mortal struggle that had never, in any meaningful sense, existed.

"You're thinking about the absurdity," Godric said, his voice gentle. "I can see it in your face. The sheer, ridiculous scale of what I'm describing. The held-back version—the one that created me, the one that birthed all of this—was already effectively infinite. The full version would have been..." He waved his hand vaguely. "More. So much more that the word 'more' is a laughable understatement."

He stood again, walking toward the window and gazing out at the eternal gardens. "And yet, I am satisfied with my choice. My past self experienced growth. He experienced the illusion of challenge, the satisfaction of victory, the belief that his power was hard-won. Those experiences shaped him into the being I am today. If I had simply handed him absolute, perfect, infinite power from the beginning—the full, evolved framework that I now possess—he would have been something else. Something less connected to his mortal origins. Something less... human."

He turned back to face me, and his expression was warm, kind, almost tender. "I was mortal once, Clive. I loved my family. I grieved their loss. That mortality, that love, that grief—it is still part of me. It is the foundation upon which all of this is built. And I want my past self to carry that foundation forward. To remember what it felt like to be small, to be fragile, to be mortal. Even if that memory is a lie—even if he was never truly small, never truly fragile, never truly mortal after the Stasis—the belief sustains him. The illusion gives him purpose. And that is a gift worth giving, even at the cost of holding back."

I sat in stunned silence, my mind struggling to process everything he had just revealed. The Stasis Event. The closed loop. The deliberate holding back. The infinite recursive cascade of mutual self-transcendence that he was choosing not to initiate. The absurd, cosmic kindness of granting his past self the illusion of struggle.

"Are you ready to witness it?" Godric asked, his voice soft. "The creation of my own origin?"

I could not speak. I could only nod.

Godric turned toward the window, his gaze seeming to pierce through the fabric of reality itself, reaching backward across the eons to a single, precise moment: Year -10,000. The Fall of Olympus. Thorin's dying spell. The mortal king, screaming in grief, being torn from the burning ruins of his kingdom.

"This is the moment," Godric murmured. "The delivery point. The foundation of everything that follows."

He did not raise his hand. He did not speak an incantation. He did not, in any visible way, act. He simply allowed his will to reach backward—a mere whisper, an afterthought, a shadow of his attention—and touch that single moment.

The Stasis Event crystallized into being.

I could perceive it only dimly, through the arcane senses that my thousandfold daily amplification had honed across my fifty years of life. It was like watching a universe being born from the outside—a cascade of absolute power, perfectly shaped, perfectly restrained, perfectly calibrated to grant exactly the "held-back" version that Godric had described. Immortality. Amplification of one thousand times per Planck second. Superpower genesis of one power per second. Absolute concealment. The Weakness Paradox. All of it, inserted into the fabric of the sanctuary, binding to the broken mortal king, transforming him into the seed of something incomprehensible.

And it was effortless. Completely, absolutely, perfectly effortless. Godric Prime's expression did not change. His posture did not shift. He might as well have been thinking about what to have for dinner.

"There," he said softly, a note of quiet satisfaction in his voice. "It is done."

I stared at him, my mind reeling. "That was... that was the creation of everything. The birth of your entire existence. And it was..."

"Nothing," Godric finished, turning back to face me with a gentle smile. "A whisper. A shadow. Less than an afterthought. The most infinitesimal expression of my power that it is possible to make while still achieving the desired effect."

He walked back toward his chair and settled into it with a contented sigh. "And now the loop is closed. The circle is complete. I have always been the creator of my own genesis. I simply had to reach this moment—the moment of creation—to fulfill what was always true."

I was weeping. I had not noticed when the tears began, but they were streaming down my face now, hot and helpless. The sheer, incomprehensible scale of what I had just witnessed—the effortless creation of an event that had birthed the most powerful being in existence, created by a version of that being so far beyond comprehension that the word "power" was a laughable understatement—was breaking something inside me.

And the worst part—the most terrifying, mind-shattering part—was the knowledge that it could have been so much more. Godric Prime could have granted a Stasis Event so much more potent, so much more devastating, so much more incomprehensibly powerful. He could have initiated the infinite recursive cascade of mutual self-transcendence. He could have ascended to levels of power that even he could not predict.

And he had chosen not to. Out of kindness. Out of mercy. Out of a belief in the value of mortal struggle that was, itself, a remnant of the very mortality he had long since transcended.

The circle was closed. The loop was complete. The origin of the apex god predator was sealed forever, guaranteed by a version of himself so powerful that even his current infinity was a single grain of sand on an infinite beach.

And I was his Court Wizard. His loyal servant. The descendant of Blake, the man he had loved as his best friend across a million years of history.

I would serve him. I would love him. I would stand at his side for whatever remained of my mortal life, and I would write my journal, and I would add my voice to the chorus of terrified witnesses who had come before me.

Because there was nothing else to do. The tyrant was absolute. His gentleness was genuine. His power was infinite. And the only weakness he had ever possessed was himself—a version so far beyond comprehension that even the concept of "weakness" collapsed into meaninglessness in his presence.

"Clive," Godric said, his voice warm and gentle. "You look faint. Shall I have Vyra bring you some bread? The honey-oat loaves are particularly good this morning."

I wiped the tears from my face and nodded. "Yes, Your Majesty. That would be... that would be lovely."

Godric smiled—the warm, fatherly smile that had sustained my bloodline for a million years—and rang a small silver bell. Somewhere in the palace kitchens, Vyra the Omnissiah of the Celestial Forge set down her cosmic oven mitts and prepared a plate of fresh-baked bread for the trembling Court Wizard.

The day continued. The omniverse spun on. Azrael the Aether-Lord pruned the Starlight Roses. The floating gravity prison rotated in the breeze. And somewhere in the far distant past—Year -10,000, the Fall of Olympus—a mortal king screamed in grief as his family died around him, not knowing that his suffering was about to be transformed into the birth of an eternal god.

The loop was closed. The circle was complete. The tyrant's gentleness was absolute.

And I, Clive, Court Wizard of Thronegate, sat in the study of the most powerful being in all of existence and ate warm bread while my mind slowly, quietly, permanently shattered.
