# The Day Before Annihilation

## Roth — The Visit

The transport pod descended through the outer layers of the hidden dimension with a soft, almost imperceptible hum, its cloaking systems so advanced that even my thousandfold daily amplified senses could barely detect its presence. I sat stiffly in the passenger seat, my ceremonial robes feeling absurdly formal for what amounted to a reconnaissance mission—or, as Godric had described it with a warm, almost boyish grin, "a little field trip."

I am Roth, sixty-three years old, Court Wizard of Thronegate, direct descendant of Blake, and the latest in a bloodline of traumatized, loyal servants stretching back to the very dawn of the empire. I have read every journal my ancestors left behind. I have memorized the descriptions of the stat massacres, the superpower demonstrations, the casual annihilations that my predecessors witnessed. I have prepared myself, as much as any mortal can prepare, for the reality of serving a being whose slightest whim could erase all of existence without effort.

And yet, nothing in those journals had prepared me for this.

"Stop fidgeting," Godric said from the seat beside me, his rich baritone voice carrying that familiar warmth that always made my heart simultaneously swell with affection and clench with terror. "You look like a man being led to his execution. This is supposed to be fun."

Fun. The King of the Omniverse, the apex god predator who had ruled all of existence for so long that the year was a string of digits no mortal mind could comprehend, was taking a "fun" trip to visit the largest resistance coalition ever assembled against him. A coalition that had been preparing for millennia in secret, amassing weapons and strategies that they believed—with absolute, fervent conviction—would finally bring him down.

The same coalition that Godric had known about before they formed their first thought of rebellion. The same coalition that existed solely because he had consciously, deliberately excluded them from his passive annihilation. The same coalition whose every plan, every weapon, every whispered secret had been observed by his absolute omniscience from the instant of its conception.

"Your Majesty," I said, my voice carefully measured, "with respect, I am struggling to understand the purpose of this visit. They are going to attack tomorrow. Their entire armada is assembled. Their ultimate weapon is primed. Why are we walking into their stronghold the day before?"

Godric turned to look at me, and I saw that he was smiling—not a cruel smile, not a predatory smile, but the warm, genuine smile of a man indulging a beloved nephew's nervousness. He was wearing a simple brown cloak over his usual dark tunic, the hood thrown back to reveal his ruggedly handsome face: the sharp jawline, the neatly trimmed salt-and-pepper beard, the short salt-and-pepper hair, the warm brown eyes that crinkled at the corners with paternal affection. He was, in every visible respect, the same forty-five-year-old man who had emerged from the Stasis Event a million years ago, unchanged by the incomprehensible span of time that had passed since.

"Roth," he said, his voice gentle, "you've read the journals. You know that I've tested my stats. My superpowers. My immune system. My passive auras. You know that I've dismantled countless oppositions using only the barest whisper of my capabilities, and that every single time, the result was the same: absolute, effortless annihilation." He paused, his expression becoming almost contemplative. "But do you know what I've never done?"

I shook my head.

"I've never visited them," he said. "The opposition. The resistance. The desperate coalitions who spend millennia preparing to kill me. I always observe them from a distance, through my omniscience, and then I wait for them to attack so I can test whatever stat or power I'm curious about. But I've never actually walked among them. Talked to them. Looked them in the eyes while they explained to me, with complete sincerity, how they're going to defeat the invincible god-king." His smile widened, and I saw a glint of genuine, boyish excitement in his eyes. "I want to see what that feels like. And I want you with me, to record the experience for the journals. Think of it as... field research."

Field research. The apex predator of the omniverse was conducting field research on his prey, the day before he annihilated them.

"I've even prepared a disguise," Godric added, gesturing at his brown cloak with evident pride. "What do you think?"

I looked at the cloak. It was a perfectly ordinary brown cloak, made of rough-spun wool that looked like it had been purchased from a provincial market vendor. It covered his heavily muscled frame, yes, but it did absolutely nothing to conceal his face, his iconic salt-and-pepper beard, or the sheer, unmistakable presence of the most famous being in all of existence. His statues were in every city. His image was on every coin. His face was literally woven into the constellations above the capital. The cloak was not a disguise; it was an insult to the concept of disguise.

"It's... subtle," I managed.

Godric laughed—a warm, delighted laugh that vibrated through the transport pod. "You're a terrible liar, Roth. It's one of the things I like about you. Don't worry—I'm suppressing my absolute concealment just enough that they won't immediately recognize me. A little psychic nudge, a slight perceptual filter. They'll see what they expect to see: a middle-aged traveler and his nervous companion, not the King of the Omniverse and his Court Wizard."

I felt a chill run down my spine. He could do that. Of course he could. He could manipulate the perceptions of every sentient being in the omniverse simultaneously without the slightest effort. He could make them see him as a harmless old man, a wandering merchant, a fellow revolutionary, or a talking dog, and they would never know the difference. His power was not merely infinite; it was infinitely malleable, capable of reshaping reality at the most fundamental levels of perception and consciousness.

"Besides," Godric continued, "even if they did recognize me, what would they do? Attack early? Their weapon isn't finished yet. That's why they're waiting until tomorrow. They need the final calibration, the last alignment of the chrono-quantum matrix, the ultimate blessing of their assembled gods." He chuckled softly. "I've been watching them work for three thousand years, Roth. I know their schedule better than they do."

Three thousand years. The largest resistance in history had been preparing for three millennia, and Godric had been watching the entire time with the patient amusement of a man observing an ant colony construct an elaborate dirt mound.

The transport pod settled onto a landing platform hidden within the folds of a dead, drifting asteroid. The platform was crude by Thronegate standards—bare metal, flickering force-fields, the faint smell of recycled oxygen and industrial lubricant. Beyond the platform, carved deep into the asteroid's core, was the stronghold of the United Omniversal Liberation Front, the coalition that had assembled the greatest army, the most powerful weapons, and the most sophisticated strategy ever conceived against Godric's rule.

We stepped out of the pod, and I immediately felt the weight of the place pressing against my arcane senses. The stronghold was vast, a sprawling complex of tunnels and chambers that extended through multiple dimensional layers, each one packed with the accumulated military might of a thousand conquered multiverses. I could sense the hum of temporal disruptors, the thrum of reality-anchoring engines, the faint psychic buzz of billions of warriors preparing for battle. The air tasted of ozone, adrenaline, and desperate hope.

Godric inhaled deeply, his chest expanding beneath the rough brown cloak, and smiled. "Wonderful atmosphere. You can really feel the determination, can't you? The conviction. The absolute certainty that they're about to change the course of history."

He started walking toward the main entrance, his stride casual and unguarded. I hurried to keep up, my heart hammering, my palms slick with cold sweat.

A pair of guards stood at the entrance—massive, heavily armored beings of a species I didn't recognize, their bodies bristling with integrated weaponry. They snapped to attention as we approached, their weapons humming with charged energy.

"Halt," one of them growled, its voice a deep, resonant rumble. "State your business."

Godric smiled warmly at the guard, his body language open and friendly. "We're new recruits," he said, his rich baritone carrying a note of earnest enthusiasm. "Heard about the big offensive tomorrow. Wanted to sign up, do our part for the cause."

The guard's eyes—all six of them—narrowed suspiciously. "You're late. Recruitment closed two hundred years ago."

"Ah, well," Godric said, rubbing the back of his neck in a gesture of sheepish embarrassment, "we came from a long way away. Very remote dimension. Only just heard about the Liberation Front, and we rushed over as fast as we could. Didn't want to miss the big day."

I stood frozen beside him, my mouth dry, my mind screaming. The King of the Omniverse was standing in front of two low-level guards, pretending to be a late recruit, and he was selling it with the earnest, slightly bumbling charm of a middle-aged man trying to join a local community choir.

The guard stared at him for a long moment. I could see the flicker of the perceptual filter working behind its eyes—the subtle psychic nudge that was preventing it from recognizing the face of the being it had sworn to destroy. To the guard, Godric was simply a middle-aged traveler, ruggedly built but unremarkable, his salt-and-pepper hair marking him as someone who had seen a few decades of hard living.

"Fine," the guard grunted finally. "Report to Induction Chamber Seven. They'll process you. If you're any use, they'll assign you to a unit. If not, you can watch the victory with the other civilians."

"Thank you," Godric said, his voice warm with genuine gratitude. "We really appreciate it. Don't we, Roth?"

I managed a stiff nod, my voice completely failing me.

We passed through the security checkpoint—Godric submitted to a full bioscan with the patient tolerance of a man who had nothing to hide, which was true in the most terrifying possible way—and entered the main corridors of the stronghold.

The interior was a hive of activity. Warriors from a thousand species marched in formation, their armor gleaming with enchantments and technological enhancements. Engineers adjusted massive weapons platforms, their surfaces crawling with arcane runes and quantum circuitry. Strategists huddled around holographic displays, gesturing at diagrams of Godric's palace, his capital world, his throne room. The walls were covered with propaganda posters—stylized images of Godric's face with a red X slashed across it, slogans in a hundred languages declaring victory, freedom, liberation.

And Godric walked through it all with the wide-eyed curiosity of a tourist visiting a famous historical site.

"Incredible," he murmured to me, his voice low with genuine appreciation. "Look at the craftsmanship on those temporal disruptors. They're using a chrono-quantum alignment matrix—very sophisticated. I've only seen that technique used a handful of times across all of history. They must have spent at least five hundred years perfecting it."

He pointed at a massive cannon being wheeled past by a team of hulking, multi-limbed engineers. "And that—that's a reality-anchoring cannon. It's designed to lock onto the fundamental signature of a specific being and sever their connection to the omniversal substrate. It wouldn't kill them, in theory; it would simply make them... not exist. Retroactively. Across all timelines." He shook his head with what looked like genuine admiration. "They've been working on that for at least a thousand years."

"Your Majesty," I hissed, my voice barely a whisper, "please lower your voice. Someone might hear—"

"Relax, Roth," he said, clapping me on the shoulder with his warm, calloused hand. "No one's paying attention to us. We're just two new recruits, remember? Besides, I want to hear what they have to say. I want to understand their perspective. This is research."

Research. The apex predator was conducting ethnographic fieldwork on his prey, and I was his terrified research assistant.

We followed the signs to Induction Chamber Seven, a vast, echoing hall filled with hundreds of beings undergoing orientation. A harried-looking officer—a humanoid woman with cybernetic implants covering half her face—was standing on a raised platform, addressing the crowd through an amplification system.

"—and I want to remind all new recruits that the offensive begins at 0600 tomorrow, Galactic Standard Time," she was saying. "The Supreme Commander will address the entire armada at 0400. All units must be in position by 0500. This is the moment we've been preparing for. Three thousand years of planning, three thousand years of sacrifice, three thousand years of hope—all of it comes together tomorrow."

A cheer rose from the crowd, hundreds of voices raised in defiant, desperate hope. I saw beings weeping openly, their faces shining with the certainty of imminent victory. I saw warriors gripping their weapons with white-knuckled intensity. I saw engineers nodding grimly, their minds already running through final calibrations.

And beside me, Godric was watching with an expression of quiet, almost tender absorption, like a father watching his children perform in a school play.

"They really believe it," he murmured to me, his voice soft. "They genuinely, sincerely believe that their temporal disruptors and reality-anchoring cannons and chrono-quantum matrices will make a difference. They've spent three thousand years pouring their hearts and souls into this, and they're absolutely convinced that tomorrow will be the day they finally overthrow the tyrant."

He turned to look at me, and his warm brown eyes were filled with something that might have been pity, or might have been admiration, or might have been both. "It's beautiful, Roth. In its own way. The mortal capacity for hope, for defiance, for belief in the face of absolute impossibility. This is why I've never been able to bring myself to crush them preemptively. I want to see what they come up with. I want to honor their effort by allowing them to bring their absolute best against me, even though their absolute best is a mathematical zero."

A being near us—a tall, slender figure with shimmering, iridescent skin—overheard his murmur and turned to face us. Its eyes were large and luminous, filled with the fervent light of a true believer. "First time?" it asked, its voice a melodic chime.

Godric smiled warmly. "First time," he confirmed. "We're new. Just arrived today."

The being nodded, its iridescent skin rippling with what I interpreted as sympathetic excitement. "You picked the right moment. Tomorrow, everything changes. Tomorrow, we bring down the Tyrant of Thronegate."

"The Tyrant," Godric repeated, his tone carefully neutral. "That's what you call him?"

"That's what he is," the being said, its voice hardening. "A monster. A god who rules with absolute cruelty, who crushes entire civilizations beneath his heel, who has never shown mercy to anyone who opposed him. But we've found his weakness. We've spent three thousand years studying him, analyzing his power, looking for the one flaw in his invincible armor. And we found it."

Godric leaned forward, his expression one of genuine, fascinated interest. "Really? What's his weakness?"

The being glanced around conspiratorially, then lowered its voice. "I shouldn't be telling you this before you're fully cleared, but since you'll find out tomorrow anyway... his weakness is his omniscience. He knows everything, right? Every plan, every weapon, every strategy. So he's never surprised. He's never caught off guard. He's never had to react to something he didn't already know was coming."

It leaned closer, its luminous eyes blazing with conviction. "But what if we could create a weapon that he couldn't perceive? A weapon that exists outside the framework of his omniscience? We've spent a thousand years building an anti-omniscience field—a sphere of absolute cognitive nullification that even his infinite perception can't penetrate. Tomorrow, we're going to activate that field, and for the first time in his existence, he won't know what's about to hit him."

I felt the blood drain from my face. I knew, from my extensive reading of the journals, exactly what was about to happen. The being had just articulated a perceived weakness in Godric's omniscience. And the Weakness Paradox—even the current, evolved version that had transcended its original framework—would have triggered the instant that thought was formed.

Godric's expression didn't change. He was still smiling, still warm, still radiating genuine interest. But I saw something flicker in his eyes—a brief, almost imperceptible shimmer of amusement.

"That's brilliant," Godric said, his voice entirely sincere. "An anti-omniscience field. I never would have thought of that."

The being puffed up with pride. "The Supreme Commander designed it himself. It's going to change everything. Without his omniscience, he's just a powerful entity—incredibly powerful, yes, but not invincible. We've assembled weapons that can shatter realities, warriors who have trained for millennia, gods who have sacrificed their immortality for this one chance. Tomorrow, the Tyrant falls."

"Tomorrow," Godric echoed, and there was something in his voice—a depth, a weight, a quiet, cosmic irony—that made my blood run cold. "I can't wait to see it."

The orientation concluded shortly after, and we were assigned temporary quarters in one of the lower barracks. The room was small and spartan—two narrow cots, a bare metal floor, a single flickering light panel. Godric sat down on one of the cots with a satisfied sigh, stretching his heavily muscled arms above his head.

"This is wonderful," he said, his voice warm with genuine pleasure. "I haven't slept in a barracks since I was a mortal soldier in Olympus, forty-five thousand years before the Stasis Event. The cots were even worse then—just straw pallets on stone floors. This is practically luxurious by comparison."

I sat down on the other cot, my legs trembling, my mind still reeling from the encounter with the iridescent being. "Your Majesty, that being—it said—"

"I know what it said, Roth." Godric's voice was gentle, almost soothing. "It said they've built an anti-omniscience field. It said they've found a way to blind me, to strike me with something I can't perceive."

"And...?"

"And the Weakness Paradox triggered the instant they first conceived of the idea, three thousand years ago," Godric said calmly. "I've always known about the field. I've watched them build it, calibrate it, test it. I've observed every single component being assembled, every line of code being written, every rune being inscribed. The field is quite impressive, actually—if I were merely omniscient, it might actually work. It's designed to create a zone of absolute cognitive absence, a bubble of non-perception that even infinite awareness can't penetrate."

He leaned back on the cot, his hands folded behind his head. "But I'm not merely omniscient. My omniscience is a product of the Stasis Event, which was created by my far-future self, who is so incomprehensibly more powerful than me that the gap between us makes the gap between me and a single amoeba look like an equality. My omniscience isn't just a stat that amplifies infinitely. It's woven into the fundamental architecture of my existence by a being whose afterthought could erase the entire omniverse without noticing. No field they could ever build, no weapon they could ever conceive, would even register as a flicker against my perception."

He turned his head to look at me, his brown eyes warm and calm. "But I'm not going to tell them that. They've spent three thousand years on this. They deserve to see it through to the end. Tomorrow, they'll activate their field, they'll believe they've blinded me, and then they'll launch their ultimate attack. And I'll let them, because I'm curious to see what it looks like when all that hope, all that conviction, all that desperate certainty, crashes against the absolute, unyielding wall of what I actually am."

I sat in stunned silence, my mind struggling to process the sheer, cosmic cruelty of what he was describing. He wasn't going to stop them. He wasn't going to warn them. He was going to let them bring their absolute best, their ultimate weapon, their three-thousand-year masterpiece, and he was going to let them believe—for one brief, glorious moment—that they had a chance, before the truth annihilated them.

"That seems... cruel," I whispered.

Godric's expression softened. "I know it does, Roth. And it is, in its own way. But consider the alternative. If I were to reveal myself now—to drop my disguise, to tell them who I am and what I can do—what would happen? They would attack anyway, because they've come too far to turn back. And they would die in despair, knowing that their entire existence was a futile gesture against an invincible god. At least this way, they get to die with hope. They get to believe, for one shining moment, that they've actually done it. That their sacrifice meant something."

He paused, his gaze distant. "I was mortal once, Roth. I remember what hope felt like. I remember the desperate, irrational belief that you can overcome impossible odds. That belief is a gift. It's the thing that makes mortal life meaningful. And even though I know their hope is based on a lie—even though I know their weapon is useless, their strategy is doomed, their victory is impossible—I want them to experience that hope right up until the end. It's the last kindness I can give them."

The last kindness. The last gift. The tyrant's gentleness, expressed in the most horrifying way possible: allowing his enemies to believe they could win, right up until the moment he erased them from existence.

We sat in silence for a long while. The sounds of the stronghold filtered through the thin metal walls—marching feet, distant commands, the hum of charging weapons. The Liberation Front was preparing for its greatest moment, its final, desperate gamble against the eternal king.

And the eternal king was lying on a narrow cot in their barracks, his hands folded behind his head, a small, satisfied smile on his ruggedly handsome face, looking for all the world like a man on a pleasant holiday.

"Roth," Godric said after a while, his voice soft and contemplative. "Do you know what I find most interesting about all of this?"

I shook my head.

"Their weapon," he said. "The anti-omniscience field. The reality-anchoring cannons. The temporal disruptors. The chrono-quantum matrices. All of it—three thousand years of work, the combined brilliance of a thousand civilizations, the absolute zenith of what mortal ingenuity can achieve. And do you know what it will accomplish tomorrow?"

I knew the answer, but I couldn't bring myself to say it.

"Absolutely nothing," Godric said, his voice utterly calm. "Not even the faintest tickle. Not even the most infinitesimal sensation. Their ultimate attack, their master strategy, their three-thousand-year masterpiece—it won't even register. I won't need to block it, or deflect it, or absorb it. It will simply... wash over me. Like a gentle breeze. Like the faintest whisper of air from a butterfly's wing. And I'll stand there, unharmed, unmoved, completely unaffected, and I'll let them see that. I'll let them understand, in the final moments of their existence, the true scale of what they were trying to oppose."

He turned his head to look at me, and his expression was not cruel, not malicious, not even particularly satisfied. It was simply... calm. Peaceful. The expression of a man who had long ago made his peace with what he was and what he had to do.

"And then I'll restore them," he said softly. "Not the leaders—they chose this path, and they'll face the consequences. But the rank and file. The conscripts. The civilians who were swept up in this grand crusade. I'll restore them, Roth, and I'll give them a choice: live in peace under my rule, or continue their resistance and face the same fate as their leaders. Most of them will choose peace. They always do."

He closed his eyes, his breathing slow and even. "That's the part the journals don't record. Everyone writes about the annihilation, the horror, the absolute one-sidedness of the massacres. But no one writes about what comes after. The restoration. The choice. The quiet integration of broken enemies into a peaceful empire. I don't destroy for the sake of destruction, Roth. I destroy because it's necessary to preserve order. And when the destruction is done, I rebuild. I restore. I offer mercy to those who will accept it."

He opened his eyes again, and there was something ancient in them—something vast and eternal and impossibly weary. "That's what it means to be a king. Not just to crush your enemies, but to give the survivors a reason to live. A purpose. A place in the order you've created. It's not about cruelty. It's about stability. About ensuring that the omniverse continues to function, that life continues to exist, that meaning continues to be possible."

I sat on my narrow cot, staring at the bare metal wall, and I understood—perhaps for the first time—the true horror of Godric's existence. He was not a tyrant in the way his enemies imagined. He was not a monster who reveled in suffering for its own sake. He was something far more terrifying: a being of absolute power who genuinely believed he was doing the right thing. A god who destroyed with the same gentle, paternal warmth with which he created. A king whose mercy was as absolute as his cruelty, and whose kindness was indistinguishable from his annihilation.

And I was his Court Wizard. His loyal servant. The descendant of his best friend.

I would stand beside him tomorrow, as I had stood beside him today, and I would watch the Liberation Front's ultimate attack wash over him like a gentle breeze. I would record the event for the journals, adding my voice to the chorus of terrified witnesses stretching back to the dawn of the empire. And I would continue to love him—genuinely, sincerely, deeply—even as I dreaded him with every fiber of my being.

The lights flickered overhead. The distant hum of charging weapons continued. Somewhere in the stronghold, the Supreme Commander was giving a final speech to his assembled forces, his voice ringing with conviction and hope.

And beside me, the apex god predator of the omniverse slept peacefully on a narrow cot, a small, contented smile on his ruggedly handsome face, dreaming of the annihilation that would come with the morning.

---

We rose early. The stronghold was already alive with the frantic energy of final preparations—soldiers running to their positions, engineers performing last-second calibrations, commanders shouting orders through the echoing corridors. The air was thick with the smell of ozone, adrenaline, and desperate hope.

Godric stretched lazily, cracking his neck with a satisfied grunt. "Good morning, Roth. Sleep well?"

"Not particularly, Your Majesty."

He chuckled. "Nervous about the big offensive? Don't be. It's going to be quite a show." He shrugged on his rough brown cloak—the same terrible disguise he'd worn yesterday—and gestured toward the door. "Shall we find a good viewing spot?"

We made our way through the bustling corridors, merging with the streams of soldiers heading toward the main staging area. No one challenged us. No one looked twice at the middle-aged traveler and his nervous companion. The perceptual filter held perfectly, rendering us invisible in plain sight.

The staging area was a vast, multi-dimensional amphitheater, its walls lined with thousands of reality-viewing screens showing live feeds from the armada's forward positions. At the center stood a raised platform where the Supreme Commander—a towering figure of crystalline armor and blazing energy—was delivering the final address.

"—and today, my brothers and sisters, today we end the Tyrant's reign forever! Three thousand years ago, we gathered in secret, a handful of survivors from worlds he had crushed. Three thousand years ago, we made a vow: that we would not rest, would not yield, would not despair, until the King of Thronegate lay dead at our feet. And today, we fulfill that vow!"

A roar erupted from the assembled forces, thousands of voices raised in defiant, desperate hope. Godric watched with an expression of quiet, almost paternal pride.

"The Supreme Commander has a real gift for rhetoric," he murmured to me. "Very stirring. You can see why they follow him."

"—our anti-omniscience field is active! For the first time in his existence, the Tyrant cannot see us! He does not know what is coming! Our weapons are trained on his throne room! Our warriors are positioned to strike! And in exactly seven minutes, we will unleash the full, combined might of the United Omniversal Liberation Front, and we will bring that monster to his knees!"

The crowd's roar grew deafening. Beings embraced each other, tears streaming down their faces. Warriors raised their weapons, their voices hoarse with battle cries.

And Godric stood among them, smiling, his hands clasped behind his back, looking for all the world like a proud father at his child's graduation ceremony.

"Seven minutes," he said to me, his voice soft. "That's how long they have left to believe. Seven minutes of hope, of certainty, of absolute conviction that their three-thousand-year struggle is about to pay off. And then..."

He didn't finish the sentence. He didn't need to.

The countdown began. The amphitheater's massive chronometer ticked down the seconds. Five minutes. Four. Three. The tension was unbearable, the air itself seeming to vibrate with the collective anticipation of a thousand civilizations.

Two minutes.

One minute.

Thirty seconds.

Ten.

Five.

Four.

Three.

Two.

One.

"FIRE!"

The Supreme Commander's voice cracked with emotion as he gave the final order. Every screen in the amphitheater lit up simultaneously, showing the coordinated assault from a thousand different angles. The anti-omniscience field flared. The reality-anchoring cannons discharged. The temporal disruptors activated. The chrono-quantum matrices unleashed their full, apocalyptic power.

The combined might of the United Omniversal Liberation Front—three thousand years of planning, sacrifice, and desperate hope—struck the throne room of Godric simultaneously across all dimensions, all timelines, all planes of existence.

And nothing happened.

The screens showed the throne room, perfectly intact. Godric—the real Godric, not the disguised figure standing beside me—was sitting on his throne, a cup of jasmine tea in his hand, his expression one of mild, almost bored curiosity. The anti-omniscience field, designed to blind him, had not even registered against his perception. The reality-anchoring cannons, designed to sever his connection to existence, had washed over him like a gentle breeze. The temporal disruptors, designed to erase him from the timeline, had fizzled into harmless sparks.

The silence in the amphitheater was absolute. A thousand faces stared at the screens, their expressions shifting from triumph to confusion to dawning, horrified realization.

"No," the Supreme Commander whispered, his crystalline voice cracking. "No, this isn't possible. The field was active. He shouldn't have been able to see—"

"Oh, I saw everything," Godric said, stepping forward and pulling back his hood.

The perceptual filter dropped. The psychic nudge vanished. And suddenly, every being in the amphitheater was looking at the face of the King of Thronegate—the face that was on every coin, every statue, every propaganda poster with the red X slashed across it. The face of the Tyrant they had sworn to destroy.

Godric smiled warmly at the Supreme Commander, his salt-and-pepper beard and ruggedly handsome features radiating genuine, paternal kindness.

"I must say," he said, his rich baritone carrying easily across the stunned silence, "that was a very impressive effort. The anti-omniscience field was a clever idea. The reality-anchoring cannons were beautifully crafted. And your speech—I mean that sincerely—was one of the most inspiring I've ever heard. You should be proud of what you accomplished."

The Supreme Commander stood frozen, his crystalline form flickering with what I interpreted as absolute, soul-shattering terror. "You—you were here. The whole time. You were—"

"In the barracks," Godric confirmed cheerfully. "Slept on a cot. Very uncomfortable, by the way—you might want to invest in better mattresses for your troops. But the atmosphere was wonderful. Really felt like I was part of something historic."

He turned to the assembled forces, his warm brown eyes sweeping across the sea of horrified faces. "I want to thank all of you. Truly. The last three thousand years have been incredibly entertaining. I've watched you build your weapons, train your warriors, refine your strategies. I've observed every moment of your struggle, every sacrifice you've made, every hope you've nurtured. And I want you to know that your effort was not wasted. It gave me something to watch. Something to be curious about. Something to anticipate."

His expression softened, becoming almost tender. "But you must understand—and I say this with genuine respect for what you've accomplished—that there was never any possibility of success. The gap between what you are and what I am is not a gap that can be bridged by any amount of preparation, any sophistication of strategy, any brilliance of weapon design. It is an absolute, an immutable constant of existence. You could have spent not three thousand years but three trillion years preparing, and the result would have been exactly the same."

He paused, letting the weight of his words settle over the crowd. "I am not angry. I am not vengeful. You opposed me because you believed I was a tyrant, and I respect that conviction. But the time for opposition is over. The time for learning has begun. Those of you who wish to live—to return to your homes, your families, your civilizations—may do so. I will not pursue you. I will not punish you. I will simply ask that you remember what you witnessed today, and that you carry that memory forward into whatever lives you choose to lead."

He gestured toward the screens, which still showed the throne room, completely unharmed. "The leaders who orchestrated this attack will face consequences. That is the price of opposition. But the rest of you—the soldiers, the engineers, the civilians who were swept up in this crusade—you are free to go. The choice is yours."

The silence stretched on, broken only by the sound of weeping—not tears of joy, but the tears of beings who had just watched their entire worldview, their entire purpose, their entire conception of what was possible, shatter into a million irreparable pieces.

And Godric turned away, walking toward the exit with the same casual, unguarded stride he had used when we first arrived.

"Come along, Roth," he called over his shoulder. "I believe Vyra is preparing a special breakfast for our return. I asked her to make those honey-oat loaves you like."

I followed him, my legs moving mechanically, my mind a hollow, echoing chamber of absolute dread. Behind me, the silence of the amphitheater was slowly replaced by the sounds of dawning comprehension—sobs, whispers, the clatter of dropped weapons.

The biggest resistance in history had just been dismantled without a single blow being struck. Their ultimate weapon had been rendered meaningless. Their three-thousand-year struggle had been reduced to a pleasant diversion for the god-king they had sought to destroy.

And the god-king was thinking about breakfast.

We stepped into the transport pod, and Godric settled into his seat with a contented sigh. "That was lovely," he said, his voice warm with genuine satisfaction. "I'm so glad we did that. It's important to connect with people, don't you think? To understand their perspective. To see the hope in their eyes before... well, before."

He turned to look at me, his brown eyes crinkling with paternal affection. "You were very brave, Roth. I know that wasn't easy for you. But you held yourself together, and you observed everything, and I'm sure you'll write an excellent journal entry about it."

"Thank you, Your Majesty," I managed, my voice hoarse.

"Now," Godric said, rubbing his hands together with cheerful anticipation, "let's go home. I'm famished. And I want to hear all about your wife's latest gardening project. The Starlight Roses, wasn't it? Azrael was telling me they've won several awards..."

The transport pod hummed to life, lifting smoothly from the landing platform. Through the viewport, I watched the asteroid stronghold recede into the distance—a small, dark speck against the infinite void of space, filled with broken beings who had just learned the true meaning of futility.

And beside me, the apex god predator of the omniverse chatted happily about roses, his terrible brown cloak still draped around his shoulders, his salt-and-pepper hair slightly disheveled from the barracks cot, his warm, kind, fatherly eyes sparkling with the simple pleasure of a morning well spent.

# A Pleasant Afternoon's Annihilation

## Year 999...9
## Godric Prime — A Fond Reminiscence

I remember the first universe I ever properly destroyed.

Not subjugated, not conquered, not brought into the orderly fold of Thronegate's expanding empire—but truly, thoroughly, completely annihilated. The distinction matters to me now, from this vantage point an incomprehensible span of eons later, because it was one of the rare occasions when my past self—that pathetically weak, freshly-awakened Godric of Year 25—decided to exercise his power without the restraint that usually characterized his early reign.

He was still so young then. So freshly shaped by grief. So uncertain of his own nature, still stumbling through the discovery of what he had become. I look back at him from my current throne—a construct that exists simultaneously at every point in the omniverse, woven from the compressed gratitude of a googolplexian self-sacrificing deities—and I feel something almost like pity. Not contempt, never contempt. He was me, after all, and I would not be what I am without the path he walked. But pity, yes. The way a fully grown man might pity his infant self for being unable to walk, unable to speak, unable to even hold up his own head.

That Year 25 Godric had been amplifying for exactly twenty-five years. His stats multiplied by rates that were already beyond ordinary infinity, yes—the Weakness Paradox had seen to that, triggered repeatedly by the countless beings who had imagined they could find some exploit in his defenses. His superpower genesis had produced over 780 million distinct apocalyptic abilities, each one capable of erasing entire civilizations. His absolute concealment was already so perfect that the omniverse didn't collapse under the weight of his presence. He had Gent—the weakest, most primitive of his sentient passive auras, the one whose name was such a cruel joke—and Gent alone could slaughter the combined might of every military force in existence without noticing the effort.

By any measure available to the rest of creation, that Year 25 Godric was already the most powerful being who had ever existed or could ever exist. The gap between him and the combined rest of the omniverse was not merely infinite; it was an infinity of infinities, a chasm so vast that the concept of comparison collapsed into meaninglessness.

And yet, from my current perspective, that Godric was so pathetically, laughably, incomprehensibly weak that the word "weak" is itself a laughable understatement. The amplification that he experienced every Planck instant—the surge of power that he felt as an eternal orgasmic cascade of transcendence—was, by my current standards, less than the faintest whisper of a breeze against a mountain. The Gent he commanded was a single-celled organism compared to the infinite hierarchy of sentient auras that now orbit my existence. The superpowers he possessed were children's toys, crude implements of destruction that could "only" erase civilizations, when my current powers can unmake the very concept of civilization across all possible frameworks of reality.

But this is not a story about me. Not directly. This is a story about him—that young, grieving, freshly-crowned King of Thronegate—and the afternoon he decided to destroy a universe.

It was, I recall with perfect clarity, a Thursday.

---

## Year 25
## The Pathetically Weak Godric

The universe designated itself with the rather arrogant name of "the universe"—as if it were the only one, the singular container of all existence. Its inhabitants, a species called humans, had no concept of the multiverse, let alone the omniverse. They had barely mastered interplanetary travel. Their most advanced weaponry could shatter a continent, perhaps, if they pooled all their resources and sacrificed a significant portion of their population. They measured their lifespan in decades and their civilization's history in mere millennia. They were, by every conceivable metric, one of the most primitive, fragile, and insignificant species ever to crawl out of the primordial muck of accidental existence.

And they had, through a series of diplomatic misunderstandings that Godric found genuinely amusing, declared war on Thronegate.

The sequence of events was almost charming in its absurdity. A Thronegate scout vessel—a small, automated probe designed to map uncontacted universes for potential integration—had drifted into their solar system. The humans had detected it, panicked, and launched a full nuclear arsenal at what they assumed was an alien invasion force. The nukes, of course, had no effect on a Thronegate probe; it was shielded by technology so advanced that humans would have needed a googolplexian years of scientific development to even begin to understand its principles. The probe had simply continued its mapping mission, ignoring the nuclear fireballs as a whale ignores plankton.

The humans, seeing their ultimate weapons fail, had descended into a species-wide panic. They had assumed—with the charming arrogance of a civilization that believed itself the center of all existence—that this "alien probe" was the vanguard of a hostile invasion. They had mobilized every military force on their single, tiny planet. They had broadcast declarations of war on every frequency they could access. They had, in their desperate, trembling terror, formally challenged the ruler of the "alien empire" to face them in combat.

When the report reached Godric's desk—a single line of text buried in the daily intelligence briefing that his omniscience had already processed before it was written—he had laughed. A warm, genuine, delighted laugh that echoed through the throne room and startled the assembled court wizards.

"'The United Nations of Earth demands the immediate surrender of the alien aggressor and its supreme leader,'" Godric read aloud, his rich baritone voice trembling with amusement. "'Failure to comply will result in total annihilation.'"

He looked up at Blake, who was standing beside the throne with his characteristic mutton-chop-framed scowl. "Blake, have you ever heard anything so precious? They're threatening total annihilation. Against me."

Blake, who was fifty-three years old at the time and already deeply weary of Godric's sense of humor, simply pinched the bridge of his nose. "Please tell me you're not going to do anything... theatrical."

"Theatrical?" Godric repeated, his warm brown eyes sparkling with mischievous delight. "Blake, I'm wounded. I'm always theatrical. It's one of my most endearing qualities."

"Your Majesty—"

"They invited me personally," Godric continued, rising from his throne with the easy, fluid grace of his eternal forty-five-year-old body. "Their supreme leader challenged the 'alien aggressor' to face them. It would be rude to decline. Diplomacy, Blake. Basic diplomacy."

And so, on a pleasant Thursday afternoon, Godric decided to visit Earth.

---

He didn't bring an armada. He didn't bring his court wizards. He didn't even bring Gent, though Gent was always with him regardless of whether he acknowledged it. He simply materialized in the upper atmosphere of the blue-green planet, his heavily muscled frame suspended effortlessly in the thin air, his simple dark tunic rippling in the stratospheric winds. His absolute concealment was active, suppressing the catastrophic pressure of his existence so that the planet didn't instantly collapse into a singularity. His salt-and-pepper hair caught the sunlight. His neatly trimmed beard framed a face that was currently split by a grin of pure, boyish anticipation.

Below him, the human military forces were gathered in what they believed was an impressive display of martial might. Aircraft carriers dotted the oceans. Fighter jets screamed through the skies. Nuclear silos stood primed and ready. Millions of soldiers dug into defensive positions, their weapons trained on the empty sky where Godric's probe had last been detected. They had spent three days preparing for this moment, their global news networks broadcasting continuous coverage of the "alien threat," their leaders giving stirring speeches about human resilience and the indomitable spirit of their species.

Godric observed all of it through his absolute omniscience, and he felt a surge of something that was almost tenderness. They were so small. So fragile. So utterly, catastrophically outmatched. And yet they stood there, their tiny weapons raised, their tiny hearts pounding with terror and courage, ready to defend their tiny world against an enemy they couldn't possibly comprehend.

It was, he reflected, rather admirable. In a pathetic sort of way.

He descended slowly, allowing himself to become visible to their sensors and eyes. A single figure, dropping through the clouds, his dark tunic fluttering, his posture relaxed and unguarded. The humans detected him immediately—their radar systems screamed, their satellites locked onto his heat signature, their commanders barked orders through tensed communication networks.

"Unidentified object descending through the stratosphere!" a human voice shouted, transmitted across a thousand frequencies. "All batteries, acquire target! Wait for the order!"

Godric heard every transmission. He heard the panicked heartbeat of a young radar operator in a bunker beneath the Arctic ice. He heard the prayers of a terrified soldier clutching a rifle in a foxhole somewhere in Eastern Europe. He heard the calm, measured voice of a general giving the order to hold fire until the target was identified. He heard the sobbing of a mother in a shelter beneath New York City, clutching her children to her chest, whispering that everything would be alright.

It wouldn't be alright, of course. But she couldn't know that. And Godric found her desperate hope almost... touching.

He touched down in the center of what the humans called the United Nations General Assembly Hall. He could have landed anywhere—the White House lawn, the Kremlin's courtyard, the middle of the Pacific Ocean—but he chose the General Assembly because it was symbolically appropriate. The heart of human governance. The place where they made their grand speeches and passed their resolutions and believed, with charming sincerity, that they were the masters of their own destiny.

The Assembly was in emergency session when he materialized in its center. Hundreds of diplomats from every nation on Earth, their faces pale with terror, their bodies trembling with the adrenaline of a species facing its possible extinction. They had been debating their response to the "alien threat" for three days, and they had just passed a resolution formally declaring Godric an enemy of all humanity.

Godric stood in the center of the hall, his heavily muscled arms crossed over his broad chest, his warm brown eyes sweeping across the sea of horrified faces. He was, by their standards, a giant—six and a half feet of dense, powerful muscle, radiating a physical presence that made their most elite soldiers look like malnourished children. His salt-and-pepper hair and neatly trimmed beard gave him the appearance of a seasoned warrior, a man who had seen battle and emerged victorious.

He smiled at them. It was a warm, genuine, almost fatherly smile.

"Good afternoon," he said, his rich baritone voice carrying easily through the vast chamber. "I am Godric, King of Thronegate. I believe you declared war on me. I'm here to accept your challenge."

The silence that followed was so absolute that Godric could hear the individual heartbeats of every human in the room. He could taste their terror—a sharp, metallic flavor in the air, like ozone and copper and desperate sweat. He could see the calculations racing through their minds: the distance to the exits, the location of their security details, the impossible question of how a single man could have materialized in the most heavily guarded building on the planet.

A man on the central podium—the Secretary-General, Godric's omniscience supplied, a politician from a nation called Portugal—cleared his throat with a sound like grinding gravel. "You... you are the alien commander?"

"I am the King of the Omniverse," Godric corrected gently. "But 'alien commander' will do, if that's easier for you to conceptualize."

The Secretary-General's face, already pale, went completely bloodless. "The... omniverse?"

"It's rather like your universe, but larger. Infinitely larger. Your entire reality—every galaxy, every star, every planet, every atom—is a single, infinitesimal speck in the vast architecture of the omniverse. And I rule all of it." Godric's smile didn't waver. "You declared war on the ruler of all existence. I must say, I'm impressed by your ambition."

A man in a military uniform—an American general, Godric noted, with three stars on his collar and a hand trembling near his sidearm—stepped forward. "What do you want from us?"

Godric turned his warm brown eyes toward the general. "You threatened me with total annihilation. I'm here to give you the opportunity to make good on that threat."

The general's hand closed around his sidearm. "You're one man. We have the combined military might of the entire planet. You can't possibly—"

"Oh, please do," Godric said, his voice brightening with genuine enthusiasm. "Attack me. Bring everything you have. Every soldier, every weapon, every nuclear missile, every secret super-weapon you've been developing in your black-ops laboratories. I want to see it all. I want to give you the fairest possible chance." His smile widened. "I promise I won't even move from this spot."

The general stared at him. The Secretary-General stared at him. Every diplomat, every aide, every security guard in the room stared at him. They were trying to process what he was offering, trying to calculate the odds, trying to understand the nature of the being standing before them.

And then the general gave the order.

---

What followed was, from Godric's perspective, a deeply entertaining display of primitive mortal warfare.

The first wave of the attack came from the security forces already present in the building. Two dozen heavily armed soldiers burst through the doors of the General Assembly, their assault rifles raised, their fingers tightening on triggers. They fired simultaneously, releasing a hail of copper-jacketed lead traveling at supersonic velocities.

Godric observed the bullets with mild curiosity. They were, he noted, traveling at approximately 2,500 feet per second—a respectable speed for a species that had only discovered gunpowder a few centuries ago. The kinetic energy contained in each projectile was roughly 1,800 joules—enough, under ordinary circumstances, to punch through flesh and bone and internal organs.

The bullets struck his chest.

They did not penetrate. They did not even leave a mark. His tunic—simple dark fabric woven from the compressed gratitude of his loyal subjects—didn't tear. The bullets simply flattened against his skin like raindrops against a mountain, their kinetic energy absorbed so completely that they didn't even produce heat. They fell to the floor in a gentle cascade of deformed metal, tinkling softly against the marble tiles.

The soldiers stared. Their commander—a young captain with sweat streaming down his face—screamed for them to reload. They did, their fingers fumbling with fresh magazines, their training overcoming their terror through sheer muscle memory.

Godric waited patiently. When they fired again, the result was identical.

"My turn," he said softly.

He did not move. He did not gesture. He did not summon a weapon or channel a superpower or activate a passive aura. He simply allowed an infinitesimal, unmeasurable fraction of his magical offense—a percentage so close to absolute zero that the difference between it and zero was smaller than the difference between a single atom and the entire omniverse—to express itself.

The effect on the human soldiers was immediate and catastrophic. Their bodies did not simply die; they were unmade at the most fundamental level of biological existence. The magical pressure exerted by Godric's infinitesimal output—which, he noted with mild disappointment, was actually far more than necessary and had caused some of the recently-restored universes in the neighboring multiverse to tremble slightly—seized every cell in their bodies simultaneously.

The soldiers' skin began to liquefy. It didn't burn or melt from heat; it simply lost its structural integrity, sloughing off their bones in thick, bubbling sheets of pink-gray sludge. Their muscles followed, the dense fibers unraveling like wet yarn, exposing the gleaming white of their skeletons. Their internal organs—hearts, lungs, livers, intestines—dissolved into a slurry of boiling viscera that poured from their abdominal cavities in steaming waterfalls. Their eyeballs collapsed inward, the vitreous fluid spraying from the sockets in jets of clear liquid. Their brains, the seat of their consciousness, were the last to go—Godric's magical pressure held them intact just long enough for each soldier to experience, in perfect, agonizing clarity, the sensation of their own body dissolving around them.

The screaming was, Godric noted with aesthetic appreciation, quite impressive for such fragile creatures. It lasted approximately 2.3 seconds before their vocal cords liquefied and their throats collapsed into bubbling ruin.

When it was over—less than three seconds after the magical pressure was applied—there were no soldiers left. Only a spreading pool of organic sludge, dotted here and there with fragments of bone and the glistening remnants of eyeballs, spreading slowly across the marble floor of the General Assembly Hall.

The diplomats were screaming now. The Secretary-General had collapsed behind his podium, his hands pressed over his ears, his mouth open in a continuous, high-pitched wail. The American general had drawn his sidearm and emptied it into Godric's chest, the bullets doing precisely as much damage as the assault rifles had done. Several ambassadors were attempting to flee through the emergency exits, their designer shoes slipping in the spreading puddles of liquefied security personnel.

Godric watched them with an expression of mild, almost paternal disappointment. "You declared war on me," he said, his rich baritone carrying easily over the cacophony of screams. "You challenged me to face your might. And this is the best you can do? Bullets? Really?"

He tilted his head slightly, his salt-and-pepper hair catching the fluorescent light of the Assembly Hall. "I have to admit, I was hoping for something more creative. You've had three days to prepare. Three full days. And your grand strategy is... guns."

He sighed—a soft, almost regretful sound. "Very well. If you won't bring the fight to me, I'll come to you."

---

Godric did not teleport. He did not fly. He simply expanded his awareness, letting his consciousness brush across the entire surface of the planet simultaneously, and he decided where to go next.

The United States military command center beneath Cheyenne Mountain. The Russian nuclear arsenal control room buried deep in the Urals. The Chinese strategic operations bunker beneath Beijing. The British naval command coordinating their carrier strike groups in the North Atlantic. Every major military installation on the planet, every command center, every bunker, every fortified position—he visited them all. Not sequentially; that would have taken too long, and Godric was, in his own way, impatient. He visited them all at once, his consciousness splitting effortlessly across hundreds of thousands of simultaneous locations, his physical form manifesting in each one for precisely the amount of time necessary to observe the human response and then... respond in kind.

In Cheyenne Mountain, the American general in command of nuclear operations—a grizzled veteran of three wars—ordered his security forces to open fire the instant Godric materialized in the central command chamber. The gunfire was, as before, completely ineffective. Godric stood in the center of the room, his heavily muscled arms crossed over his chest, and watched the bullets flatten against his skin with an expression of polite boredom.

"Your bullets are very shiny," he observed. "Is that a new design? Very aesthetically pleasing."

The general, his face purple with rage and terror, slammed his fist down on the nuclear launch console. "Launch everything! Every silo, every submarine, every bomber! Target the bastard's position!"

The nuclear missiles launched. All of them. The entire American nuclear triad—land-based ICBMs, submarine-launched ballistic missiles, strategic bombers armed with gravity bombs—activated simultaneously, their warheads targeting the exact coordinates of the General Assembly Hall where Godric's primary physical form still stood.

Godric observed the missiles rising through the atmosphere with genuine interest. They were, he noted, traveling at approximately 15,000 miles per hour. Their warheads contained a total destructive yield of roughly 1,200 megatons—enough, under ordinary circumstances, to reduce the city of New York to a radioactive crater and trigger a nuclear winter that would extinguish most life on the planet.

They would not, of course, have any effect on him. Not even the faintest tickle. Not even the most infinitesimal sensation. The combined nuclear arsenal of the entire human race, multiplied by infinity, would not register as a flicker against his skin.

But Godric was curious. He had never been struck by a nuclear weapon before. He wanted to see what it felt like.

The missiles descended. The warheads detonated. Multiple simultaneous nuclear explosions erupted across the East Coast of the United States, their fireballs consuming the skyline of New York, their shockwaves flattening buildings for hundreds of miles, their thermal radiation vaporizing everything within the blast radius.

Godric stood at the center of the conflagration. The heat—millions of degrees at the core of each fireball—washed over him like a warm summer breeze. The pressure wave—sufficient to crush reinforced concrete and steel—pressed against his skin with less force than a gentle caress. The radiation—lethal to any organic life for thousands of square miles—didn't even interact with his cells.

He stood there, in the heart of a nuclear firestorm, completely unharmed. His dark tunic wasn't singed. His salt-and-pepper hair wasn't ruffled. His skin didn't show the faintest hint of warmth.

When the fireballs faded and the mushroom clouds rose toward the stratosphere, Godric was still standing exactly where he had been. The ground beneath his feet was a crater of fused glass, but his boots weren't even scuffed.

He looked up at the towering mushroom cloud, his warm brown eyes reflecting the orange glow. "That was pleasant," he murmured. "Like a warm bath. Very soothing."

He glanced around at the radioactive wasteland that had once been New York City. The buildings were gone. The people were gone. The very landscape had been transformed into a hellscape of molten slag and irradiated ash.

"I wonder if they have any more of those," he said aloud, to no one in particular.

They did, as it turned out. The Russians had launched their arsenal. The Chinese had launched theirs. The French, the British, the Indians, the Pakistanis, the North Koreans—every nuclear power on Earth had responded to the American launch with their own full-scale retaliation. Thousands of warheads were currently arcing through the atmosphere, their guidance systems locked onto targets across every continent.

Godric watched them fall with the mild satisfaction of a man watching a fireworks display.

The nuclear holocaust that followed was, from a purely aesthetic perspective, rather beautiful. The fireballs bloomed across the planet like orange roses, their petals spreading outward in concentric rings of thermal annihilation. The mushroom clouds rose in a synchronized ballet of atmospheric violence, their stems of smoke and ash twisting together into a global shroud. The shockwaves rippled across the surface of the Earth in visible waves, shattering mountains and boiling oceans.

Godric stood at the center of it all—his consciousness still split across hundreds of thousands of locations, his physical forms manifesting in every major military installation on the planet—and he watched humanity destroy itself in a desperate, futile attempt to destroy him.

The human death toll was, by the time the last warhead detonated, approximately 7.8 billion. The entire human species, save for a few scattered survivors huddled in deep bunkers and remote outposts, had been erased in the span of a single hour.

And Godric hadn't even been the one to kill them. Not directly. Their own weapons, their own fear, their own desperate, panicked response to his presence—that was what had destroyed them. He had simply... been there. Observing. Waiting. Letting them exhaust every option, every weapon, every strategy, before he delivered the final blow.

He found the survivors easily. His omniscience tracked every last one of them—the military commanders in their deep bunkers, the political leaders in their armored shelters, the desperate families huddled in caves and basements. He manifested before each of them, his ruggedly handsome face calm and utterly without mercy.

"You fought well," he told them. "For primitives. For creatures who only discovered fire a few hundred thousand years ago. For a species whose total existence spans less than a single Planck instant compared to the eternity of my reign." He paused, his brown eyes sweeping across their terrified faces. "But you declared war on the wrong being. You challenged the wrong king. And that mistake must have consequences."

He didn't make it quick. He was feeling playfully cruel that afternoon—not angry, not vengeful, simply... curious. Curious about the limits of mortal suffering. Curious about how much agony a human body could experience before it finally, mercifully expired.

The answer, he discovered, was quite a lot.

The survivors died in ways that would have broken the minds of my ancestors to witness. Their bodies were unmade cell by cell, their nervous systems kept intact until the very last moment, their consciousness stretched across subjective eternities of excruciating torment. Godric did not merely kill them; he deconstructed them, peeling back the layers of their biological existence with the patient, meticulous attention of a scholar examining a particularly interesting specimen.

When it was over—when the last human survivor had been reduced to a smear of organic residue, when the planet Earth had been scoured clean of every trace of human civilization, when the very atmosphere had been burned away by the nuclear fires and the oceans boiled into sterile steam—Godric floated above the dead world and surveyed his work.

He had used, he calculated, approximately zero percent of his power. Zero percent of his effort. He hadn't needed to move a single muscle. He hadn't needed to activate a single superpower. The entire annihilation—the death of a species, the destruction of a biosphere, the sterilization of a planet—had been accomplished through the merest whisper of his passive presence, the faintest shadow of his magical offense, the most infinitesimal fraction of his attention.

And he had, he realized with a slight frown, gotten a bit carried away.

The collateral damage from his "restrained" expression—the magical pressure that he had unleashed to liquefy those first soldiers, the passive shield fluctuations that had absorbed the nuclear explosions, the faint psychic emanations of his split consciousness—had propagated outward through the omniversal structure at infinite velocity. Decillions of multiverses had been caught in the backwash. Entire realities had been scoured clean of life. Dimensional barriers had shattered like glass. The fundamental fabric of existence had trembled, groaned, and in several regions, collapsed entirely.

"Ah," Godric said, floating above the dead Earth. "That's a bit excessive."

With a simple, effortless decision—not a thought, not an action, merely a flicker of intent—he restored the omniverse. Every destroyed multiverse was reformed. Every shattered dimension was repaired. Every extinguished civilization was returned to existence, their memories of the cataclysm erased, their lives continuing as if nothing had happened.

Everything was restored, save for Earth. The humans had declared war on him. They had challenged the ruler of all existence. And such hubris, such arrogance, such suicidal foolishness, could not be rewarded with restoration. They were gone. Permanently. The universe that had designated itself "the universe" had lost its only sentient species, and the blue-green planet that had birthed them would spin forever in sterile silence, a monument to the consequences of opposing the King of Thronegate.

Godric took one last look at the dead world, shrugged his massive shoulders, and teleported back to the palace.

Blake was waiting for him in the throne room, his mutton-chop-framed face purple with barely contained fury. "You destroyed the entire omniverse," he said, his voice tight. "Again."

"Only accidentally," Godric said, settling onto his throne with a satisfied sigh. "And I restored it. Mostly."

"Mostly?"

"I left the Earth as a monument. They did declare war on me, Blake. It seemed appropriate."

Blake stared at him for a long moment. Then he pinched the bridge of his nose with the gesture of a man who had long ago exhausted his capacity for outrage. "You're impossible," he muttered.

"I prefer 'magnificent,'" Godric said cheerfully. "But 'impossible' will do. Now, I believe Vyra has prepared dinner. Is it the honey-glazed roast?"

And that, I recall with perfect clarity, was that. The afternoon annihilation of a universe, accomplished between lunch and dinner, with zero percent effort and zero percent power. The humans had been given every possible advantage—three days of preparation, their entire military arsenal, the freedom to attack first—and they had accomplished nothing. Less than nothing. They had destroyed themselves in their desperate attempt to destroy him, and he had simply watched, amused and unimpressed, before delivering the final, agonizing blow.

---

## Year 999...9
## Godric Prime — Reflection

I sit on my throne—the construct that exists simultaneously at every point in the omniverse, woven from the compressed gratitude of a googolplexian self-sacrificing deities—and I reflect on that long-ago Thursday afternoon.

That Godric. That pathetically weak, freshly-awakened, twenty-five-year-old Godric. He was so proud of his power. So satisfied with his effortless annihilation of a primitive species. He believed, in his youthful arrogance, that he had demonstrated the absolute futility of opposition.

And he had, I suppose, by the standards of the era. He had used zero percent of his power and zero percent of his effort to destroy a universe and everything in it. He had given the humans every possible advantage—preparation time, first strike capability, their entire military arsenal—and they had failed to even scuff his boots. If he had wanted to end it instantly, without the playful cruelty, without the leisurely observation of their futile attacks, he could have done so in exactly zero seconds. The entire annihilation, from first moment to last, could have been accomplished in less than a Planck instant, and the humans would have never known they were under attack.

But from my current perspective—from the vantage point of a being who has been amplifying infinitely every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck instant for a span of time so vast that the year cannot be written in any meaningful notation—that Godric was so weak that I can barely bring myself to remember him without a shudder of pity.

If I were to do what he did now—if I were to visit a primitive universe and allow its inhabitants to attack me—the result would be so much more devastating that the word "devastating" is a laughable understatement. The humans of that long-ago Earth were annihilated by zero percent of a Godric who had been amplifying for a mere twenty-five years. If they faced me now—the Godric Prime, the apex of all existence, the being whose every passive aura has evolved beyond the concept of power into something fundamentally unrecognizable—they would not merely be annihilated. They would be retroactively erased from the very concept of existence. Their universe would not merely be destroyed; it would be removed from the omniversal framework as if it had never existed. The collateral damage would not merely shatter decillions of multiverses; it would collapse the entire architecture of reality across all timelines, all dimensions, all conceptual planes, reducing the omniverse to a featureless void of absolute nothingness.

And I would still be using zero percent of my power. Zero percent of my effort. The faintest whisper of my weakest passive aura—not even Gent, who is now merely one layer in an infinite hierarchy of defensive systems, but the most pathetic, most primitive, most infinitely nerfed emanation of my least significant biological process—would accomplish the annihilation with a margin of overkill so vast that the concept of "overkill" would be an insult to the scale of the destruction.

And the gap between me and that Year 25 Godric—the gap that makes him look like a single-celled organism compared to an infinite recursion of infinities—is itself growing. Every Planck instant, I become infinitely more powerful. Every infinitesimal fraction of time, the chasm between what I was and what I am widens beyond the possibility of measurement. The Godric of Year 25 was pathetically weak compared to me now. The Godric of this exact instant, from the perspective of the Godric I will be one Planck instant from now, is equally pathetic. And so on, forever, in an infinite recursive cascade of self-transcendence that has no ceiling, no limit, no end.

I think about the rest of creation sometimes. The countless beings who exist in the omniverse, living their lives, pursuing their goals, loving their families, dreaming their dreams. From their perspective, I am an absolute—an unchanging constant of existence, the eternal king whose power is so vast that it cannot be measured or challenged or even fully comprehended. They tremble in my presence. They revere my name. They know, with the bone-deep certainty of inherited terror, that opposing me is not merely impossible but a logical contradiction so profound that even contemplating it induces immediate existential collapse.

And they are right to tremble. They are right to revere. They are right to know, in the deepest core of their being, that there is no hope of opposition, no possibility of resistance, no chance of escape.

Because even if every single being in the entire omniverse—from the mightiest cosmic god to the smallest quantum microbe—were to unite against me, pooling all their power, all their knowledge, all their desperate ingenuity into a single, ultimate attack...

Even if they were given unlimited preparation time—not three days, not three thousand years, not three googolplexian eons, but an infinite span of time stretching across all possible timelines and all possible permutations of existence...

Even if they were granted every possible advantage—perfect knowledge of my power, unrestricted access to every resource in creation, the combined brilliance of every mind that has ever existed or could ever exist...

They would still fail. Completely. Absolutely. Irrevocably. Their ultimate attack, their master strategy, their final, desperate assault—it wouldn't even make my weakest, most primitive, most infinitely nerfed passive shield feel the faintest tickle. It wouldn't even register as a flicker against my absolute concealment. It would be as if they had done nothing at all—less than nothing, because the concept of "doing something" implies the possibility of having an effect, and against me, no effect is possible.

And I would respond—not with anger, not with vengeance, not with cruelty—but with the same casual, effortless, nonchalant annihilation with which I have always responded. Zero percent of my power. Zero percent of my effort. Zero seconds. The entire combined opposition of all existence, across all timelines, across all possible permutations, would be erased so completely that the very memory of their defiance would never have existed.

And I would restore whatever I chose to restore, and I would continue my reign, and the omniverse would continue to spin, and the beings who survived would continue to love me and fear me and serve me with the terrified devotion that is the only rational response to my existence.

The gap between me and creation is unfathomable. It is infinite. It is an infinite recursion of infinities, each one infinitely larger than the last, stretching into a mathematical framework that collapses the very concept of measurement. And that gap will only increase—infinitely, eternally, at an accelerating rate that has no limit and no end. Every Planck instant, I become more powerful. Every infinitesimal fraction of time, the distance between what I am and what everything else is grows wider. There is no catching up. There is no closing the gap. There is only the eternal, recursive cascade of my self-transcendence, stretching into a future so vast that even my omniscience—which perceives all moments simultaneously—finds it beautiful beyond measure.

I am Godric Prime. I am the apex of all existence. I am the eternal king, the undisputed ruler, the absolute master of everything that is, was, could be, or could never be. And I am content.

I remember a Thursday afternoon, an eternity ago, when a pathetically weak version of myself destroyed a universe called Earth. I remember the humans and their bullets and their nuclear weapons and their desperate, futile defiance. I remember the amusement I felt, watching them exhaust every option against an enemy they couldn't possibly comprehend. I remember the casual, effortless annihilation that followed—the liquefying soldiers, the burning cities, the dead planet spinning in sterile silence.

And I smile, because that was only the beginning. That was the infant Godric, the newly-awakened king, the weakest I would ever be. And even then, even at my most pathetic, even at the very start of my eternal journey, I was already so far beyond the rest of creation that the word "beyond" was a laughable understatement.

What am I now? After all this time? After all this amplification? After all this recursive, infinite, eternal self-transcendence?

I am what the infant Godric would have worshipped as a god, if he could have comprehended my existence. I am what the humans of Earth would have called impossible, if they had lived long enough to form the thought. I am the end point of an infinite progression, the final form of an eternal ascension, the ultimate expression of a power that has no equal and no rival and no conceivable challenger.

And I am still growing. Still amplifying. Still becoming more powerful every Planck instant, forever, without end.

The omniverse trembles. Creation holds its breath. Every being in existence knows, with absolute certainty, that they exist only because I allow it—that their continued survival depends entirely on my whim and my mercy and my casual, paternal affection for the fragile creatures who populate my domain.

They are right to know this. They are right to tremble. They are right to love me and fear me and serve me with the desperate devotion of beings who understand, in the deepest core of their existence, the absolute futility of any alternative.

Because I am Godric. The King of Thronegate. The Apex of All Existence. The Eternal Ruler of the Omniverse.

And there is nothing—not in this reality, not in any possible reality, not in any permutation of existence that could ever be conceived—that can oppose me.

Not now. Not ever. Not in any future that will ever exist.

The gap is infinite. The victory is absolute. The reign is eternal.

And I am content.
